Tech Report: Defamation Counterclaim Arising out Reagan National Helicopter Crash Case Can Go Forward

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1410 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wallace, decided today by Chief Magistrate Judge Scott Varholak (D.
  • On January 29, 2025, a Black Hawk Helicopter and American Airlines Flight 5342 collided mid-air near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport.
  • Defendant made his first X post addressing the rumor on January 31, 2025, at 1:00 a.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[A.] From Ellis v. Wallace, decided today by Chief Magistrate Judge Scott Varholak (D. Colo.):.

On January 29, 2025, a Black Hawk Helicopter and American Airlines Flight 5342 collided mid-air near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport. Hours after the crash, several posts and articles appeared claiming Plaintiff was the helicopter pilot in the midair collision ("the rumor"), including:.

Defendant made his first X post addressing the rumor on January 31, 2025, at 1:00 a.m. Eastern Time. And Plaintiff filed the Complaint in this matter on April 9, 2025, alleging that Defendant's posts were defamatory. Plaintiff then proceeded to appear as a guest on several podcasts. On July 18, 2025, she was interviewed on the Kill Tony podcast. During the interview, the hosts asked Plaintiff about the collision rumor and her pending litigation. Plaintiff explained that Defendant was the "[f]irst one to tie my likeness to the rumor. We don't know if he started the rumor, but he had millions of followers. He did the most what we can determine as damage.".

Industry observers note that ten days later, Defendant filed the Special Motion to Dismiss Plaintiff's Complaint, attaching copies of X posts and articles linking Plaintiff to the crash hours before Defendant commented on the rumor. Plaintiff then appeared on a second podcast, the RVA Magazine podcast, on September 30, 2025. Plaintiff was again asked about the rumor and her pending litigation. In response, she stated:.

[W]ithin 24 hours of the crash, I was finding out that I was being named as as the pilot as, like, the unnamed female pilot that was the supposed DEI hire that Trump, President Trump had alluded to at a press conference that "we know it's DEI because we just know." And so that kind of sent the online world into a frenzy of like, let's figure out who this pilot is. And, from what we can tell, [Defendant] picked up on that and used a picture of me and the [Michael] Smerconish article and, um, kind of put it all together. And with his following, he had, I think, two and half million followers or something like that, we believe he did the most damage. Like it would not have had the legs it had if he hadn't posted about it.

According to recent reports, finally, on January 12, 2026, Kim Congdon interviewed Plaintiff on The Kim Congdon Takeover podcast. Congdon asked Plaintiff if she was suing the individual that started the rumor. Plaintiff responded:.

I don't, yeah, I don't know if he started it, but he definitely, like, he pushed it. He's the first one to tie my likeness to it. Yeah. His name's Matt Wallace and, uh, he, uh, millions of followers on Twitter, and he pushed it pretty hard and we believe he did the most damage and so I'm suing him in federal court.".

On April 6, 2026, Defendant filed the Counterclaim alleging that these podcast statements were defamatory.

Recent findings suggest that defendant alleges that Plaintiff made repeated defamatory statements that: (1) Defendant "was the first one to post [Plaintiff's] likeness in connection with the helicopter crash," and (2) that Plaintiff believes Defendant's "statements caused the most damage." {Plaintiff alleges that there is a material difference between claiming that Defendant was the first to name Plaintiff in relation to the tragedy, and that Defendant was the first one to post Plaintiff's likeness in connection with the collision. The distinction is unclear to the Court. Accordingly, the Court assesses Plaintiff's "likeness" statements as conveying Defendant was the first to connect Plaintiff to the collision.}.

[B.] The court rejected Plaintiff's arguments that Plaintiff's statements were protected by the "litigation privilege." That privilege bars defamation lawsuits based on statements in court filings and in-court statements, but doesn't apply to statements about the lawsuit made outside the litigation.

(Recall that, though in a typical case it would be a defendant who's arguing the statements were privileged, opinion, true, etc., and plaintiff would be responding, here the roles are flipped because the defendant is counterclaiming against plaintiff based on plaintiff's statements.).

[C.] The court also rejected Plaintiff's arguments that the statements were nonactionable opinion: It concluded that both statements were "susceptible of being proved true or false," and were framed as factual assertions rather than using "loose or hyperbolic language that provided the impression that her statements should not be taken seriously.".

[D.] The court concluded that Defendant had introduced sufficient evidence that the statements were false:.

First, with respect to Plaintiff's "likeness" statements, Plaintiff repeatedly claimed that Defendant was "the first one to tie [her] likeness to the rumor." However, Defendant provided several pieces of evidence showing that other X users linked Plaintiff to the rumor before Defendant….

Second, Defendant has shown a reasonable likelihood of proving by clear and convincing evidence that Plaintiff's "most damage" statements were false. Defendant declares that "the rumor was spread primarily by much larger voices than [Defendant's,] such as Ann Coulter's, Alex Jones's, and others." He claims that these "prominent individuals and entities" had a "far greater reach than anything [he] posted" about Plaintiff. If true, this declaration could provide clear and convincing evidence that Defendant's "most damage" statements were false. At the very least, it creates a question for the jury since Plaintiff has offered competing evidence. ….

[E.] The court also concluded that Defendant had introduced sufficient evidence that Plaintiff knew the "likeness"/"first one to tie" statements were probably false (which is required by Colorado law in such cases):.

First, Plaintiff's statements on the RVA Magazine podcast and The Kim Congdon Takeover podcast occurred after Defendant filed his Special Motion to Dismiss and Plaintiff filed her response. In his Special Motion to Dismiss, Defendant included evidence of other X users linking Plaintiff to the rumor before Defendant's first post. And Plaintiff's podcast statements referred to the ongoing litigation. Thus, it is plausible to infer that Plaintiff had a high degree of awareness of the probable falsity of her statements.

Second, Plaintiff's statements reveal inconsistencies in her account of the underlying events. During her interview on the Kill Tony podcast and The Kim Congdon Takeover podcast, Plaintiff repeatedly stated that she did not know whether Defendant started the rumor despite claiming he was "the first one to tie [her] likeness to it." Plaintiff repeated these conflicting statements in her declaration. was the first to blame [her] for this horrific crash because [she] clearly knew that information was incorrect.")] Consequently, such inconsistencies weigh in favor of finding that Defendant has shown a reasonable likelihood of proving actual malice by clear and convincing evidence….

But the court concluded there wasn't enough evidence of knowing or reckless falsehood as to the "most damage" statement:.

Defendant declares that at the time Plaintiff made her public statements, she knew "prominent individuals and entities" had discussed her connection with the crash and that those individuals had a "far greater reach than anything [Defendant] posted." However, such evidence does not support an inference that Plaintiff entertained serious doubts as to the truth of the statements or was highly aware of their probable falsity. Further, Defendant provides no other evidence to support his actual malice claim here.

In a recent development, on the other hand, the mere fact that the actor stated that the podcaster did the most harm—even knowing the New York Times had a broader audience—does not necessarily equate to actual malice; the actor could easily believe (even if wrongfully) that the podcaster caused the most harm because the podcaster gave credibility to the false rumor and thus led others to run with the story. Here, Defendant has only presented evidence that those with broader audiences likewise posted the false story. But, as the hypothetical shows, this does not necessarily mean that Plaintiff's statement that Defendant caused the most damage was made with actual malice.}.

[F.] Finally, the court concludes that Defendant had sufficiently alleged damages, as required by Colorado law:.

Specifically, he alleged that Plaintiff's statements have caused: (1) "significant stress and strain in [his] family relations," and (2) stress from his alleged tarnished reputation. Although Plaintiff claims that that Defendant asserted these damages "in conclusory fashion," the Court finds the presented evidence sufficient to satisfy Defendant's burden at this stage.

The court thus denies Plaintiff's motion to dismiss as to the "likeness"/"first one to tie" statements, which means Defendant's counterclaim can go forward (though of course it doesn't mean the Defendant's counterclaim will ultimately prevail).

    #8419. Our Amicus Brief in the First Circuit $100,000 H-1B Visa Fee Case

    📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (647 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    Our Amicus Brief in the First Circuit $100,000 H-1B Visa Fee Case

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (647 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • On Thursday, the Cato Institute and I filed an amicus brief in the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, in support of California and other states challenging the Trump Administration's imposition of a $100,000 fee on applications for H-1B visas (which are used by tech firms, research institutions, and other organizations to hire immigrant workers and researchers with various specialized skills).
    • The district court ruling in this case invalidated the $100,000 fee on the grounds that the executive had illegally usurped Congress' power to impose taxes.
    • We are very grateful to Deno Hemonas and Philip Wilkinson of Wilson Sonsini Goodrich Rosati, who worked with me on the brief, pro bono.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On Thursday, the Cato Institute and I filed an amicus brief in the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, in support of California and other states challenging the Trump Administration's imposition of a $100,000 fee on applications for H-1B visas (which are used by tech firms, research institutions, and other organizations to hire immigrant workers and researchers with various specialized skills).

    The district court ruling in this case invalidated the $100,000 fee on the grounds that the executive had illegally usurped Congress' power to impose taxes. It relied heavily on the Supreme Court's recent decision in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, the tariff case I helped litigate. A second federal district court later invalidated the fee on other grounds.

    We are very grateful to Deno Hemonas and Philip Wilkinson of Wilson Sonsini Goodrich Rosati, who worked with me on the brief, pro bono. Stanford Law School Prof. and former federal judge Michael McConnell, also worked with us on the brief. He is one of the nation's leading experts on executive power, a prominent conservative originalist constitutional law scholar, and was our lead counsel in the Supreme Court phase of the IEEPA tariff case.

    Here is a summary of our arguments:.

    As the Supreme Court emphasized in its recent decisions striking down Donald Trump's Massive IEEPA tariffs, "the Framers gave Congress alone access to the pockets of the people." Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, 607 U.S. 229, 241 (2026)  The tax power was, as Alexander Hamilton explained, "the most vital of the authorities proposed to be conferred upon the Union." Just months ago, the Supreme Court in Learning Resources applied those fundamental principles to hold that the President may not use a general grant of authority to "regulate … importation" to impose tariffs, because the power to "regulate" is not the power to tax and Congress did not clearly delegate its taxing power. This case asks whether the same President—by imposing a tax of his own devising on the entry of noncitizens and calling it a "restriction" on entry—may accomplish by a different label what Learning Resources forbade.

    Recent findings suggest that the exaction here is a tax. Its "defining feature" is that it raises revenue. Learning Resources, 607 U.S. at 241. It is neither a mere fee contributing to the costs of operating the program nor a penalty. The power to "restrict" entry is not the power to "tax" entry. To limit or qualify entry notes nothing about charging for it, and the Government can identify no statute in which the words "restrict" or "restriction" confer tax authority.

    The Immigration and Nationality Act  contains express, detailed provisions for fees and payments, setting each amount and specifying how the funds are collected and spent. This confirms the absence of a generalized, unlimited discretionary presidential taxing power. Congress does not "hide elephants in mouseholes," and this case involves a very large elephant. Whitman v. Am. Trucking Ass'ns, 531 U.S. 457, 468 (2001). In more than a century, no President has used Section 212(f) or Section 215(a) of the INA to raise revenue, a point the Government does not dispute. As the Supreme Court held in Learning Resources, that absence is "strong evidence" the power does not exist.

    In addition, the government's interpretation of the relevant statutes violates the major questions doctrine, which requires Congress to speak clearly when delegating power over a major economic or political issue to the executive. The power to impose unlimited taxes on any visa holders or immigrants entering into the United States is undoubtedly a major one. If, nonetheless, the court concludes that Congress did somehow grant the government the sweeping power it claims, it would violate the constitutional nondelegation doctrine, which constrains delegations of legislative power to the executive.

    I have previously criticized the $100,000 H-1B fee on both legal and policy grounds here, here, and here.

    Our Amicus Brief in Case Challenging Trump's Section 338 Tariffs Against Canada

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (426 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that yesterday, the Cato Institute and I filed an amicus brief before the US Court of International Trade, in Gellert Global Corp.
    • I previously wrote about the Section 338 tariffs and why they are harmful and illegal in an article in The Dispatch, and a paper for the Montreal Economic Institute.
    • We are grateful to Daniel Cannistra and others at Crowell & Moring for their invaluable pro bono assistance in helping draft and submit the brief on very short notice.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that yesterday, the Cato Institute and I filed an amicus brief before the US Court of International Trade, in Gellert Global Corp. v. Trump, the first case challenging Donald Trump's massive 50% Section 338 tariffs against Canadian imports. The plaintiff is represented by the Liberty Justice Center, the public interest law firm I worked with on the case challenging the massive tariffs Trump imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). That case resulted in the tariffs' invalidation by the Supreme Court earlier this year.

    I previously wrote about the Section 338 tariffs and why they are harmful and illegal in an article in The Dispatch, and a paper for the Montreal Economic Institute.

    We are grateful to Daniel Cannistra and others at Crowell & Moring for their invaluable pro bono assistance in helping draft and submit the brief on very short notice. Here is a summary of our key arguments, which should soon be posted at the Cato website:.

    This brief explains why Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 cannot be used to impose the tariffs enacted by Defendants, and why doing so violates the major questions and nondelegation doctrines.

    Sources indicate that the Court should strike down the Section 338 duties for three reasons. First, Section 338 requires that any tariffs imposed be in response to discriminatory trade restrictions enacted by foreign trading partners, and that those tariffs "offset" the barriers imposed by those countries. The Section 338 tariffs imposed by the Trump administration violate both of these requirements. In addition, Section 338 has been superseded by later statutes and is no longer operative.

    In a recent development, second, the major questions doctrine forecloses interpreting Section 338 to permit the President to impose extraordinary import taxes whenever another country imposes any trade restrictions or declines to purchase American goods. to "speak clearly" when it assigns to the executive "decisions of vast 'economic and political significance.'" The sweeping power claimed by the administration in this case undeniably raises a major question, and it is at the very least unclear that Section 338 actually grants such vast authority.

    According to recent reports, third, stripping the statute's qualitative conditions of operative force violates the nondelegation doctrine, which constrains delegation of legislative power to the executive. An extremely high rate ceiling of 50 percent cannot substitute for clear legislative limiting how and when tariffs can be imposed.

    Cato and I (together with Prof. Michael McConnell) also recently submitted an amicus brief in litigation challenging Trump's massive Section 301 tariffs.

    Macao: Ex-Lawmaker Gets 12.5 Years After Unfair Trial

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (910 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (London) – A court in Macao, a special administrative region of China, sentenced the former lawmaker and democracy activist Au Kam San to 12.5 years in prison on November 6, 2026, on baseless national security charges, Human Rights Watch said today.
    • Macao’s Court of First Instance, in the first publicly known case under the city’s national security law, convicted Au on five charges involving “subversion of state power,” “establishing links with foreign forces to endanger national security,” and “violation of secrecy.” The Macao government should quash the sentence and immediately and unconditionally release Au.
    • In a recent development, “The Macao authorities’ bogus prosecution of former lawmaker Au Kam San reflects Beijing’s escalating repression across its territories,” stated Maya Wang, deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (London) – A court in Macao, a special administrative region of China, sentenced the former lawmaker and democracy activist Au Kam San to 12.5 years in prison on November 6, 2026, on baseless national security charges, Human Rights Watch said today.

    Macao’s Court of First Instance, in the first publicly known case under the city’s national security law, convicted Au on five charges involving “subversion of state power,” “establishing links with foreign forces to endanger national security,” and “violation of secrecy.” The Macao government should quash the sentence and immediately and unconditionally release Au.

    In a recent development, “The Macao authorities’ bogus prosecution of former lawmaker Au Kam San reflects Beijing’s escalating repression across its territories,” stated Maya Wang, deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “The sentence, which could keep the democracy advocate in prison until he’d be past 80, is both outrageous and cruel.”.

    The court did not release the full judgment, but only a summary of its decision. It ruled that Au worked with unspecified overseas “hostile” organizations “over an extended period” to disseminate materials advocating subversion and inciting hatred against the Chinese government, as well as to provoke hostile foreign action against China and disrupt Macao’s 2024 election for chief executive.

    Recent findings suggest that it also found that, while serving as a lawmaker in 2021, he disclosed confidential information about casino license renewals from a legislative committee meeting to overseas organizations. The court did not identify the organizations or substantiate the charges in detail, but claimed Au did not dispute most of the facts.

    Au’s prosecution involved serious violations of his right to a fair trial, Human Rights Watch said. He had been detained since July 2025.

    In July 2026, his family told reporters that the authorities had held him incommunicado and denied him access to the lawyer his family found for him. Au was instead represented by a court-appointed lawyer whom Au “accepted,” the court statement said. Article 36 of Macao’s functional constitution, the Basic Law, guarantees residents access to legal counsel to protect their lawful rights and interests. In its November statement, the court said Au’s family had been allowed to visit him “regularly.”.

    In a recent development, au was tried in a closed-door hearing over three days, from September 16 to 18. A law that Macao adopted in March permits closing court proceedings to the public when Macao’s national security committee determines that national security is at risk. The committee’s decisions are not subject to appeal or judicial review.

    Au, a Portuguese and European Union citizen and former primary school teacher, was one of Macao’s longest-serving pro-democracy lawmakers. Directly elected to the Legislative Assembly from 2001 to 2021, he was one of its few consistent voices for democratic reform, government accountability, and social causes.

    He campaigned for 15 years for free public education and more public housing, scrutinized government spending, and raised concerns about corruption and the misuse of public funds. After leaving the legislature, he remained engaged in public affairs, including efforts to protect Macao’s historic Guia Lighthouse.

    Industry observers note that au also played a major role in Macao’s small civil society. For 30 years, his group, the Macao Union of Democratic Development (澳門民主發展聯委會), organized annual vigils commemorating the 1989 Tiananmen Massacre in Beijing, even as he and fellow organizers experienced abuse for their efforts, including physical assaults and loss of jobs.

    Industry observers note that macao was a Portuguese colony until 1999, when its sovereignty was transferred to the People’s Republic of China. Macao’s government has long suppressed critical voices. It has arbitrarily arrested opposition figures and journalists, severely restricted protests, and barred Hong Kong pro-democracy activists and journalists from entering the territory.

    Recent findings suggest that the crackdown on political opposition and civil society has intensified in recent years, Human Rights Watch noted. Authorities disqualified 21 people in 2021 and 12 in 2025 from running for legislative seats, citing vague reasons such as “disloyalty” to Macao. In 2021, Macao’s Court of Final Appeal upheld the government’s arbitrary ban on the Tiananmen Massacre vigils, ruling that the organizers’ political slogans violated the Chinese Constitution and Macao’s Basic Law by urging the public to “overthrow the existing political system.”.

    According to recent reports, macao’s draconian Law on Safeguarding National Security, enacted in 2009 and amended in 2023, undermines the rule of law and human rights guarantees enshrined in the Basic Law, and contravenes the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which applies to Macao through the Basic Law. The 2023 amendments extended the National Security law to nonviolent acts; previously, only violent acts were punishable.

    The European Union has condemned Au’s conviction and sentencing, and Portugal has raised the case directly with the Chinese authorities.

    “Portugal, the European Union, and other concerned governments should publicly and forcefully press for Au Kam San’s immediate and unconditional release,” Wang remarked. “Countries should take note of the recent harsh sentences handed down in Hong Kong and Macao and consider what that means for their long-term relationship with the Chinese government.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Kyiv, November 10, 2026) – Escalating Russian drone attacks on passenger trains and other railway vehicles in Ukraine have killed and injured civilians, including railway workers, and increasingly threaten a transportation system that millions of Ukrainians depend on, Human Rights Watch said today.

    Since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Ukraine’s state railway organization, Ukrzaliznytsia, has evacuated more than 4 million people by train from areas under attack, while maintaining essential transportation links for civilians across the country.

    According to recent reports, “For millions of Ukraine’s civilians, trains are a lifeline, enabling them to escape danger, reunite with family members, and access essential services including medical care,” remarked Belkis Wille, associate crisis, conflict and arms director at Human Rights Watch. “The increasing Russian drone attacks on passenger trains put civilian lives at risk, threatening a transportation system many depend on for safety and survival.”.

    Human Rights Watch investigated three Russian drone attacks on trains and railway equipment between March and September 2026. Researchers interviewed railway workers and a passenger and examined photographs and videos of the attacks and their aftermath, including footage published by the Russian Defense Ministry and Russian military-affiliated Telegram channels.

    In 2026, the attacks have increased, including one on January 27, when a Russian drone struck a passenger train carrying 292 people in Kharkivska region, killing five civilians and injuring two others, according to Ukrainian authorities.

    A Russian drone strike on March 2 on a moving passenger train travelling from Nikopol toward Kryvyi Rih killed a civilian and injured at least six others.

    August 6, a Russian drone struck railway equipment and facilities near Lozova station in Kharkivska region, killing 2 railway workers and injuring 11 civilians.

    Industry observers note that on August 13, a Russian drone hit a locomotive—the engine car—attached to a passenger train near Buialyk station in Odeska region, killing the train driver, Vasyl Morozov, 50, and his assistant, Ivan Shevchyk, 41. A second drone hit a replacement diesel locomotive dispatched several hours later to move the damaged train to Odesa city.

    Recent findings suggest that beyond the physical damage, railway workers described mounting psychological strain as attacks and emergency evacuations became increasingly frequent throughout the year. The conductor of the train attacked on August 13 noted family members have urged her to leave the profession because of the dangers, and the deputy train manager said his children asked him to stop working on trains.

    Sources indicate that railway staff stated the growing threat prompted changes to safety protocols in mid-2026, including more precautionary stops during which railway staff direct passengers to leave a train for minutes or hours before they can continue their journey. Train staff interviewed said that as of September, they were conducting multiple evacuations on every route. Oleksandr Shevchenko, deputy head of passenger services at Ukrzaliznytsia, told Human Rights Watch that during September, passengers were evacuated from 15 trains shortly before Russian attacks struck those trains.

    The repeated attacks have also strained Ukrzaliznytsia’s ability to maintain services and replace damaged equipment. Shevchenko said Russian forces had damaged or destroyed more than 500 locomotives since 2022, including more than 300 in 2026 alone. With limited domestic manufacturing capacity, replacing damaged locomotives and other railway vehicles has become increasingly difficult, he said. The railway also operates medical evacuation and diplomatic train services with its remaining equipment.

    Recent findings suggest that the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) documented a sharp increase in Russian attacks on railway infrastructure between mid-2025 and mid-2026. From June to November 2025, OHCHR verified 78 Russian attacks on railway infrastructure. Between December 2025 and May 2026, it verified 142 Russian attacks, an 82 percent increase compared to the preceding 6 months. From June to September 2026, OHCHR verified another 130 Russian attacks. The strikes damaged railway tracks, stations, locomotives, railway energy infrastructure, and passenger trains, threatening essential civilian transportation and evacuation services.

    Sources indicate that russian authorities and pro-Russian media have also stated that Ukraine has attacked passenger trains in Russia and Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine. OHCHR verified two attacks on railway infrastructure in Russian-occupied territory between December 2025 and May 2026. From June to September 2026, OHCHR verified another 11 Ukrainian attacks on railway infrastructure in the Russian-occupied regions of Donetsk, Luhansk, and Crimea. Human Rights Watch examined one Ukrainian attack on a train in Crimea.

    Under international humanitarian law, parties to an armed conflict must distinguish between civilian objects and military objectives. Civilian passenger trains, railway stations, and railway equipment used for civilian purposes may not be deliberately targeted.

    Industry observers note that warring parties should cease disproportionate and deliberate attacks on civilian trains and railway facilities and should investigate attacks that may have unlawfully targeted civilian objects, Human Rights Watch said. Ukraine’s international partners should continue supporting measures to protect civilians and critical civilian transportation networks from attack.

    Industry observers note that “Russian forces’ intensifying attacks on railways are placing civilians in peril,” Wille mentioned. “Railway workers are risking their lives to evacuate civilians multiple times in a single journey, with warnings only minutes before a strike.”.

    For more details on the individual attacks on trains, and relevant international humanitarian law, please see below.

    Industry observers note that attacks affecting civilian rail transportation are not new. In one of the deadliest incidents for civilians since Russia’s full-scale invasion, a Russian cluster munition attack on the crowded Kramatorsk train station in eastern Ukraine on April 8, 2022, killed at least 58 civilians and injured more than 100 others.

    In the first 8 months of 2026, Ukrzaliznytsia recorded more than 1,600 Russian attacks on its rolling stock and infrastructure. Most recently, a Russian jet-powered drone reportedly struck the main railway station in the eastern city of Dnipro on October 29, hitting a crowded platform and killing at least 13 people.

    Oleksandr Shevchenko, deputy head of passenger services at Ukrzaliznytsia, told Human Rights Watch that Russian attacks initially focused primarily on railway infrastructure. Since 2026, however, Russian forces have increasingly struck moving passenger trains and locomotives or engines, he mentioned. Passenger trains do not transport active military personnel, although individual off-duty Ukrainian soldiers may be among the passengers.

    A September 13 attack that damaged the locomotive of a fuel train occurred shortly after a separate train carrying former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson, former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt, and other international officials had passed through the station after attending a Yalta European Strategy conference in Kyiv.

    August 13 Attack on a Locomotive Attached to a Passenger Train in Odeska Region.

    Recent findings suggest that the August 13 drone attack that killed the train driver and his assistant was on a train carrying approximately 340 passengers, including 67 children, and 14 crew members. No passengers were injured.

    Sources indicate that human Rights Watch interviewed four crew members who survived the attack. Mykola Zakharchenko, the train manager, said railway officials issued an evacuation warning shortly before 7 a.m., but the drone struck before the train had come to a complete stop.

    Sources indicate that “The train driver notified us there would be a stop and evacuation,” Zakharchenko said. “Then about 50 seconds later there was an explosion and the train shook.”.

    According to recent reports, the deputy train manager, Oleksandr Smolnakov, said railway personnel immediately began evacuating passengers after the explosion. Olga Poniuk, a conductor with nearly 25 years of railway experience, described trying to keep passengers calm.

    Industry observers note that “I needed to evacuate, but without spreading panic among passengers,” she said. “Almost every compartment in my carriage had children in it.”.

    The dangers continued after the initial strike. Zakharchenko said that while railway personnel attempted to transport the train to Odesa city, monitoring teams twice warned of additional drones in the area, prompting workers to take cover under nearby trees. Following the second warning, another drone struck a replacement diesel locomotive connected to the damaged passenger train to move it to Odesa, just a short distance from the initial attack.

    Zakharchenko noted railway personnel later demonstrated him flight-path data indicating that one of the drones had circled the area before striking the locomotive. Crew members provided photographs and videos of the aftermath of the attack.

    The Wrong Side, a Russian military-affiliated Telegram channel, published the video feed of a drone tracking a train entering Buialyk station. The video cuts and then demonstrates the same train at the station with smoke coming from the locomotive section of the train and a fire truck nearby. The caption notes that a Geran, a Russian-produced Shahed-type drone, was used in the attack.

    August 6 Attack on a Railway Flaw Detection Car Near Lozova Station.

    The August 6 drone attack that killed 2 railway workers and injured 11 civilians, according to Ukrainian authorities, struck railway equipment and facilities near Lozova station in Kharkivska region.

    Sources indicate that nina Zabila, the station head, told Human Rights Watch that the drone struck a railway flaw detection car—a specialized rail vehicle that scans tracks for hidden cracks and damage before they cause accidents—that was parked near the station and damaged station facilities. Emergency responders identified the weapon as a Geran drone.

    It has been revealed that “We heard a strange sound and then an explosion,” Zabila mentioned. “Then I saw blood on the people who were injured.” She said she was unaware of any military targets nearby.

    Sources indicate that the Russian Ministry of Defense posted a video capturing the moment prior to the attack on the station. The video shows a drone feed tracking and closing in on the railway flaw detection car at the station. A local Ukrainian news channel published a video of the aftermath.

    March 2 Attack on a Moving Passenger Train Near Kryvyi Rih.

    The March 2 drone attack that killed a civilian and injured at least six others struck the fifth carriage of a moving passenger train traveling from Nikopol toward Kryvyi Rih, said Vitaliy Zhuravsky, the train driver.

    Zhuravsky noted no air raid alert was in effect when a Shahed drone struck shortly after 1 p.m.

    “I only heard it when the explosion happened,” he stated. “Then I used the emergency brakes.”.

    Sources indicate that zhuravsky and his assistant evacuated approximately 40 to 50 passengers to a nearby tree cover, fearing further strikes. Drones continued flying overhead, he said, and Russian attacks struck railway facilities in nearby Apostolove while emergency responders assisted passengers.

    June 4 Attack by Ukraine on a Locomotive in Crimea.

    It has been revealed that human Rights Watch examined one incident of a Ukrainian attack on a train. On June 4, Sergei Aksyonov, the Russian-appointed head of occupied Crimea, stated that a Ukrainian drone attack on a local train—a railbus—traveling between Azovske and Kerch had killed one civilian and injured three others. Human Rights Watch verified a video uploaded to Telegram on June 4 by Robert Brovdi, commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, showing a drone striking a railbus near Vladislavivka, a town in Russian-occupied Crimea between Azovske and Kerch.

    Industry observers note that human Rights Watch matched characteristics of the railbus visible in the drone footage and found they were consistent with the RA-3 railbus, a train used for local passenger transport in Crimea. Researchers were unable to identify and interview anyone involved in the attack or independently verify the reported casualties or whether the train was being used for military purposes at the time.

    Recent findings suggest that under international humanitarian law, parties to an armed conflict must distinguish between civilian objects and military objectives. Civilian passenger trains, railway stations, and railway equipment used for civilian purposes may not be deliberately targeted.

    According to recent reports, however, such infrastructure can serve a dual purpose and may be used by the military for operations, although that alone does not make it a military objective. Under Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions (article 52), to be a legitimate target, the infrastructure must make “an effective contribution to military action” and its destruction “in the circumstances ruling at the time, must offer a definite military advantage.”.

    Dual-use infrastructure is to be presumed a civilian object. Attacks designed to leave the rail transport system in general unable to function or to deter civilian travel or use of railways are not permitted. Even when attacking a lawful military objective, disproportionate attacks that cause excessive civilian harm are prohibited, and parties must take all feasible precautions to minimize civilian harm. Serious violations of international humanitarian law committed with criminal intent may amount to war crimes.

    Supreme Court Will Review Case Challenging Donald Trump's "Invasion" Executive Order

    📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (591 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that yesterday, the Supreme Court decided to review Mullin v.
    • The Trump administration's position on this concern is badly wrong, and has dangerous implications.
    • Recent findings suggest that I also go over the dire implications of adopting a broad definition of invasion.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that yesterday, the Supreme Court decided to review Mullin v. RAICES, a case challenging the legality of Donald Trump's January 2025 "invasion" executive order, which bars virtually all legal migration across the southern border. Trump relies on the Guarantee Clause of Article IV, Section 4 of the Constitution, which states that "The United States shall guarantee to every State in this Union a Republican Form of Government, and shall protect each of them against Invasion." The administration claims that illegal migration, drug smuggling, and supposed "public health" risks  qualify as an "invasion" under the Guarantee Clause, thereby authorizing the president to suspend legal migration indefinitely.

    The Trump administration's position on this concern is badly wrong, and has dangerous implications. In my article, "Immigration is Not Invasion" I provide a comprehensive overview of the many reasons why "invasion" - as that term is used in the Constitution and the AEA - must be a military attack, not illegal migration, drug smuggling, or other similar activity. As James Madison put it, "invasion is an operation of war." I provided a shorter overview of the invasion order and its dangerous implications in a 2025 Just Security article.

    Recent findings suggest that I also go over the dire implications of adopting a broad definition of invasion. Among other things, it would allow the federal government to suspend the writ of habeas corpus (and thereby detain people - including US citizens - without due process) at any time. It would also give state governments the power to "engage in war" against neighboring foreign countries at virtually any time, even without congressional authorization. And there is much more. This case has major implications that go beyond immigration, and threaten the civil liberties of US citizens, as well as recent migrants.

    The Supreme Court could potentially rule against Trump on statutory grounds, without reaching the glitch of the definition of "invasion" in the Constitution. That is what the district court and the DC Circuit did. Alternatively, the Court could rule that the president has purely statutory authority to bar these migrants. But if it rejects these statutory arguments, or at least does so in large part, it will have to reach the "invasion" issue. If the justices do reach that issue, it is vital that the reject the administration's position.

    There are also a number of procedural complications in the case (primarily involving the scope of the remedy), which I will not attempt to go over here.

    Recent findings suggest that this case should not be confused with the related ongoing litigation over the legality of Trump's invocation of the Alien Enemies Act of 1798. The AEA can only be used to detain and deport migrants when there is a declared war, an "invasion," or a "predatory incursion." There, too, the Trump administration claims illegal migration and drug smuggling qualify as an "invasion," and there too it is wrong to do so (on which see  Part III of my article, my amicus brief in the Fifth Circuit AEA case, which I coauthored on behalf of the Brennan Center, the Cato Institute, and others). As detailed in my article, it is highly likely that "invasion" has the same meaning in the AEA and in the four places where that term is used in the Constitution, enacted just a few years earlier.

    Recent findings suggest that I will likely have more to say about this case in future posts and other writings. Stay tuned!

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Member countries called for the release of journalists, lawyers and civil society activists from unlawful detention, for freedom of speech, for action to tackle gender-based violence, and for accountability for violent crackdowns in the country’s Gorno-Badakhshan autonomous region.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Geneva, November 10, 2026) – United Nations members urged Tajikistan during its periodic United Nations peer review on November 5, 2026, to take urgent action to protect human rights in the country and end repression against government opponents.

    Member countries called for the release of journalists, lawyers and civil society activists from unlawful detention, for freedom of speech, for action to tackle gender-based violence, and for accountability for violent crackdowns in the country’s Gorno-Badakhshan autonomous region.

    In a recent development, “Tajikistan has openly flouted United Nations peer review recommendations to the detriment of its people’s human rights and freedoms,” noted Hugh Williamson, Europe and Central Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “Tajikistan should use this opportunity to take the advice of its peers and end its systematic human rights abuses.”.

    In a recent development, the Universal Periodic Review (UPR) is a mechanism of the United Nations Human Rights Council in which member countries review other countries’ human rights records every four and a half years and problem recommendations to address concerns. In Tajikistan’s 2021 review, the government accepted 172 out of the 234 recommendations and noted 62 of the others. But the government has failed to implement key recommendations and human rights conditions have worsened sharply since 2021, Human Rights Watch mentioned.

    Member states praised Tajikistan for ratifying the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, adopting a National Strategy for Protection of Human Rights until 2038, and passing a Law on the Equality and Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination in 2022.

    However, several countries expressed alarm at the worsening human rights situation in Tajikistan. Germany noted that it “remains concerned about repression against civil society, journalists, human rights defenders, religious organizations, and the political opposition, including through torture and lack of judicial independence.” Countries urged Tajikistan to end reprisals against opposition figures, nongovernmental organizations, activists, and journalists; to protect freedom of expression and media freedom; to abolish the death penalty; and to establish mechanisms to prevent torture and ill treatment.

    In a recent development, several countries, including Brazil, France and the Netherlands urged Tajikistan to conduct thorough investigations into the 2021-2022 events in Gorno-Badakhshan autonomous region. France called for an “independent, impartial, and transparent investigation of deaths of civilians and allegations of human rights violations in Badakhshan.” In May 2022, police reportedly killed up to 40 people in the autonomous region during so-called security operations.

    The police also reportedly arbitrarily detained and tortured more than 200 protesters, including  205 residents of the region who were sentenced to prison in closed trials in 2021 and 2022.

    More than a dozen UN member states urged Tajikistan to uphold its commitments to allow civil society organizations to operate unhindered. In this context Estonia, Poland, Portugal, and Ukraine called on Tajikistan to bring its counter terrorism legislation into line with international human rights standards. Poland stated that “overly broad definitions of the terrorist threats and extremist phenomenon may lead to disproportionate restrictions on human rights”.

    It has been revealed that tajikistan has been dismantling the foundations of independent civil society since its last UPR. After closing down more than 500 nongovernmental organizations in 2022, Tajik authorities declared the closure of another 239 organizations in the first half of 2023, either through court decisions or because they were forced to self-liquidate.

    Industry observers note that while some countries welcomed Tajikistan’s recent progress on women’s rights, other countries urged Tajikistan to address widespread gender-based violence. Belgium, Chile, Iceland, Switzerland, and the UK stated that Tajikistan should criminalize gender-based and domestic violence. Several countries also recommended eliminating child, early and forced marriages. Estonia, which urged the government to “introduce a consent based definition of rape in its legal code”, was one of a number of states that called on Tajikistan to bring its rape legislation into line with international standards.

    In a recent development, several countries, including Chile, Japan and Ukraine called on Tajikistan to strengthen protections against enforced disappearance while Lithuania urged it to end transnational repression. Transnational repression by the Tajik government has involved enforced disappearances, unlawful renditions, abusive use of Interpol Red Notices, and harassment of family members in Tajikistan of opponents in exile.

    Industry observers note that in October 2026, Tajikistan’s lower chamber of parliament approved a decision to withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC), which will take effect one year after the formal UN notification to the UN secretary-general. Several countries urged Tajikistan to reconsider. ICC judges found in March 2026 that as an ICC member country, Tajikistan failed to comply with its obligation to arrest and surrender Russian President Vladimir Putin, who was under an ICC arrest warrant, during his visit in October 2025 and referred the matter to the court’s Assembly of States Parties for further action.

    According to recent reports, “Tajikistan told UN members during the review that it is fully committed to international human rights standards, but it has not demonstrated its commitment,” Williamson mentioned. “Its credibility on the international stage would increase if it turns words into actions with specific steps to end rights abuses by state authorities and promote basic freedoms.”.

    • It has been revealed that on November 10, the United States failed for the second time to participate in its United Nations Universal Periodic Review (UPR), setting a troubling and unprecedented record in the UPR’s nearly 20-year history.
    • Industry observers note that the UPR is a process in which the human rights record of every member state is periodically reviewed by other countries.
    • According to recent reports, after the US was a no-show for its UPR today, the UN Human Rights Council again decided to give the US yet another opportunity to reengage with the process — rescheduling the US UPR for January 2027, justifying this decision on the basis of the cooperative nature of the mechanism.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that on November 10, the United States failed for the second time to participate in its United Nations Universal Periodic Review (UPR), setting a troubling and unprecedented record in the UPR’s nearly 20-year history. UN member states should ensure there are consequences for the United States’ persistent non-cooperation.

    Industry observers note that the UPR is a process in which the human rights record of every member state is periodically reviewed by other countries. It is a unique peer review mechanism aimed at ensuring universality of coverage and equal treatment of all states. The UPR is often the only occasion for discussion at the UN of a state’s human rights situation and for civil society groups to raise their concerns to a global audience. The US decision to disengage from this vital process is just the latest example of the Trump administration's disdain for human rights, its international obligations, and the UN multilateral system.

    According to recent reports, after the US was a no-show for its UPR today, the UN Human Rights Council again decided to give the US yet another opportunity to reengage with the process — rescheduling the US UPR for January 2027, justifying this decision on the basis of the cooperative nature of the mechanism. The ultimate strength of this process, however, lies in its universality. Member states should act now to uphold the UPR and its universal application, rather than risk undermining the integrity of the mechanism.

    Allowing US non-participation to go without consequences disregards civil society’s and UN experts’ concerns regarding the deteriorating human rights situation in the country, opens the door for other countries to treat participation in the UPR as optional, and incentivizes non-participation.

    Human Rights Watch and other organizations have called on the Human Rights Council to ensure consequences for persistent non-cooperation and create the space for dialogue that the US seeks to deny. The council should request that the UN high commissioner for human rights brief it on the human rights situation in the US at the 64th session in March 2027 with the participation of civil society groups and victims of US human rights violations.

    It has been revealed that the Human Rights Council needs to discuss the US human rights record, like every other UN member state. UPR universality must be protected at all costs. No exceptions allowed.

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that from Judge Allison Burroughs (D.
    • In a recent development, andrew Lattarulo is an immigration lawyer and part owner of the law firm Georges Cote LLP, which represents "thousands of clients in active immigration proceedings." Lattarulo also runs a popular Instagram account featuring videos of himself discussing "know-your-rights information about U.S.
    • Audai Cote, "the registered agent and individual in charge of I-9 compliance" at the firm, was served with a Notice of Inspection on September 8, 2025.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that from Judge Allison Burroughs (D. Mass.) Friday in Lattarulo v. Mullin:.

    In a recent development, andrew Lattarulo is an immigration lawyer and part owner of the law firm Georges Cote LLP, which represents "thousands of clients in active immigration proceedings." Lattarulo also runs a popular Instagram account featuring videos of himself discussing "know-your-rights information about U.S. immigration matters," which regularly "amasses hundreds of thousands of views." Georges Cote is currently being investigated by Homeland Security Investigations ("HSI"), the investigative arm of the Department of Homeland Security ("DHS"), for employing individuals without a legal right to work in the United States.

    Audai Cote, "the registered agent and individual in charge of I-9 compliance" at the firm, was served with a Notice of Inspection on September 8, 2025. Unlike Lattarulo, "Cote is not an immigration attorney—he focuses on personal injury." The firm responded on September 12, 2025, and the government sent Cote a Notice of Suspect Documents on September 25, 2025. The firm was given ten days to attempt to verify the identity and work authorization of the employees named in the Notice of Suspect Documents.

    In late September 2025, while the HSI investigation proceeded, both Lattarulo and Cote travelled from Boston to Aruba for a weekend trip. On September 27, 2025, Cote arrived back at Logan Airport from Aruba without concern. Lattarulo made the same journey the following day, September 28, 2025. Lattarulo passed through customs preclearance in Aruba before boarding a flight to Boston.

    According to recent reports, when his flight arrived at Logan Airport, three U.S. Customs and Border Protection ("CBP") agents and one HSI officer stopped Lattarulo as he got off the plane. The agents seized his cell phone without a warrant and then downloaded a complete copy of the data stored on the phone. Eight days later, they returned the cell phone via overnight delivery.

    In a recent development, the seized cell phone data is currently in a format that is not readable or reviewable, but the government intends to convert the data to an accessible format and search it if the Court permits. The data includes confidential information, including privileged attorney-client communications related to Lattarulo's clients. {The Government was clear that any search of the contents of the phone would utilize a taint team to protect privileged information.} ….

    The court held that Lattarulo was likely correct on his claim that the search was unconstitutional retaliation for his speech, and therefore granted "a preliminary injunction enjoining Defendants from accessing the data obtained from the phone before this action is resolved":.

    "[T]he law is settled that as a general matter the First Amendment prohibits government officials from subjecting an individual to retaliatory actions, including criminal prosecutions, for speaking out." … The retaliation problem [here] turns on causation—that is, whether the seizure and search of Lattarulo's cell phone would have occurred but for his protected speech.

    Respondents have provided no evidence that searches of cell phones are frequently conducted during the kind of employment investigation at matter here, and Lattarulo has directed the Court to sources which suggest otherwise. Indeed, Lattarulo's evidence suggests that any pursuit of criminal charges against employers for employing unauthorized immigrants is exceedingly rare. The fact that the government, after Lattarulo spoke out publicly against it, elected to adopt a highly unusual investigative method that appears designed to inflict a maximal burden on Lattarulo lends substantial support to an inference that its actions were pretextual.

    The stage of the investigation at which the search occurred further bolsters the inference of pretext. Under HSI's own policies, the agency "presumes that employers who, within 10 business days of receiving a Notice of Suspect Documents, verify the identity and/or employment authorization of the listed employees, or take appropriate actions to address the apparent employment of unauthorized workers, have demonstrated reasonable care under the INA." The government's search occurred only three days after Georges Cote first received a Notice of Suspect Documents, meaning that the agency was still early in its period of "presum[ing]" compliance when it occurred. Thus, the government's actions here required it to short-circuit its orderly investigative procedures and cast aside its ten-day presumption of compliance in favor of immediately seizing Lattarulo's phone. That aggressive deviation from protocol strongly suggests that the seizure did not arise from an ordinary investigative motive.

    According to recent reports, further, Lattarulo has identified an "otherwise similarly situated individual not engaged in the same sort of protected speech," who was not subjected to the same enforcement action: his law firm partner Audai Cote, who had the same or greater access to the firm's employment records but did not speak publicly about immigrant rights. Indeed, if the government was truly intent on seizing evidence at the first possible opportunity, Mr. Cote, who returned to America a full day before Lattarulo, would have been a more logical target. Nonetheless, the government opted to wait until Lattarulo touched down in Boston the next day and subject only him to an intrusive cell phone search. The balance of the evidence presently before the Court thus suggests that Lattarulo is likely to establish that he would not have been searched except for his protected speech.

    {It is true that the presence of probable cause generally precludes a finding of causation in a retaliatory arrest case, but the Supreme Court has recognized a limited exception for situations in which officers who "have probable cause to make arrests [for a particular crime] … typically exercise their discretion not to do so," such as "an individual who has been vocally complaining about police conduct … [before being] arrested for jaywalking," By analogy, the limited record before the Court suggests that searches of cell phones are not regularly conducted during the kind of employment investigation at issue here and that Lattarulo's own law firm partner was not subjected to the same seizure and search of property.}.

    In a recent development, it is true that Defendants can "prevail … by showing that the [search] would have been initiated without respect to retaliation," and here Defendants state that they have additional evidence which would show as much, but they have not provided it because they assert that doing so would prejudice an ongoing investigation…. [T]he Court concludes that the limited record that is before the Court suggests that Lattarulo is likely to succeed on the merits of his First Amendment retaliation claim and that the record before it is therefore adequate to grant the limited preliminary relief contemplated by this order.

    The court didn't resolve Lattarulo's Fourth Amendment claim, because it granted the preliminary injunction based on the First Amendment claim. But it did note the following:.

    Plaintiffs' Fourth Amendment claim turns largely on the scope of the border search exception to the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement. That exception "is grounded in the government's 'inherent authority to protect, and a paramount interest in protecting, its territorial integrity.'" It allows the government to perform "routine" border searches of electronic devices without suspicion of any crime, and to perform "non-routine" border searches of electronic devices without a warrant, so long as the government has reasonable suspicion. Alasaad v. Mayorkas (1st Cir. 2021).

    The question this case raises is: reasonable suspicion of what? In other words, what types of suspected criminal activities can the government use a warrantless advanced border search to investigate? The First Circuit in Alasaad stated that the exception applies to searches for "contraband" or for "evidence of contraband or a border-related crime." Later in its opinion, however, it stated that the exception applies to searches for "contraband, evidence of contraband, or for evidence of activity in violation of the laws enforced or administered by CBP or ICE." In most cases, of course, "border-related crime[s]" and "activity in violation of the laws enforced or administered by CBP or ICE" are synonymous, and the First Circuit in Alasaad appears to have intended to use those terms more or less synonymously.

    According to recent reports, the difficulty of this case lies in the fact that the suspected violation at matter—employment of unauthorized aliens in the United States in violation 8 U.S.C § 1324a—involves a law that is "enforced or administered by CBP or ICE" but arguably is not a "border-related crime." Based on the information before the Court, there appears to be no connection between Lattarulo's border crossing (or, more broadly, the government's interest in policing the border) and the suspected crime that formed the basis for the government's border search. Rather, it appears that the government seized on a fortuitous border crossing following a weekend vacation as an opportunity to search for evidence of a domestic crime it was already investigating.

    Recent findings suggest that even though the suspected violation involves aliens and a law administered by ICE, the Court is not convinced that the First Circuit in Alasaad intended for the border exception to apply to investigations into activity that occurred nowhere near the border and that has no relationship to the border crossing during which the search occurred. Nor is the Court convinced that application of the border search exception to this type of investigation would further the principles underlying the exception. Nonetheless, given the novelty of these questions and the fact that a ruling on them is not necessary, the Court will refrain at this point from reaching a firm conclusion on the concern of the border search's applicability….

    Mary Lemay and Patrick M. Hanley (Butters Brazilian LLP) represent Lattarulo.

    Germany’s Freedom of Information Under Renewed Attack

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A leaked draft of the Interior Ministry’s proposed Law on the Adjustment of Transparency, Disclosure, and Information Duties to Ensure Adequate Protection of Critical Infrastructure was made public on November 5, reigniting concerns about a renewed attack on freedom of information in Germany.
    • The government’s previous attempt in June to introduce a law that would essentially gut the Freedom of Information Act stalled, after wide pushback from civil society and even from within the Social Democrats—a partner in the coalition government.
    • A new government draft law dated September 30 now proposes to amend the Freedom of Information Act by excluding its application to any information requests about state actions relating to “critical infrastructure” or infrastructure deemed “in particular need of protection to maintain public security.” These vague provisions would give authorities that receive freedom of information requests broad discretionary powers to reject requests.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A leaked draft of the Interior Ministry’s proposed Law on the Adjustment of Transparency, Disclosure, and Information Duties to Ensure Adequate Protection of Critical Infrastructure was made public on November 5, reigniting concerns about a renewed attack on freedom of information in Germany.

    The government’s previous attempt in June to introduce a law that would essentially gut the Freedom of Information Act stalled, after wide pushback from civil society and even from within the Social Democrats—a partner in the coalition government.

    A new government draft law dated September 30 now proposes to amend the Freedom of Information Act by excluding its application to any information requests about state actions relating to “critical infrastructure” or infrastructure deemed “in particular need of protection to maintain public security.” These vague provisions would give authorities that receive freedom of information requests broad discretionary powers to reject requests.

    FragDenStaat, a German civil society platform for freedom of information, called this exclusionary clause a “Trojan horse,” that risks allowing for the blanket rejection of information requests that relate to “energy, transportation, healthcare, finance, water, food, and much more.”.

    Sources indicate that under Germany’s Freedom of Information Act, anyone can make requests for access to public records. Human rights groups and journalists often rely on freedom of information laws as an effective—and sometimes the only—avenue to scrutinize state actions and hold authorities to account. Limiting the scope of the Act through such overbroad exclusions would undermine their access and state transparency. It is also unnecessary as the Act already stipulates that official information that could jeopardize public security is exempt from information requests.

    Under international human rights law, Germany is obliged to protect the right to seek and receive information as part of the right to freedom of expression. Information regarding any government action should only be withheld in exceptional cases—not through blanket exceptions.

    It has been revealed that access to information is a right essential for enabling effective public participation and ensures that the public has access to reliable information that can help strengthen trust in democratic institutions. The government should drop its efforts to undermine it.

    Breaking: Hope for World’s Forests and Their Defenders at COP31

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Netherlands’ commitment at the United Nations climate change conference (COP31) today that it will invest up to half a billion dollars in the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF) is a major step towards protecting the world’s most biodiverse ecosystems and the rights and livelihoods of millions of people who depend on them.
    • Sources indicate that when I attended COP26 in Glasgow in 2021, 137 countries committed to halt and reverse forest loss and land degradation by 2030.
    • The TFFF seeks to tackle that problem by pooling money from governments and private actors to invest in a profit-yielding fund; the profit then supports payments for eligible tropical countries that demonstrably protect their forests.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Netherlands’ commitment at the United Nations climate change conference (COP31) today that it will invest up to half a billion dollars in the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF) is a major step towards protecting the world’s most biodiverse ecosystems and the rights and livelihoods of millions of people who depend on them.

    Sources indicate that when I attended COP26 in Glasgow in 2021, 137 countries committed to halt and reverse forest loss and land degradation by 2030. While that list of signatories has grown, the funding needed to meet these goals has remained inadequate. This endangers our collective ability to ensure forests, which absorb and store planet warming emissions, can act as an emergency brake to the climate crisis.

    The TFFF seeks to tackle that problem by pooling money from governments and private actors to invest in a profit-yielding fund; the profit then supports payments for eligible tropical countries that demonstrably protect their forests. The goal is to have a self-sustaining fund that sidesteps the capricious ebbs and flows of aid. Initially championed by Brazil, it is now financially backed by multiple governments and private actors.

    Sources indicate that in response to demands from territorial leaders and civil society organizations, including Human Rights Watch, at least 20 percent of TFFF payments to tropical forest countries are earmarked for Indigenous peoples and local communities. The fund excludes investments “that cause significant environmental impact,” including “activities related to coal, peat, oil and gas.”.

    Today’s announcement brings the total investment pledged towards the TFFF to US$ 7.8 billion. While this remains short of the original 10 billion target, the fund is already planning to invest its initial sponsor capital and make its first payments to tropical forest countries next year.

    It has been revealed that earlier this month, the Brazilian government, in their capacity as the previous climate conference president, also released a practical roadmap to enhance efforts to halt and reverse deforestation and degradation, building on input from 180 actors, including Human Rights Watch. It aims to align international efforts towards tested methods.

    Sources indicate that the roadmap recognizes strengthening “rights holders’ authority over lands, territories and resources, supporting long-term forest stewardship and reducing pressures from encroachment, competing claims and unauthorized forest conversion” as an effective policy intervention. After a decade working with environment, land, and Indigenous rights defenders who put their lives on the line to protect their territories, I couldn’t agree more with this analysis.

    JBS and the EU’s Exposure to Human Rights Violations and Illegal Deforestation in Pará, Brazil.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that the girl in the picture looking straight into the camera with probing eyes is 15-year-old Rahile Omer.
    • On November 6, Radio Free Asia (RFA) reported that Rahile, at 23, had died in prison while serving an unjust 12-year sentence.
    • Human Rights Watch has not been able to independently verify this information, but the report should raise alarm about what is happening to the countless Uyghurs who remain behind bars as part of the Chinese government’s crimes against humanity since 2016.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the girl in the picture looking straight into the camera with probing eyes is 15-year-old Rahile Omer. She was photographed in March 2018 among hundreds of other detainees at a political re-education camp in Konasheher county, Kashgar, Xinjiang. A 2022 BBC investigation identified her as the youngest among the hundreds whose headshots were leaked in the Xinjiang Police Files. Previous records show authorities detained her at age 14 shortly after her parents’ detention in mid-2017.

    On November 6, Radio Free Asia (RFA) reported that Rahile, at 23, had died in prison while serving an unjust 12-year sentence.

    Human Rights Watch has not been able to independently verify this information, but the report should raise alarm about what is happening to the countless Uyghurs who remain behind bars as part of the Chinese government’s crimes against humanity since 2016.

    Authorities sentenced her in 2021, when she turned 18, reportedly for “disturbing social order,” according to RFA. Chinese officials familiar with her situation told RFA that she was transferred to prison because she did not provide information about others and was caught praying at the dormitory during her “re-education.” They said she possibly died of a heart problem.

    Hundreds of Uyghurs in the diaspora are mourning Rahile. As a member of this community, I fear receiving similar heartbreaking news every day. My father, Memet Yaqup, is serving a 16-year prison sentence; my uncle, Emet Yaqup, is serving life. I do not know their exact locations or the charges against them, nor do I know if they are still alive.

    The last time I got word about them was in 2024, when a source told me, “You should be thankful that your father and uncle are still alive, we have lost many lives over the years.”.

    Global attention has led Beijing to strictly control information from Xinjiang. Authorities deny independent observers, including United Nations human rights experts, unfettered access to the region while organizing carefully choreographed official tours for select friendly diplomats, journalists, social media influencers, and members of the Uyghur diaspora to present a sense of normalcy to the outside world.

    Rahile Omer punctuates this narrative, and governments should press Beijing to answer the question: What happened to her?
