    Türkiye: COP31 Host Continues Support for Coal Expansion

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (832 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Istanbul, November 11, 2026) – While world leaders gather in Antalya for the United Nations climate change conference (COP31) on November 11 and 12 to discuss how to accelerate global climate action and implement their climate commitments, Turkish authorities’ reluctance to stop expansion of coal operations in the country and strategy an exit from fossil fuels sends the wrong message as the co-host of COP31 and undermines the credibility of its commitments and agenda, Human Rights Watch said today.
    • Industry observers note that in July 2026, the Turkish government appealed a June court ruling rejecting a proposal to add two latest units to the Afşin-Elbistan coal power plant A in Türkiye’s southeastern Kahramanmaraş province.
    • In a recent development, “The court cancellation of the Afşin-Elbistan power plant expansion felt like a turning point in longstanding local community efforts to halt Türkiye’s coal expansion plans,” remarked Deniz Bayram, assistant Europe and Central Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Istanbul, November 11, 2026) – While world leaders gather in Antalya for the United Nations climate change conference (COP31) on November 11 and 12 to discuss how to accelerate global climate action and implement their climate commitments, Turkish authorities’ reluctance to stop expansion of coal operations in the country and strategy an exit from fossil fuels sends the wrong message as the co-host of COP31 and undermines the credibility of its commitments and agenda, Human Rights Watch said today.

    Industry observers note that in July 2026, the Turkish government appealed a June court ruling rejecting a proposal to add two latest units to the Afşin-Elbistan coal power plant A in Türkiye’s southeastern Kahramanmaraş province. In the same month, the government embarked on the permit process to expand the capacity of an existing coal power plant in the northwestern Çanakkale province.

    In a recent development, “The court cancellation of the Afşin-Elbistan power plant expansion felt like a turning point in longstanding local community efforts to halt Türkiye’s coal expansion plans,” remarked Deniz Bayram, assistant Europe and Central Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch. “Yet Turkish authorities seem determined to expand coal, even as they host COP31, taking Türkiye in the wrong direction when it comes to combatting climate change and protecting community members’ right to health.”.

    Two administrative courts in Kahramanmaraş issued rulings rejecting the expansion plan in June. These rulings concerned five separate court challenges brought against the expansion by local governments, civil society organizations, and community members.

    According to recent reports, human Rights Watch submitted an amicus curiae brief in June 2025 in one of the five cases brought to the Kahramanmaraş administrative courts by the Turkish Medical Foundation. The brief drew on Human Rights Watch research findings in a 2024 report documenting the serious public health and environmental concerns arising from the existing operation of the power plant.

    It has been revealed that the Kahramanmaraş Administrative Court No. 3 ruling cancelled the project, drawing on two court-commissioned expert reports to inform its decision. In setting out its grounds for cancellation the court cited these reports. Human Rights Watch cited some of the same grounds in its amicus brief. The grounds included the lack of a proper air quality assessment and the superficial assessment of chronic exposure to air pollution, including inadequate consideration given to the cumulative impacts from a public health standpoint in the environmental impact assessment approving the expansion.

    The court expert reports noted in particular that the impact assessment had not properly evaluated health impacts for at-risk groups such as children, older people, and individuals with chronic illnesses, and made no comprehensive assessment of the long-term respiratory and cardiovascular risks posed by chemicals and pollutants released from fossil fuel combustion.

    Further grounds in the expert report included the finding that the authors had falsified the number of participants recorded at a public participation meeting about the project in the context of the environmental impact assessment procedure, and that a majority of those who did attend opposed the coal power plant expansion.

    According to recent reports, in Türkiye’s Aegean region, clearance of the Akbelen forest and olive groves to pursue coal mining to supply two old coal power plants is proceeding, despite local opposition. In 2025, coal accounted for 33.9 percent (120.86 billion kWh) of Türkiye’s total electricity generation. Türkiye is one of the only four European countries, together with Poland, Kosovo, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, that have not committed phase out coal or set a timeline for ending coal-fired power generation.

    The National Energy Plan announced by the Turkish government on November 5 aims to advance electrification and energy independence by 2040 but sets no concrete target to phase out fossil fuels despite ambitious commitments to invest in renewable energy and electrification.

    Recent findings suggest that türkiye is not alone in sending mixed signals on climate leadership, however, Australia, COP31’s co-host and one of the biggest coal exporters, is also pursuing fossil fuel expansion at home, exposing the growing disconnect between both countries’ international climate rhetoric and their domestic energy policies. While the emphasis both countries have placed on electrification is an important step toward climate action, their failure to address the need to halt new fossil fuel projects and ensure a fair and equitable phase-out of fossil fuels risks undermining this progress.

    In a recent development, “The COP31 co-hosts Türkiye and Australia should adopt resolute policies to end the expansion of upcoming fossil fuel projects and set a clear timeline for phasing out existing coal power plants,” Bayram noted. “Cancelling coal projects that are still in the permit procedure could be an important step toward this.”.

    #8403. Indonesia: US Aid Cuts Fuel HIV

    📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1152 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hrw ↗ Open Full Page

    Indonesia: US Aid Cuts Fuel HIV

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1152 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that (Jakarta) – United States foreign aid cuts in 2025 abruptly ended essential community-based HIV prevention and care for lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) people in Indonesia who already face discrimination and arbitrary arrest, Human Rights Watch stated in a report released today.
    • Recent findings suggest that the 33-page report, “‘We Want to Be Treated as Human’: Impact of US Foreign Aid Cuts on HIV/AIDS Prevention and Care in Indonesia,” documents the Trump administration’s dismantling of the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and finds that it eliminated services for people at greatest risk of HIV, creating additional barriers to testing, prevention, and lifesaving treatment.
    • Impact of US Foreign Aid Cuts on HIV/AIDS Prevention and Care in Indonesia.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that (Jakarta) – United States foreign aid cuts in 2025 abruptly ended essential community-based HIV prevention and care for lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) people in Indonesia who already face discrimination and arbitrary arrest, Human Rights Watch stated in a report released today. Globally, more than 170,000 additional people are estimated to have died in one year because of the cuts to HIV/AIDS response, which especially affect populations at increased risk of HIV infection.

    Recent findings suggest that the 33-page report, “‘We Want to Be Treated as Human’: Impact of US Foreign Aid Cuts on HIV/AIDS Prevention and Care in Indonesia,” documents the Trump administration’s dismantling of the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and finds that it eliminated services for people at greatest risk of HIV, creating additional barriers to testing, prevention, and lifesaving treatment. The Indonesian government and international donors should urgently restore support for community-led HIV/AIDS services.

    Impact of US Foreign Aid Cuts on HIV/AIDS Prevention and Care in Indonesia.

    Download the full report in English.

    Annex I: Human Rights Watch Letter to the Indonesia Ministry of Health.

    Annex II: Human Rights Watch Letter to the Indonesia Ministry of Home Affairs.

    Annex III: Human Rights Watch Letter to the US Department of State.

    “The Trump administration’s gutting of USAID eliminated services that helped LGBT people in Indonesia get lifesaving services in an environment of stigma, discrimination, and fear,” mentioned Julia Bleckner, senior health researcher at Human Rights Watch. “Indonesia and international donors should restore care before more people are pushed out of treatment, more people die from preventable causes, and decades of progress against HIV is lost.”.

    Human Rights Watch interviewed 35 people living with HIV, outreach workers, activists, academics, aid recipients, and staff of nongovernmental organizations in Jakarta, Depok, and Serang in November 2025 and June 2026, and reviewed budget and policy documents.

    Human Rights Watch wrote to the US Department of State and to the Indonesian Department of Health and the Ministry of Home Affairs on September 24, 2026, regarding the impact of the cuts, but has received no responses.

    The US government’s foreign assistance tracking website states that obligated funds for HIV in Indonesia dropped from $11.9 million in fiscal year 2024 to $7.9 million in FY25. These cuts included all USAID-funded community-based prevention and care directed to LGBT populations.

    Indonesia’s HIV/AIDS epidemic is concentrated among populations that face severe barriers to care due to discrimination and stigma. HIV prevalence is about 0.4 percent among the general population, compared with 22 percent among men who have sex with men and 25 percent among transgender people. Yet the most recent comprehensive spending data show that in 2020 only 0.1 percent of Indonesia’s domestic HIV/AIDS spending went to programs for men who have sex with men, and none went specifically to transgender people. International donors covered 98 percent of HIV programming for these populations, who frequently rely on community-led and outreach services due to the discrimination and stigma they encounter in public health facilities.

    According to recent reports, outreach workers had distributed condoms and information about preexposure prophylaxis, helped people obtain confidential testing, accompanied clients to clinics, and supported adherence to antiretroviral treatment. They also paid for transportation and tests, advocated for these patients with clinic staff, and trained health workers to provide respectful care. Outreach workers said that since the cuts they had lost contact with clients, that some clients were late collecting medication or missing doses, and that local organizations no longer had the capacity to track new infections and treatment interruptions.

    It has been revealed that “Just leaving the house as a trans person is scary,” noted a transgender outreach worker living with HIV. “Without an outreach worker, the person will be alone and they won’t get care.”.

    It has been revealed that the loss of services coincided with the Indonesian government's increasing attempts to criminalize and target at-risk groups. Indonesia’s newly introduced criminal code, which took effect on January 1, 2026, makes all consensual sex outside heterosexual marriage a criminal offense subject to complaints by close family members, effectively criminalizing same-sex conduct for the first time. Police raid private gatherings and have used possession of condoms and purported HIV medication as evidence of crimes. These practices deter people from carrying prevention supplies, gathering for outreach, testing for HIV, and seeking treatment.

    Industry observers note that transgender people whose identity documents do not reflect their gender identity may be publicly called by a former name, opening them up to humiliation or discrimination. Outreach workers have accompanied patients, advocated respectful treatment, helped people obtain identification and health insurance, and trained clinic staff. With funding gone, many people must now navigate these obstacles alone.

    A gay activist living with HIV spoke about the severity of the crisis: “If you are LGBT and living with HIV, it’s the end of the story. You are doomed.”.

    Sources indicate that after the US funding cuts, several governments promptly followed with their own. France, Japan, Germany, and others withdrew from financing the HIV/AIDS response. In June, Winnie Byanyima, executive director of the United Nations organization UNAIDS, said of the global funding cuts: “There’s no question that this is the most serious disruption in the HIV response since the world came together to fight this disease.”.

    It has been revealed that the Indonesian government should adequately fund HIV prevention and care for men who have sex with men and transgender people, support community-led organizations, ensure consistent supplies of antiretroviral medicines, and train health workers to provide nondiscriminatory care. The government should also repeal discriminatory laws, end unlawful raids targeting LGBT people, stop using possession of condoms and HIV medication as evidence of crimes, investigate and appropriately punish abuses by the police, and protect LGBT people from vigilante violence.

    In a recent development, the US government should ensure continuity and timely release of funding for the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) created in 2003, disclose the impact of terminated programs, and withdraw its “Promoting Human Flourishing in Foreign Assistance Policy,” which restricts work to protect the rights of transgender people and other issues. International donors should increase contributions to the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria and directly support LGBT-led community organizations responding to HIV in Indonesia.

    “Indonesia should stop targeting LGBT people and start investing in the community services proven to prevent HIV and keep people in treatment,” Bleckner noted. “The United States and other donors should help rebuild these lifelines, not abandon the people who depend on them.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Geneva, November 12, 2026) – The failure of states to take decisive action on autonomous weapons next week at the Review Conference of the Convention on Conventional Weapons (CCW) would leave civilians dangerously exposed to rapidly advancing military technologies, Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, and Stop Killer Robots stated today.
    • The CCW is an international treaty prohibiting or restricting the use of weapons considered excessively injurious or whose effects are indiscriminate.
    • In a recent development, “Autonomous weapons systems are no longer a hypothetical future threat, with reports growing that they are already being tested, integrated, and deployed,” remarked Carolyn Horn, Programme Director for Law and Policy at Amnesty International.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Geneva, November 12, 2026) – The failure of states to take decisive action on autonomous weapons next week at the Review Conference of the Convention on Conventional Weapons (CCW) would leave civilians dangerously exposed to rapidly advancing military technologies, Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, and Stop Killer Robots stated today.

    The CCW is an international treaty prohibiting or restricting the use of weapons considered excessively injurious or whose effects are indiscriminate. Governments should use the upcoming meeting to begin time-bound negotiations for a upcoming protocol to the CCW on autonomous weapons systems, also known as killer robots. Such a protocol should impose legally binding prohibitions and controls on these fast-evolving, potentially catastrophic technologies.

    In a recent development, “Autonomous weapons systems are no longer a hypothetical future threat, with reports growing that they are already being tested, integrated, and deployed,” remarked Carolyn Horn, Programme Director for Law and Policy at Amnesty International. “Meaningful constraints need to be put in place now. Countries should seize this moment to open negotiations on new international law before these systems become entrenched in military practice, with potential to lead to devastating consequences for humanity.”.

    Recent findings suggest that from November 16 to 20, 2026, states parties to the CCW will meet in Geneva for one of the most consequential Review Conferences of the era, the three organizations remarked. After more than a decade of expert discussions, states have clarified the core issues and identified the elements needed for a latest international treaty. The Review Conference, held only every five years, is a critical opportunity to convert that work into concrete action.

    In a recent development, autonomous weapons systems select and engage targets based on sensor processing rather than human input. Their use raises profound ethical, legal, humanitarian, and security concerns, including the risk of unlawful killings, indiscriminate attacks, algorithmic bias, and erosion of accountability for violations of international human rights and humanitarian law. The organizations warned that widespread deployment could weaken long‑standing legal restraints designed to protect civilians and limit harm during armed conflict.

    The Review Conference will consider the final report of the Group of Governmental Experts (GGE) on Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems, a United Nations body set up under the CCW, which sets out “elements for an instrument” that could serve as the basis for negotiations. This provides a clear pathway for states to adopt a one‑year mandate to negotiate a latest protocol prohibiting certain autonomous weapons systems and regulating others, the organizations mentioned.

    It has been revealed that “After years of stalemate largely due to some states weaponizing the consensus-based decision-making under the CCW against meaningful progress, states parties finally have an opportunity to move from discussion to action,” noted Verity Coyle, deputy crisis, conflict and arms director at Human Rights Watch. “A time‑bound treaty negotiation process is the only credible way to ensure UN member states effectively respond to the existential dangers posed by autonomous weapons systems.”.

    In a recent development, geopolitical instability and accelerating military investment in artificial intelligence make action at this Review Conference imperative, the groups remarked. Without a mandate to negotiate a treaty, discussions would continue to stall even as research, development, and subsequent operational deployment are expanding.

    The organizations also urged states to ensure meaningful civil society participation throughout the Review Conference, noting that independent expertise has been essential to clarifying risks, shaping policy options, and keeping humanitarian concerns at the center of discussions.

    “The Convention on Conventional Weapons was created to address emerging threats, and this Review Conference should show that it still can,” remarked Nicole van Rooijen, Executive Director of Stop Killer Robots. “States parties to the convention have a responsibility to act before autonomous weapons systems reshape warfare in ways that undermine human dignity and civilian protection.”.

    A brutal attack on trans women sex workers in Buenos Aires has sparked outrage in Argentina, raising questions about hate-motivated violence and the responsibility of public officials to protect groups vulnerable to discrimination.

    Industry observers note that although consensual adult sex work is not a crime under Argentine national law, Buenos Aires imposes administrative penalties on offering sexual services in unauthorized public spaces. President Javier Milei’s administration has repeatedly attacked gender diversity initiatives, dismantled institutions and policies promoting equality, and tried to restrict access to gender-affirming healthcare for trans youth. Government officials have also used stigmatizing rhetoric about LGBT people.

    In a recent development, public discourse and government actions matter. When political leaders portray minorities as threats, dismiss their identities, or weaken protections against discrimination, they risk reinforcing prejudice and creating an environment in which hostility becomes socially acceptable.

    Recent findings suggest that argentina has notably long been a regional leader on protections based on sexual orientation and gender identity, adopting landmark legislation recognizing same-sex marriage and diverse gender identity. Yet despite these significant steps, trans people continue to face entrenched discrimination and violence.

    Following the attack, trans sex workers and activists are demanding not only accountability but meaningful protection, effective steps to reverse the discrimination that limits employment opportunities, and an end to harassment. Argentina’s leaders should respond to their calls with public policies that uphold the dignity and rights of trans people and sex workers.

    Indonesia: Alleged Excessive Force Against Protesters

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, (London) – Indonesian authorities should impartially investigate allegations that military and police officers on November 10, 2026, responded to youth protests with excessive force and may have deliberately provoked violence, Human Rights Watch remarked today.
    • Student and activist groups had organized protests across several cities against corruption, environmental damage, and the rising cost of living on National Heroes’ Day, November 10, and called for the resignation of President Prabowo Subianto.
    • It has been revealed that “Indonesian authorities should impartially investigate alleged excessive force against largely peaceful protesters in Yogyakarta,” said Meenakshi Ganguly, deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, (London) – Indonesian authorities should impartially investigate allegations that military and police officers on November 10, 2026, responded to youth protests with excessive force and may have deliberately provoked violence, Human Rights Watch remarked today. Security forces in the city of Yogyakarta on Java Island used rubber bullets, water cannons, and tear gas to disperse protesters, injuring several and detaining over 150 people, including children.

    Student and activist groups had organized protests across several cities against corruption, environmental damage, and the rising cost of living on National Heroes’ Day, November 10, and called for the resignation of President Prabowo Subianto. Police stated that some protesters hurled rocks and firebombs at the provincial parliament building, leading to heavy security force deployment with columns of troops and armored vehicles.

    It has been revealed that “Indonesian authorities should impartially investigate alleged excessive force against largely peaceful protesters in Yogyakarta,” said Meenakshi Ganguly, deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “Reports that the police instigated some of the worst violence are especially troubling.”.

    That evening, the generally peaceful protest turned violent when a group gathered outside Yogyakarta’s Legislative Council building in the Jalan Malioboro area, a commercial hub and tourist landmark. After clashes broke out between protesters and police, security forces used water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds as the protests continued into the early hours of the morning.

    A medical volunteer stated the violence began around 7 p.m. when a group of unidentified people—suspected plain-clothes policemen and government supporters—appeared and began attacking students and other protesters. She said she saw security forces, both in uniform and in civilian clothes, assaulting at least 40 people then arresting them.

    “I saw one person being beaten by 10 people,” she told Human Rights Watch. “They kicked and stomped on him repeatedly. There was blood everywhere. I tried to protect the victim and was hit as well.” She remarked that while she was recording the violence, an unidentified person seized her phone, and some men sexually harassed her when she was trying to assist victims.

    A Papuan student was struck in the face by a teargas canister while riding a motorcycle through the area around Tugu Yogyakarta, the city’s main landmark. “I fell, immediately felt disoriented, and lost consciousness,” he said. Police subsequently arrested him and then took him to the hospital.

    Overnight, police entered Gadjah Mada University to track down protesters and arbitrarily rounded up people, accusing them of violence.

    In a recent development, “Tear gas was fired at us,” stated Diana Nuraini, a student journalist from Pijar Press at the university. “Teargas canisters were also launched about 100 meters from [nearby] Panti Rapih Hospital. The crowd ran into the campus.” One protester suffered a skull fracture near the campus, while eight students were arrested.

    Ova Emilia, the Gadjah Mada University rector, criticized acts of violence against university community members.

    The Yogyakarta Legal Aid Institute (LBH) reported that at least 13 demonstrators could not be contacted in the aftermath of the clashes and expressed concern they had been unlawfully detained. The Yogyakarta Representative of the Office of the Ombudsman of the Republic of Indonesia urged police not to treat protest as a criminal offense.

    The Yogyakarta Regional Police remarked officers detained 157 people suspected of involvement in rioting and damage to public facilities. Police said they recovered Molotov cocktails, firecrackers, gasoline, and bladed weapons. On November 11, police released 154 people.

    The national police chief, Gen. Suyudi Ario Seto, and the House of Representatives deputy speaker, Sufmi Ahmad Dasco, visited the protest site on November 11 and remarked that those responsible for using dangerous items such as Molotov cocktails and bladed weapons would be identified and prosecuted. General Seto said that the police would assess whether the demonstration was “genuine” or a deliberate attempt to foster violence. Neither criticized abuses by the security forces.

    Under National Police Chief Regulation No. 8 of 2009, police officers are prohibited from using force on the pretext of serving the public interest or restoring order during riots.

    Industry observers note that the violence in Yogyakarta occurred amid large-scale deployments of security forces in several cities ahead of National Heroes’ Day, which commemorates a battle for independence in 1945. In Jakarta, the government brought in tens of thousands of military personnel, while in Surabaya, a joint force of nearly 3,000, including 500 military personnel, was deployed to secure two demonstration sites.

    The right to peaceful assembly and protest is a fundamental right protected under international human rights law. The United Nations Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials provide that officers should apply nonviolent means as much as possible and only use force when strictly necessary. When using force, law enforcement officials should exercise restraint and act in proportion to the seriousness of the offense and to the legitimate objective to be achieved.

    The 2020 UN Guidance on Less-lethal Weapons in Law Enforcement provides that tear gas should only be employed when necessary to prevent further physical harm and should not be used to disperse nonviolent demonstrations.

    The deployment of military forces for crowd control—responsibilities that ordinarily fall to the police—raises serious concerns about the misuse of force and the intimidation of protesters, Human Rights Watch said.

    “Indonesia has a long history of military repression, and it’s critical for the Prabowo government to ensure that there is no return to past practices,” Ganguly remarked. “The government should recognize that its response to protests and respect for human rights will shape how the world views Indonesia’s democracy.”.

    The Mayflower Extract

    📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (575 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that the 2026 Federalist Society Convention is a wrap.
    • Recent findings suggest that I think much of the press coverage failed in attempt to to consolidate a very broad movement into a few paragraphs.
    • Sources indicate that I think there are a range of opinions about how the conservative legal movement should respond to the current political situation.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that the 2026 Federalist Society Convention is a wrap. I have attended every NLC since I was a 1L in 2006 (except for the cancelled COVID year). At each convention, the focus is a bit different but the overall takeaway is similar. There is a healthy a mix of timeless topics and topical topics, with an infusion of the political landscape of the day. It is very hard to capture the essence of a convention by watching some or even all of the panels, as so much business transpires in the hallways and at the bars.

    Recent findings suggest that I think much of the press coverage failed in attempt to to consolidate a very broad movement into a few paragraphs. For example, CNN blared "After blue wave, Federalist Society is ready to move on from Trump." Really? Secretary of State Marco Rubio delivered the Olson Lecture, White House Counsel Will Scharf had a fireside chat, White House Advisor May Mailman discussed over-regulation, and Gene Hamilton favored restrictive immigration policy on behalf of America First Legal Foundation. Plus there were other members of the administration from the EPA and OLP.

    Sources indicate that I think there are a range of opinions about how the conservative legal movement should respond to the current political situation. I don't think anyone actually knows exactly what to do. The midterm election, of course, was the elephant in the room. I offered my take here. A lot can happen over the next two years.

    It has been revealed that I'm flummoxed by the uproar about the commemorative coins celebrating Calais, Slaughter, and other decision. These were in fact generational wins at the Supreme Court. Justice Scalia established overruling Humphrey's Executor as a founding principle of FedSoc. Since the 1980s, conservatives--including John Roberts--have seen the Voting Rights Act as violating the Constitution. And West Virginia v. B.P.J. was such an obvious outcome--except perhaps at CNN. Plus, this was the swaggiest NLC I've ever been to. There was an entire room to pick up FedSoc swag. The coins were a nice touch.

    Industry observers note that perhaps the biggest disruption at the convention was the groundstop. My flight home Saturday evening was cancelled, as were many others. I was able to get a room at the Mayflower for another day. Fortunately, one of the few remaining perks of United status is priority rebooking during "irregular operations." I was originally scheduled to fly home Sunday evening around 7:30 p.m. The United App has a latest feature that lets you be on standby for up to three flights at once without losing your confirmed seat. United will send you a text notifying you that a seat opened up on an earlier flight, and you have twenty minutes to accept it. I was able to jump from the 7:30 p.m. flight to the 12:50 p.m. flight. A few hours later, I was given a chance to jump from the 12:50 p.m. flight to the 10:58 a.m. flight. For both of these flights, I was number one on the standby list. Around 5:00 a.m., I was offered the chance to move to the 8:20 a.m. flight, but I was sleeping and missed the window. The system worked very well. And without my status, I doubt I would have been able to get the earlier flight. As things turned out, the 12:50 p.m. flight was cancelled. I will get home today.

    France: Sweeping Bill Threatens Peaceful Protest, Rights

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1226 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that (Paris, November 12, 2026) – A draft law that passed in its first reading by the French Senate on October 27, 2026, contains measures that would severely undermine the rights to peaceful assembly and freedom of expression, and are incompatible with France’s human rights treaty obligations, Human Rights Watch noted today.
    • Industry observers note that “Penalizing people engaged in their right to peaceful protest is the wrong answer to tackling violent disorder in France,” remarked Eva Cossé, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch.
    • The bill was introduced by the government on September 16 under a fast-track procedure.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that (Paris, November 12, 2026) – A draft law that passed in its first reading by the French Senate on October 27, 2026, contains measures that would severely undermine the rights to peaceful assembly and freedom of expression, and are incompatible with France’s human rights treaty obligations, Human Rights Watch noted today. The so-called “vandals pay” bill is now pending review by the National Assembly.

    Industry observers note that “Penalizing people engaged in their right to peaceful protest is the wrong answer to tackling violent disorder in France,” remarked Eva Cossé, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch. “Lawmakers in both houses should reject this problematic bill entirely.”.

    The bill was introduced by the government on September 16 under a fast-track procedure. It was pushed forward and significantly toughened by opposition conservative senators in response to weeks of nationwide high school protests over what students see as the government’s under-investment in their education, and the violence that took place alongside school and cost-of-living protests on October 17 that included significant clashes with law enforcement and widespread looting and property damage across France. The bill builds on the momentum of legislation adopted in August to address serious public disorder, developed in response to concerns over illegal dance parties, football-related rioting, and racing vehicles on the streets.

    While the purpose of the current legislation is ostensibly to address and deter violence and property damage, the text adopted by the Senate introduces measures that pose a serious threat to human rights, including the essence of the right to peaceful protest, Human Rights Watch noted. The French authorities have also failed to put forward evidence that existing criminal justice measures are insufficient to address violent disorder or criminal damage.

    Sources indicate that the draft law provides for joint civil liability for property damage during a protest. It would allow courts to order individual participants, including the parents of children who participated, to pay up to €10,000 in damages—or perform community service—whether or not the individual committed acts of violence or caused the damage.

    Sources indicate that people could be penalized simply for “knowingly” participating in an “unlawful assembly” (attroupement), defined in the French criminal code as “any gathering of people on a public highway or in a public place that is likely to disturb public order,” or for failing to disperse after the police issue orders for a second time. Legal commentators have remarked that the requirement for prior dispersal orders is not an effective safeguard, because such orders are in practice either not issued or are not sufficiently audible.

    Being present during a protest considered an unlawful assembly, or failing to leave the area fast enough following police orders to disperse, could trigger severe financial consequences. The bill requires prosecutors to share suspects’ identities with prefects, the interior minister’s local representative, and local authorities so they can pursue damage claims in civil court, even if the prosecutor has decided not to pursue criminal charges.

    In a recent development, the bill would allow criminal penalties of up to one year in prison and a €15,000 fine for organizers of banned protests, and six months in prison and a €7,500 fine for participants, or in some cases, a summary fine of €500 to avoid prosecution. Existing law allows six months in prison and a €7,500 fine only for protest organizers. Punishments can be doubled for people who cover their faces. The bill also gives prefects the power, without prior judicial oversight, to preemptively ban individuals from protests for 24 hours on the basis of police intelligence or evidence of repeated or serious violent behavior during the three preceding years.

    The bill broadens existing security and administrative measures that jeopardize rights, Human Rights Watch said. To recover court-ordered damages, after a conviction, the draft law allows the state to confiscate social security payments—child benefit, early-years child allowance, family supplement, family support allowance, back-to-school allowance, and solidarity allocation—from parents to pay for damages caused by their children under age 18. This measure risks disproportionally affecting low-income households.

    It would also allow the authorities to deny social housing to adults convicted of “unlawful assembly” or serious public order offenses near residential buildings in the preceding three years, and to seek to evict families from social housing if a member of the household repeatedly engages in such acts.

    The bill broadens existing powers under counterterrorism, child protection, and drug laws, that oblige tech companies, without a court order, to take down within 24 hours online content that authorities deem capable of provoking offenses, under the threat of blocking the site and massive fines.

    Industry observers note that the draft law extends the use of video surveillance to monitor public gatherings, and permits algorithmic processing to potentially identify protesters, measures first introduced for the Paris 2024 Olympics. Senators added a upcoming provision to authorize recording and transmitting footage from drones and other police aircraft to track, identify, and prosecute individuals for protest-related offenses, raising the prospect of general drone surveillance by police. Previous laws imposed stricter conditions on police drone deployments to monitor protests.

    This draft law is part of a broader trend of erosion of the civic space and the rule of law in France, Human Rights Watch stated.

    The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the European Convention on Human Rights, to which France is a party, protect the rights to peaceful assembly and association and to freedom of expression. Although the treaties allow for restrictions on these rights, they must be subject to strict tests of necessity and proportionality.

    In particular, the European Court of Human Rights has consistently emphasized that peaceful participants in a protest may not be held responsible for reprehensible acts committed by others, and that “this is true even when the demonstration results in damage or other disorder.” The court has previously found France violated this standard, ruling that even a lower end disciplinary sanction imposed on a protester who did not commit any culpable act, was not permitted. The court reminded France that in seeking to pursue a legitimate aim, the result must not to be to discourage people, for fear of sanctions, from being able to express their views including through peaceful protest.

    Punishing individuals for the actions of others, and jailing and fining people simply for engaging in peaceful protest as a means of deterring violent disorder are not legitimate restrictions on those rights. The other measures in the bill also raise human rights concerns including in relation to the right to a fair trial, the right to privacy, and the rights to social security and housing.

    In a recent development, “This bill is a human rights disaster,” Cossé said. “It undermines human rights that are central to a functioning democracy, punishes people for the actions of others and not only risks, but seems designed to deter, participation in peaceful protest.”.

    This news release has been corrected to accurately reflect commentators’ concerns about the criminal code’s requirements for dispersing a protest.

    • Recent findings suggest that in 2013, I interviewed 37-year-old Lívia from Budapest for Human Rights Watch’s report Unless Blood Flows which documented domestic violence in Hungary.
    • The new government package would strengthen enforcement of restraining orders, make misuse of intimate images a distinct criminal offense, and provide special protections for victims and survivors of intimate partner violence in criminal proceedings.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that on November 12, Hungary's Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced that his government intends to ratify the Council of Europe Convention on preventing and combatting violence against women and domestic violence, also known as “Istanbul Convention,” as part of a comprehensive package of measures seeking to strengthen protection and dignity of women and girls. It is a welcome and timely step.

    Recent findings suggest that in 2013, I interviewed 37-year-old Lívia from Budapest for Human Rights Watch’s report Unless Blood Flows which documented domestic violence in Hungary. She told me she had repeatedly called the police about her husband’s abuse and that the police even witnessed him beating her. Officers told her they could do nothing “unless blood flows.” Other women described similar responses, some telling me they had stopped calling for help.

    The new government package would strengthen enforcement of restraining orders, make misuse of intimate images a distinct criminal offense, and provide special protections for victims and survivors of intimate partner violence in criminal proceedings.

    The government also intends to end the prescription requirement for emergency contraception and the requirement under the so-called “heartbeat decree” that forces women seeking abortions to listen to any embryonic or fetal cardiac activity. It also aims to help women and girls in need to access menstrual products. These measures are urgently needed and very welcome.

    In a recent development, parliament, then controlled by a two-thirds majority from the Fidesz/KDNP ruling coalition, blocked an earlier ratification effort in 2020. Ratification commits Hungary to binding standards on preventing violence, protecting victims and survivors including those without secure immigration status, and holding perpetrators accountable.

    According to recent reports, alongside ratifying the convention, authorities should develop an implementation proposal in consultation with victims, survivors and women’s rights organizations; Police should receive specialized training on intimate partner violence, how to assess risks and to act on credible threats, and how to work with the courts to enforce protection orders. And the government should adequately fund sufficient numbers of shelter spaces, legal aid, and counseling services nationwide. To ensure reforms are effective, authorities should collect and publish data on police responses and breaches of protection orders to facilitate assessment.

    Industry observers note that the real test of these reforms will be when a survivor like Lívia next calls the police for help. No one should have to bleed before police and authorities act.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Joseph Bottum in the Wall Street Journal explains how "Anti-Zionism" turned him into a Zionist.

    I am a Zionist because on the ground, activist anti-Zionism is becoming indistinguishable from antisemitism. Whatever linguistic differences exist, whatever distinctions activists say they hold, the metonymy that glides from shouting against Israel to violence against Jews is too easy, too well-greased, for public figures to refuse blame for the rhetoric that allows it. Jews who own restaurants labeled "zio" and "disgusting humans" in Philadelphia, a Jewish center's mural painted over with "Zionism is not welcome" in California, a synagogue's signs defaced with initials for the slogan "All Zionists Are Bastards" in Maryland—the tropes of anti-Zionism slip rapidly into the tropes of antisemitism. . . .

    Industry observers note that I have come to full-blown Zionism—because that is the most coherent way to oppose the activists, left and right, who aim at something profoundly antithetical to the American spirit. "It is now no more that toleration is spoken of, as if it was by the indulgence of one class of people, that another enjoyed the exercise of their inherent natural rights," George Washington wrote in 1790 to a Jewish congregation. "For happily the Government of the United States, which gives to bigotry no sanction, to persecution no assistance requires only that they who live under its protection should demean themselves as good citizens, in giving it on all occasions their effectual support.".

    Industry observers note that this doesn't mean uncritical agreement with everything the government of Israel does. It means that our current forms of activist anti-Zionism would make the U.S. a place wildly different from the one Washington envisioned. . . .

    As long as we have a social politics in which antisemitism wears the cloak of anti-Zionism, the duty of Americans is clear: When Jews are targeted as Jews, the solidarity the moment requires from the rest of us is standing up as Zionists.

    • According to recent reports, emirati authorities detained the residents, who had been in the UAE between 2 and 40 years, between March and May.
    • It has been revealed that “Emirati authorities appear to be rounding up residents simply based on their religious beliefs as Shia Muslims in a largely Sunni country rather than providing any evidence of wrongdoing, while trampling over people’s due process rights,” mentioned Joey Shea, senior UAE researcher at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that (Beirut) – Emirati authorities have arbitrarily detained at least five Shia Muslim foreign residents since the United States and Israel carried out military strikes on Iran in February 2026, Human Rights Watch said today. The detentions appear to be based on the detainees’ religious identity.

    According to recent reports, emirati authorities detained the residents, who had been in the UAE between 2 and 40 years, between March and May. They have not been brought before a judge or formally charged, three informed sources said.

    It has been revealed that “Emirati authorities appear to be rounding up residents simply based on their religious beliefs as Shia Muslims in a largely Sunni country rather than providing any evidence of wrongdoing, while trampling over people’s due process rights,” mentioned Joey Shea, senior UAE researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The authorities should immediately release anyone targeted because of their religion.”.

    Between September and October, Human Rights Watch interviewed the three sources and reviewed CCTV footage of a raid on the firm that one of the detainees owned. The detainees’ and sources’ names are withheld for fear of reprisals against them and their relatives.

    The sources said that security authorities asked at least one of the detainees about his religious affiliation before his arrest and interrogated at least one family member about their religious views. Another Shia community member warned at least one detainee and a relative to leave the UAE.

    On March 23, Emirati state security arrested one man, 44, in Sharjah, as he was in his car near his home at midnight, a relative mentioned. He was not allowed to contact a lawyer or his family that night.

    The following night, Emirati security forces took the man to his family home for a search. The officers took money, jewelry, books, and credit cards, his relative said. Security forces did not inform him or his family of any charges against him.

    It has been revealed that the relative remarked that a worker at the mosque they attended had warned him to leave the country in June 2025. The government “viewed us Shias as sleeper cells,” he said. The relative left the UAE two days later.

    The same mosque worker asked the man on March 20, 2026, whether he had “any problems with the police.” The relative noted this was how the man had been warned, but he did not understand it as a warning and stayed in the UAE.

    Emirati security forces also raided the man’s organization. Human Rights Watch reviewed CCTV footage reportedly from the site, timestamped March 24. The footage demonstrates two men, one in a baseball cap and the other in traditional clothing, entering the man’s company at around 9:19 p.m. and searching offices. One enters a room with computers and appears to tamper with the equipment.

    According to recent reports, the man was held in incommunicado detention for three days, then allowed to make a one-minute call to his family. He has been allowed two-minute calls every two weeks since. Prison authorities end the call if he attempts to reveal information about his case or location. His family has not been allowed to visit.

    On September 14, the family learned through his lawyer that he had been moved to the notorious al-Sadr prison in Abu Dhabi, the source said. Emirati authorities have held the prominent Emirati human rights defender Ahmed Mansour there since 2017 in conditions that may amount to torture.

    On the evening of April 22, state security officials arrested a 38-year-old foreign Shia national at a money transfer office near his home in Sharjah, a relative noted. They took him to his home and searched it, seizing money, gold jewelry, and his laptop without informing his family of any charges.

    Industry observers note that on May 29, Emirati authorities summoned his wife for questioning, including about her husband’s religious views, the source remarked. Authorities released her at 10 a.m. on May 30.

    According to recent reports, emirati authorities held him in incommunicado detention, allowing him to make a brief call on June 3, the source stated. Authorities allow him one brief phone call every week in which he cannot reveal the details of his detention. The authorities told his wife on October 6 that he had been moved to al-Sadr prison. She has not been allowed to visit him.

    Recent findings suggest that emirati authorities arrested three more foreign Shia nationals between April and May, a third source related to the men stated. Security forces raided the homes of all three men, confiscated their passports and money, and did not inform them of the charges against them, the source said.

    Sources indicate that during one of the raids, a security officer asked a family member about their religion, job, and income, the source noted. Before the arrest, one of the men received a phone call from Emirati authorities asking about a religious concern and the names of his associates, the source said.

    The three men have been allowed to make a brief call every ten days without revealing their location, the source mentioned. Prison authorities end the call if they attempt to give details about the case or detention conditions.

    Sources indicate that “We all left the UAE in one day,” a family member said. “We wrapped up over 30 years in the UAE… We gave the UAE our hopes, dreams, and children. We sang their national anthem in schools. We loved this country.”.

    Industry observers note that human Rights Watch has previously documented Emirati authorities arbitrarily detaining and forcibly disappearing and expelling other Shia residents, without due process, between 2009 and 2021. Reuters reported that thousands of Pakistani Shia residents have been deported from Gulf Arab states since February 28. During the same period, Emirati authorities revoked visas of Iranian families who have lived in the UAE for decades and banned Iranian nationals from transiting through the UAE, media and UAE Foreign Ministry reports said.

    Sources indicate that on February 28, the United States and Israel carried out airstrikes on Iran, and Iran retaliated with strikes against Israel and Gulf states. Iran has since rolled out thousands of drones and missiles at Gulf countries, with the largest number striking the UAE.     📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Between August 28 and September 16, US military forces intercepted and destroyed eight Ecuadorian fishing vessels, alleging that they served as floating refueling stations for drug-trafficking boats. They detained 146 of the 160 crew members and transferred them to Ecuadorian authorities, who charged 90 with “unlawful association.”.

    According to recent reports, since Human Rights Watch reported on the operations, Ecuadorian courts have acquitted 40 people. In an October 29 judgment reviewed by Human Rights Watch, a Manta judge acquitted eight fishermen from a vessel named the Don Rufo. The prosecution’s own witnesses, including Ecuadorian police and Navy officials, testified that no illicit items were recovered, and that they knew of no prior investigation linking the fishermen to organized crime.

    The judge stated the prosecution rested on a “chain of successive presumptions.” He admonished the prosecutor for pursuing an unsupported case and closed it.

    Sources indicate that the ruling follows an October 7 decision acquitting another 32 crew members from the Conquista II and María Candelaria on similar grounds. The judge found no evidence supporting the unlawful association charge and admonished prosecutors for pursuing the case without even minimal evidence.

    Out of the 160 crew members intercepted by the US, 110, that is 70 percent, are now free and without charges. Fourteen were not brought before Ecuadorian authorities, 56 were released without charge by a judge, and 40 were acquitted. Fifty others are awaiting trial.

    Neither Ecuador nor the United States has publicly disclosed the operation’s legal basis, including the criteria used to intercept the vessels, and in some cases destroy them, or evidence linking the boats to drug trafficking.

    According to recent reports, the US Congress should ensure oversight over these and other US security operations in and near Ecuador, where people have been detained without evidence and, in some cases, tortured by Ecuadorian personnel. Organized crime in Ecuador is a serious threat that should be addressed with an effective and rights respecting security and justice policy, not with human rights violations.

    This article has been updated to reflect the correct number of crew members detained and overall intercepted by US military forces.

    Latest Update: Philippines: US Tech Hub to Displace Hundreds

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1423 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Manila) – The Philippine government’s impending construction of a technology manufacturing hub under the US government’s “Pax Silica” initiative will displace hundreds of Indigenous peoples and farmers in Tarlac province, Human Rights Watch stated today.
    • The Philippine government will provide the land—including territory inhabited for generations by the Indigenous Aeta tribe—while investors, including US companies, will finance the infrastructure and facilities.
    • “Indigenous communities and small farmers fear they will be unlawfully displaced by the semiconductor hub,” stated Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Manila) – The Philippine government’s impending construction of a technology manufacturing hub under the US government’s “Pax Silica” initiative will displace hundreds of Indigenous peoples and farmers in Tarlac province, Human Rights Watch stated today.

    The Philippine government will provide the land—including territory inhabited for generations by the Indigenous Aeta tribe—while investors, including US companies, will finance the infrastructure and facilities. The framework agreement between the Philippines and the United States is yet to be signed.

    “Indigenous communities and small farmers fear they will be unlawfully displaced by the semiconductor hub,” stated Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The Philippine government should follow domestic laws and international standards that protect land rights.”.

    Human Rights Watch visited two affected sites in Capas in October 2026—Sapang Kawayan in Barangay Aranguren and Sitio Binyayan in Barangay O’Donnell—and spoke to 11 residents.

    It has been revealed that pax Silica is a US initiative that began in December 2025 to secure US technology supply chains. Under Pax Silica, the US State Department has brokered agreements with other countries and international entities on issues including mineral extraction, technology hardware manufacturing, communications infrastructure, software and platforms, and trade. The Philippines joined Pax Silica in April 2026 and agreed to host a 1,618-hectare semiconductor hub in the town of Capas in Tarlac province, north of Manila, largely for mineral processing and semiconductor manufacturing.

    In a recent development, the hub development is led by the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA), a Philippine government body created by law in 1992 that owns and administers areas previously used as US military bases, including territory occupied and used by the Aeta communities. The Pax Silica hub will be inside New Clark City, a government and residential complex built by BCDA in 2018. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. mentioned the government was “terribly excited” about Pax Silica.

    Under the 1997 Indigenous Peoples Rights Act (IPRA), Indigenous peoples have the right to lands, inland waters, coastal areas, and natural resources that they have “occupied [and] possessed since time immemorial” and can receive Certificates of Ancestral Domain Title. Extended delays in processing titles have left many Indigenous communities vulnerable to encroachment.

    The Aeta Hungey tribe in Sapang Kawayan has been seeking recognition of its ancestral domain since 1994 and refiled in 1999 after the Indigenous Peoples Rights Act took effect, but has not yet received title.

    Industry observers note that in early July 2026, BCDA officials sent letters to Sapang Kawayan residents, informing them that the land they were occupying would be “affected by the project New Clark City” and inviting them to discuss it at their Clark office without mentioning the planned hub. These letters and BCDA personnel visits to measure their lands caused immediate concern among residents.

    On July 23, BCDA declared that the hub would be built inside New Clark City.

    Chieftain Petronila Capiz-Muñoz stated that visiting BCDA officials orally informed residents that they will be relocated by December and provided information that left residents worried: “They said the upcoming homes would be 30-square meters per family… We complained; they’d be turning us into a matchbox. We farm here, otherwise how would we have sustained our lives here all this time? We don’t rely on aid.”The former BCDA president, Joshua Bingcang, confirmed to media in September that 40 Aeta Hungey homes would be “pushed a little bit,” affecting about 200 people. BCDA officials told the House of Representatives on November 11 that the relocation site would be in Sitio Binyayan, Barangay O’Donnell, three kilometers from Sapang Kawayan, without access to the streams they use for water.

    “We do not want to give up our community,” Muñoz remarked. “How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood? This is where we source our water, this is where we plant.”.

    According to recent reports, BCDA has not provided a detailed map, but independent geographers who have been supporting the Aeta have mapped the proposed hub based on available information. It indicates Sapang Kawayan inside the hub and Sitio Manabayukan, where a different tribe—the Ayta Mag-Antsi—live, just outside.

    The village head of Barangay O’Donnell, Wendell Mercado, said that he and the mayor of Capas asked BCDA to hold a public consultation. “To this day, we are still waiting,” he said.

    The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples states that Indigenous peoples have the right to participate in decision-making in matters that would affect their rights, and that governments shall seek to obtain their free, prior, and informed consent before adopting measures that may affect them. The declaration also provides that Indigenous peoples shall not be forcibly removed from their lands or territories. Although the declaration is not a binding treaty, the Philippines supported the declaration when the UN General Assembly adopted it in 2007.

    Available information indicates that BCDA never secured the free, prior, and informed consent of Aeta community members, Human Rights Watch said.

    Philippine farmers in Sitio Binyayan have also received BCDA letters and were orally informed that their farmland, but not their homes, would be affected. BCDA confirmed to Mercado in a July 16 letter that 92 “affected persons in the Pax Silica project” live in Barangay O’Donnell, including the farmers in Sitio Binyayan.

    It has been revealed that “The farmers called me, confused as to why people were measuring their land, forcing them to sell, giving them 30 days, or 10 days to respond to the offer,” stated Mercado. “It’s so cruel.”.

    The farmers stated that BCDA officials offered compensation worth 300,000 pesos (about US$4,700) per hectare, which they said they do not want to accept. “I really don’t want to, but what can you do if you’re just a small person who stands alone, what will happen to you?” said Rafael Dela Cruz, a 72-year-old farmer. Mander Matias, another farmer, said he even refused the letter of invitation: “The next time they visited me, there were many of them, six of them, really reiterating they’d take my farmland.”.

    Generations of farmers have lived in Sitio Binyayan, but they have no land titles despite the 1988 Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Law, which awards landless farmers the right to collectively own lands they till. The Public Land Act also gives rights to people who have been “in open, continuous, exclusive and notorious possession and occupation of alienable and disposable agricultural lands of the public domain for at least 20 years.”.

    Industry observers note that in case of a refusal to take the compensation offer, the right-of-way act states that the government must initiate court expropriation proceedings. “If there’s a way, we will fight so the government won’t take it,” noted one farmer.

    Farmers who have cultivated land for generations even without formal ownership may have internationally protected rights and interests in continued use of that land. These touch upon the obligations of states under the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, particularly the rights to food and an adequate standard of living. Governments have obligations to recognize and protect legitimate tenure arrangements, prevent arbitrary dispossession, and ensure that any eviction complies with international human rights standards.

    The UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, in a general comment on land rights, stated: “For peasants, access to land and other productive resources is so crucial for the realization of most rights under the Covenant that it implies for them a right to land. … It includes the right to have access to, sustainably use and manage land to achieve an adequate standard of living.”.

    The farmers—who have little formal education—fear they do not have the skills for the jobs promised by Pax Silica. “Farming is the only job we know,” said Wilfredo Gutierrez, 60. Another farmer said that, “Money is temporary; land is forever.”.

    Philippine authorities should protect affected people’s access to land and livelihoods and ensure any agreements made under Pax Silica respect their human rights.

    It has been revealed that “The Philippine government shouldn’t be trampling the rights of Indigenous peoples and farmers in its haste to attract foreign technology investment,” Buan stated. “Development officials should provide information to people who will be affected and genuinely consult them before proceeding with the hub.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    “Our children are able to go to school again.” That's how one Liberian parent described the impact of a newly introduced government policy banning school registration fees for kindergarten through sixth grade. The policy is already helping families who struggled to pay the fees, removing a longstanding barrier to their children's education.

    Since the policy took effect in September, Liberian child advocates have interviewed parents in four counties to assess whether schools were complying with the ban. The findings offered encouraging early indications: nearly all 20 parents interviewed knew about the policy and had enrolled their children without paying registration fees.

    Parents described the difference the policy was making. “The decision by the ministry is so good,” stated a parent in Bong County. “It enables our children to go to school free without worry.” Another parent whose children had previously been out of school said, “For some of us that don’t have money, it helps us a lot.”.

    A Human Rights Watch investigation in late 2025 and early 2026 found that registration fees caused severe hardship for many Liberian families and put education out of reach for others. Some parents told us they had delayed enrolling their children for years because they could not afford the fees. Children described being sent home from school over unpaid fees. Others said they had dropped out of school or turned to child labor.

    It has been revealed that the upcoming policy has the potential to benefit nearly half a million families, helping children start school on time, stay in school, and avoid child labor. But ensuring that all schools comply will be essential. One parent noted that despite the policy, a primary school demanded registration fees for his three children. When he said he couldn't pay, he was told, “No registration, no school.”.

    The government should monitor and enforce compliance with the fee ban, extend the policy to junior and senior secondary schools, and address other costs—including transportation, uniforms, and textbooks—that keep children from attending school.

    In a recent development, liberia has taken a significant step toward making the right to education a reality for all children, regardless of their financial circumstances. Making education accessible to all children will help reduce inequality and create opportunities for generations to come.

    #8384. Industry News: Is Current Second Amendment Jurisprudence Premised Upon a "Misquote"?

    📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1481 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Is Current Second Amendment Jurisprudence Premised Upon a "Misquote"?

    📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1481 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This past week, the New York Times published an article by Mike McIntire and Eli Murray alleging that a "pivotal legal test" for determining whether gun control laws are constitutional is "based on a misquote." Yet it appears it is the NYT's reporters who misfired.
    • When the Supreme Court begins weighing the constitutionality of assault-weapons bans next month, the justices will be guided by the court's own precedent: a landmark ruling that such restrictions are allowed only if a firearm is both "dangerous and unusual.".
    • For nearly two decades, judges across the country have invoked this language to strike down gun-control laws.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This past week, the New York Times published an article by Mike McIntire and Eli Murray alleging that a "pivotal legal test" for determining whether gun control laws are constitutional is "based on a misquote." Yet it appears it is the NYT's reporters who misfired.

    Here is the article's basic claim:.

    When the Supreme Court begins weighing the constitutionality of assault-weapons bans next month, the justices will be guided by the court's own precedent: a landmark ruling that such restrictions are allowed only if a firearm is both "dangerous and unusual.".

    For nearly two decades, judges across the country have invoked this language to strike down gun-control laws. It is a pivotal legal test.

    It is also based on a misquote.

    Justice Antonin Scalia, writing for the majority in the 2008 case, District of Columbia v. Heller, attributed the "dangerous and unusual" language to Sir William Blackstone, an 18th-century English jurist whose writings became the basis for much of American law.

    But in his seminal 1769 treatise, "Commentaries on the Laws of England," Blackstone referred to weapons that were "dangerous or unusual," suggesting that a gun did not need to be both in order to be restricted.

    Sources indicate that but is there actually an error in the opinion? Here is the paragraph from Heller in which the alleged misquotation occurs, with the allegedly offending sentence underlined:.

    We also recognize another crucial limitation on the right to keep and carry arms. Miller remarked, as we have explained, that the sorts of weapons protected were those "in common use at the time." 307 U. S., at 179. We think that limitation is fairly supported by the historical tradition of prohibiting the carrying of "dangerous and unusual weapons." See 4 Blackstone 148–149 (1769); 3 B. Wilson, Works of the Honourable James Wilson 79 (1804); J. Dunlap, The New-York Justice 8 (1815); C. Humphreys, A Compendium of the Common Law in Force in Kentucky 482 (1822); 1 W. Russell, A Treatise on Crimes and Indictable Misdemeanors 271–272 (1831); H. Stephen, Summary of the Criminal Law 48 (1840); E. Lewis, An Abridgment of the Criminal Law of the United States 64 (1847); F. Wharton, A Treatise on the Criminal Law of the United States 726 (1852). See also State v. Langford, 10 N. C. 381, 383–384 (1824); O'Neill v. State, 16 Ala. 65, 67 (1849); English v. State, 35 Tex. 473, 476 (1871); State v. Lanier, 71 N. C. 288, 289 (1874).

    Note that the claim, with the quotation, is followed by a "See" string cite (followed, in turn, by a "See also" string cite of further authorities). If they were at all familiar with how legal citation works, this should have given the NYT reporters pause. As others have noted, the Supreme Court's style guide indicates that the "see" signal is not used for direct quotations. Rather it indicates that "the cited authority is basic source material supporting, although not stating, the text proposition" (emphasis added). Blackstone is cited first not because it is the dominant source but because the authorities are listed in chronological order.

    What makes matters worse is that it appears the authors of the story were informed of all this before the story went to press. One of the story authors contacted John Bash, who clerked for Justice Antonin Scalia the term Heller was decided and worked on the case, and Bash explained all of this to the reporter, as Bash details in this LinkedIn post. Bash writes:.

    Industry observers note that this is stunning. A recent article in The New York Times claims that District of Columbia v. Heller--the 2008 Supreme Court case holding that the Second Amendment protects an individual right to own a firearm--contains a "misquote" of Blackstone. The supposed misquote is the phrase "dangerous and unusual weapons" in this passage:.

    We also recognize another vital limitation on the right to keep and carry arms. Miller mentioned, as we have explained, that the sorts of weapons protected were those "in common use at the time." 307 U. S., at 179. We think that limitation is fairly supported by the historical tradition of prohibiting the carrying of "dangerous and unusual weapons.".

    Sources indicate that that passage is followed by the signal "See" and numerous citations, the first of which is Blackstone. The Blackstone source says "dangerous or unusual weapons" ("or" instead of "and"), but a number of the sources that follow say "dangerous and unusual weapons," in addition to sources that use the Blackstone disjunctive framing.

    Back in October the Latest York Times reporter reached out to me about this, presumably because I was the law clerk for Justice Scalia on Heller. I immediately wrote back with a full on-the-record explanation of why there was no misquote. Yet the article does not refer to my explanation at all and asserts with no qualification that it was a misquote.

    So if anyone is interested, I have posted my email below verbatim. I will also put in the comments my follow-up when the reporter asked me a question.

    Here is the e-mail Bash sent to the reporter working on the story:.

    Hi Mike, thanks for reaching out on this.

    Even if I remembered any conversation with Justice Scalia about this particular point (which I don't), it would not be ethical for me to share private conversations I had during my clerkship wth Justice Scalia about the substance of opinions.

    But just as an appellate lawyer, I don't see the matter. If the historical sources are mixed on the conjunctive or disjunctive framing, then it is true that there is an historical tradition of prohibiting weapons that are both dangerous and unusual, the narrower category that is encompassed by either framing. The fact that Blackstone is the first citation is just because the treatise citations are in chronological order (consistent with making a point about historical tradition), followed by case citations also in chronological order. The introduction of the treatise list with a "See" signal (rather than no signal) means that the quoted phrase is not necessarily a direct quote from each source (or any source)—as with the "See also" signal for the cases. And assuming that it's correct that the conjunctive sources all trace back to a single 18th Century treatise, that would not detract from the point that learned commentators had endorsed or applied that test through early American history, which is the point the text is making about historical tradition.

    Here is the first follow-up e-mail Bash sent "in response to the reporter asking if he could quote me and whether the opinion purposefully omitted the Hawkins treatise quoted in the conjunctive-framing sources so that Blackstone would be first":.

    Sure. Happy to take a look at the quote.

    Can't speak to the thinking that went into the opinion, but I really doubt that. As I mentioned earlier, I don't think the provenance of the limitation is particularly relevant; the point was that commentators had recognized it throughout history. For example, in a Fourth Amendment case, a court might make the point that the curtilage rule—that the immediate vicinity of the home is considered part of the home—has been recognized through American history, citing late Eighteenth Century and Nineteenth Century treatises and cases. Even if that rule could be traced back to a single uncited treatise, that's not really the point. It's that courts and commentators endorsed it and so that history and tradition informs the constitutional analysis.

    Industry observers note that and all that aside, I just think it is implausible that the paragraph would be understood differently if Blackstone had been the second citation rather than the first—especially since Hawkins was himself a very influential legal commentator (if I recall correctly). I've never heard of a court or litigant attributing weight to the order of sources subject to the same signal (e.g., "See"), which would seem to me especially unwarranted when the sources are presented chronologically (and so there is an obvious explanation for the ordering other than importance). As I noted before, I think all the sources together make clear a uniform historical tradition of prohibiting dangerous and unusual weapons, the category encompassed by all of their articulations of the rule.

    Interestingly enough, the NYT article concludes citing a scholar affirming Bash's contention that, as the relevant passage claims, "there is an historical tradition of prohibiting weapons that are both dangerous and unusual," or as some would put it, those arms that are "unusually dangerous." Insofar as some lower courts have applied a different analysis, it is not clear to me how that is attributable to Scalia's language in Heller, or the contested passage.

    The NYT story ends citing a scholar for the proposition that "relying on centuries-old legal precedents requires understanding how earlier generations used language." One might conclude that those writing on the Supreme Court should heed a similar admonition.
