    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that three foreign nationals are accused of using artificial intelligence to pose as corporate executives and lawyers in a fraud scheme that allegedly took in over $129 million. (Image from Shutterstock).

    Federal prosecutors in Manhattan have unsealed an indictment accusing three foreign nationals of using artificial intelligence to pose as corporate executives and lawyers in a fraud scheme that allegedly took in over $129 million, according a story published Friday in The Guardian.

    It has been revealed that according to the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Newly introduced York, Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan and Guy Sheetrit manipulated voices and images to deceive employees at companies around the world between 2024 and 2026. Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain this summer, and Sheetrit was taken into custody in the United Kingdom in September.

    Sources indicate that according to prosecutors, the scheme worked in two stages. First, the defendants allegedly posed as a company executive and told employees they needed help with a confidential financial matter. Employees were then directed to contact attorneys at a major international law firm, whom the defendants also allegedly impersonated, and to wire large sums as instructed.

    Sources indicate that prosecutors allege that the defendants stole nearly $5 million from a Missouri hospital system, about $2.7 million from a Rhode Island bank, roughly $3 million from a California hospital system, more than $4.6 million from a Massachusetts mutual fund, about $5 million from a Florida pet food firm, and over $11 million from a U.K. technology company. The defendants have been indicted on charges relating to wire fraud, money laundering, conspiracy and identity theft.

    According to recent reports, funds were allegedly routed to accounts in countries including the U.S., Spain, Portugal, Greece, the United Arab Emirates, Singapore, Austria, Slovakia and China, then converted to cryptocurrency to hide their origin and split among conspirators. Prosecutors say Soall and Hazan used several aliases, including “Rocky Balboa,” “Superman Cash” and “Ron.”.

    U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said in a statement that while AI holds great promise, it can also be turned to criminal ends.

    #8376. No Pseudonymity in Ex-Associate's Sexual Assault Claim Against Major Law Firm

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1423 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    No Pseudonymity in Ex-Associate's Sexual Assault Claim Against Major Law Firm

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1423 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Blank Rome LLP, the opinion was issued under seal in May, but just unsealed last week (at my behest):.
    • In a recent development, plaintiff is an attorney who filed a detailed, 197-paragraph Complaint under the pseudonym "Jane Doe" against Defendant Blank Rome LLP …, her former employer, alleging claims for sex discrimination, hostile work environment, and retaliation pursuant to Title VII ….
    • Doe's Complaint similarly details Associate A's professional background, including his law school and year of graduation, and the names of his prior law firms.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    From Judge W. Scott Hardy in Doe v. Blank Rome LLP, the opinion was issued under seal in May, but just unsealed last week (at my behest):.

    In a recent development, plaintiff is an attorney who filed a detailed, 197-paragraph Complaint under the pseudonym "Jane Doe" against Defendant Blank Rome LLP …, her former employer, alleging claims for sex discrimination, hostile work environment, and retaliation pursuant to Title VII …. Her claims arise from the Firm's purported failure to respond appropriately after Doe allegedly was sexually assaulted by another associate attorney, identified in the Complaint as "Associate A," while they and others were socializing at the home of a Firm partner on a Saturday evening after leaving a graduation party hosted by another partner of the Firm. The Complaint details Doe's professional background, including where she attended law school, when she began her employment at the Firm, and the type of law she practiced while at the Firm.

    Doe's Complaint similarly details Associate A's professional background, including his law school and year of graduation, and the names of his prior law firms. The Complaint does not identify Doe by her own name, nor does it identify by name "Associate A" or any other attorney at the Firm. The only person identified by name in the Complaint is the Firm's Chief Human Resource Officer, who is named 24 times….

    The court noted the strong presumption in favor of parties litigating in their own names, and concludes this presumption wasn't rebutted here:.

    A mere showing of embarrassment or economic harm is not enough [to justify pseudonymity]. Rather, there must be a showing of both: (1) fear of severe harm, and (2) that the fear of severe harm is reasonable. When a litigant sufficiently alleges that he or she has a reasonable fear of severe harm from litigating without a pseudonym, the Third Circuit instructs that "district courts should balance the plaintiff's interest and fear against the public's strong interest in an open litigation process." {"[T]he Court is sympathetic to Plaintiff's concerns, and understands that, unfortunately, victims of sexual harassment and assault often face ridicule and further harassment when they file lawsuits or otherwise publicly disclose their allegations, especially in the internet age. However, these concerns, while certainly reasonable, are not sufficient to outweigh the public's right to access court proceedings."} ….

    It also expressed its concern about one-sided pseudonymity (a concern that some courts weigh heavily and others don't, as this article lays out in detail):.

    Doe is not the only party exposed to public humiliation and reputational harm. The Firm itself and its chief human resource officer have been identified publicly in the Complaint (and other current or former Firm attorneys have been described with sufficient identifying indicia in the Complaint to be identified by implication). Permitting Doe to proceed pseudonymously while the Firm defends itself publicly, particularly where there seems to be material factual disputes between the parties, presents an unfair asymmetry that also weighs against anonymity ….

    In a recent development, doe … plead[ed] highly detailed factual averments in her 197-paragraph Complaint that inform the reader of her law school, her prior law firm affiliation, the month and year she commenced work at the Firm, the general nature of her practice, and the date of her departure from the Firm. Similar factual averments were plead regarding Associate A, including by naming three firms at which Associate A had previously been employed. The Firm's identity has also been revealed both in the caption of the Complaint and in its detailed factual averments. Many of these averments supply indicia of identity of both Doe and Associate A even though they would not have been necessary pursuant to applicable pleading standards set forth in Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a)…. [This] weighs against anonymity.

    Recent findings suggest that the court also mentioned Doe's argument "that there are social stigmas that attach to victims of sexual assault and harassment, and that using her real name would subject her to 'ridicule, scrutiny, and alienation' by her own colleagues and would jeopardize her reputation within the local legal community," but responded that (1) "Doe is an adult, not a minor" and that (2) she "does not contend that she would forgo her claims if her motion to proceed pseudonymously were to be denied and there is no indication from the record that Doe would be deterred from proceeding if she identified herself." For whatever it's worth, plaintiff dismissed the case a few months after the decision denying pseudonymity, presumably pursuant to a settlement. Because of the dismissal, neither Doe nor Associate A were publicly identified in the docket.

    Finally, the court discussed in some detail the question "whether either party stakes out their respective positions here for illegitimate ulterior motives," a factor that some courts' multi-factor tests for pseudonymity mention but that rarely gets much elaboration:.

    Doe contends that the Firm would have no reason for opposing her motion other than her bald accusation that such opposition is being undertaken to "perpetuate ongoing harm" and to "further humiliate her, undermine her professional reputation and potentially deter her form continuing with this litigation." Doe proffers no particularized basis for this accusation beyond her objection that the Firm's General Counsel circulated an internal communication within the Firm itself about Doe at or near the time her Complaint was filed, to contend that the Firm opposes her pending motion for illegitimate and "nefarious" motives, further suggesting the Firm is opposing it as a "litigation tacti[c].".

    Industry observers note that for its part, the Firm similarly accuses Doe of illegitimate tactical motives for seeking to proceed pseudonymously despite filing a factually detailed Complaint with enough content for a reader to know or surmise the identities of its personnel so that she may "cast[] aspersions upon the character of others about whom she publicly alleges information that makes them readily identifiable." The Court notes, too, that Doe filed her detailed Complaint without seeking leave to file it under seal or in redacted form and did file it on the public docket approximately a week before seeking to proceed pseudonymously. {In saying so, the Court is not suggesting that proceeding in this manner is inappropriate or that that seeking to file such a pleading under seal or in redacted form is the better course. Though, there may be circumstances when doing so is advisable.}.

    In a recent development, on the present record, the Court discerns no illegitimate or nefarious motives by either party. In reaching this conclusion, the Court notes that there are known and anticipated vicissitudes and adversities to litigants involved in presumptively public judicial proceedings.

    Here, the Defendant is a large, multi-office law firm and Doe is one of its former lawyers. Both parties are experienced with the judiciary and presumably familiar with the reasonably foreseeable extrajudicial consequences litigation has on parties and witnesses.

    Moreover, lawyers representing their clients in court, such as counsel of record here, are expected to prepare and file pleadings and briefs on court dockets for legitimate purposes that subject them to potential sanctions if such filings are presented for an improper purpose. Of course, pleadings and briefs having a proper purpose may also have attendant collateral adverse extrajudicial consequences, but such consequences do not necessarily transform a proper filing into an improper one. Sometimes those boundaries are clear, sometimes blurred. {Here, on the present record, the Court detects some potential tactical and strategic efforts by both parties within the context of otherwise legitimate and proper lawyering but cautions both parties and their counsel to stay within those boundaries going forward.}.

    As noted above, Doe has a legitimate interest in seeking to proceed pseudonymously to avoid potential embarrassment, humiliation, emotional distress, and professional reputational harm. Those are reasonable and understandable concerns. Likewise, the Firm's opposition to Doe's request is grounded on the desire for symmetry in the transparency of the Court's administration of justice so that Doe may not be permitted to "hurl accusations … from behind 'a cloak of anonymity.'" The Court agrees that such rationale, rooted in fairness and tethered to the presumption of transparency in court proceedings, is also reasonable and legitimate. Accordingly, the parties' respective motives neither favor nor disfavor Doe's continued anonymity.

    And the court concluded by noting "the presumption in favor of open judicial proceedings," and by saying that, "[w]hile the parties here are not public officials or public bodies, the strong presumption in favor of open judicial proceedings is not outweighed by the other … factors considered above.".

    #8374. School Board Member Seeks "Better Sense of How" Church "Approaches Issues of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Around Their Messaging" …

    School Board Member Seeks "Better Sense of How" Church "Approaches Issues of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Around Their Messaging" …

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2204 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, this happened when the board was deciding whether to allow a long-term lease of space on weekends to a church, pursuant to a policy that allowed such leases for community groups generally.
    • Plaintiff Matt Gioia moved his family from Colorado to Maine in the summer of 2020 to start a newly introduced church.
    • Gioia sought space from the Hermon School Department, which generally opens up its facilities to various groups:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, this happened when the board was deciding whether to allow a long-term lease of space on weekends to a church, pursuant to a policy that allowed such leases for community groups generally. And, a federal court held Friday, this violated the First Amendment. Some excerpts from the long opinion in Pines Church v. Hermon School Dep't, by Chief Judge Lance Walker (D. Me.):.

    Plaintiff Matt Gioia moved his family from Colorado to Maine in the summer of 2020 to start a newly introduced church. Gioia was born in Waterville, Maine, and lived in Guilford, Maine until he graduated high school and joined the military at seventeen years old. Initially, Gioia's church—The Pines Church—gathered at his home. In March of 2021, The Pines Church began holding Sunday morning services at a movie theater in Orono, Maine, pursuant to a month-to-month lease arrangement. As the Church grew, Gioia began to look for a new space that could accommodate a larger group.

    Gioia sought space from the Hermon School Department, which generally opens up its facilities to various groups:.

    This policy provides that "[s]chool facilities should be made available for appropriate community use when such facilities are not required for their primary purposes: the instruction of students and related school activities." The policy distinguishes between "occasional or short-term use of school facilities," which "shall be authorized by the school principal," and "long-term rental or lease," which "shall be authorized by the Hermon School Committee upon the recommendation of the Superintendent of Schools.".

    Industry observers note that but the Hermon School Committee (which consisted of "Committee Chair Jesse Keith, Vice Chair Karen Shorey, Stephanie Oiler, Haily Keezer, and Christopher McLaughlin") denied the Church's request for a year-long or six-month lease, allowing only a month-to-month lease (which appeared to be inadequate for the church, given its need for a stable meeting location). Here's part of the summary of the facts, based on the bench trial that the court held:.

    The next day [after a hearing], a former committee member emailed Keith and Shorey to share her belief "that it is not in our communities [sic] best interest to lease one of our school facilities to any religious organization," warning that "[t]here is a quiet movement in our country by some conservative religious groups who are actively working to soften the boundaries between church/state, starting with our schools" and that granting the Church a lease would lead to "a slippery slope." She wondered how the Hermon School Department would have to respond to a similar request from "an Imam who wants to open a mosque," in light of the "precedent" set by a lease to The Pines Church.

    Her email concluded with unintended irony: "There's a reason why the founding fathers wrote the constitution the way they did." Keith and Shorey denied at trial that this email influenced their decision-making with respect to the Church's lease request, which I find implausible in light of the trial record….

    McLaughlin reached out to [HSD Superintendent Micah] Grant and explained that he "had a few additional questions" for Gioia:.

    McLaughlin "wanted to get a better sense of how [T]he Pines Church approaches complications of diversity, equity, and inclusion around their messaging around some key issues relevant to marginalized communities." Those questions requested information about the Church's views on same-sex marriage, "[a]ccess to safe and affordable abortion," "[a]ccess to gender affirming medical care," "[c]onversion therapy for LGBTQIA+ individuals (youth and adults)," and "[i]nclusive sexual education and access to birth control for youth." ….

    [At a later meeting, High School Principal Brian] Walsh took the podium and explained that he had several reservations about the Church's request. He first explained that it would be difficult to find the staff to clean the building on Sunday afternoons. But apart from this, he continued:.

    [W]e've never had a long-term lease, at least over my twenty-one years here, and I think there's a number of reasons we don't do that. There's a lot of variables we just don't know. No question our students should come first, our program should come first.

    We also don't know or have the sense of how this will be promoted, to [the student representative's] question. If you put Hermon High School's name with a church or another organization with different beliefs than the school has, I see that as problematic. But again, that's where I sit and that's where I stand. Doesn't mean this organization won't do a great job, doesn't mean they won't support, hopefully, our mission as well. I just don't know, there are too many variables with that and again we have not—we have never done that.

    What I would not want is for students to feel like a group organization that we are renting to, their vision or their mission is now ours. And there's a blurred line when it comes to that. I have nothing against this church, this reverend, or anything, we've just never said yes to something like this, so probably why it's in your hands, because you guys get to make that decision. I'm looking at the facility and some other variables, so that's kind of—that's where I come from….

    [At a later meeting,] Oiler then made a motion for a month-to-month lease, citing concerns about the number of people and cleaning the space afterwards, which she was careful to emphasize had nothing to do with the organization. Keezer asked if they could ask Gioia about how the Church kept its current space clean. Oiler curiously protested that this was not about the Church (when in fact it was ostensibly about the Church and its janitorial readiness) but any organization, then adding the less than persuasive point that if fifteen people got the stomach bug at the same time, someone would have to clean it up. {At trial, Oiler testified that she had in mind a specific incident that occurred at Hermon Middle School when one of her children was a student there.}.

    It has been revealed that given the shortage of custodial staffing, she explained, she was concerned about the number of people who would be coming in and out of the building. She suggested that the Committee investigate its current rental arrangements, to make sure those organizations were paying what they should considering the costs associated with hosting them. What this had to do with the Church's application remains a mystery….

    It has been revealed that the Free Speech Clause prohibits restrictions on access to limited or designated public fora that "discriminate against speech on the basis of viewpoint," including on the basis that the viewpoint in question is a religious one. In other words, if a public school's facilities are available for public use, a religious organization cannot be denied access to those facilities because it is a religious organization. Similarly, the Free Exercise Clause "bars even 'subtle departures from neutrality' on matters of religion," and therefore prohibits "denying a generally available benefit solely on account of religious identity," unless such denial is "justified … by a state interest 'of the highest order.'" ….

    By virtue of Policy KG, the Hermon School Department made its facilities available "for appropriate community use when such facilities are not required for their primary purposes: the instruction of students and related school activities," including for "long-term rental or lease." Having done so, the School Department could not then reject the Church's lease application because it is a religious organization or because of disagreement with its religious viewpoints, without violating the First Amendment, as Plaintiffs contend has occurred….

    The court concluded that the Department indeed violate the Church's First Amendment rights, by discriminating against it based on its "religious viewpoint or out of animus against that viewpoint":.

    I start with the question of whether a majority or significant block of committee members demonstrated bad motive.

    I find without any difficulty that McLaughlin exhibited bad motive. McLaughlin's intrusive questions expressed viewpoint related concerns towards Plaintiffs, and he was the only member not to vote in favor of any lease term, including the month-to-month arrangement. Although his email itemizing political and cultural questions occurred early in the process, before the Committee received any advice from counsel, and even though he testified that he harbored no ill will toward Plaintiffs after gaining more information about them, it strikes me as very likely that McLaughlin lacked objectivity when it came to the question of leasing school space to the Church.

    According to recent reports, it appears that he based his decision directly on the Plaintiffs' religious beliefs and its associated political and culture ethics that flow from those beliefs, and the religious nature of the proposed use. McLaughlin would have approached a lease request differently had it been presented by an organization that shared his personal beliefs.

    In a recent development, I also find that Oiler was unable to overcome concerns over constitutionally permissible school-church association, notwithstanding the legal advice the Committee received, and Grant repeatedly emphasized. Though less openly hostile than McLaughlin, Oiler's attitude toward the Church was anything but neutral…. [I]t struck me during her testimony, and I find, that Oiler's chief concern was that the tenant would be a Church. This was made only more obvious by protesting far too much that this was not about the Church but instead fear, for example, of mass vomiting epidemics and the platoon of janitorial assistance that would be required to mop it up.

    Industry observers note that all of her other concerns about space and the like were definitively answered by Grant as not remotely problematic. I find based on the trial record that her motive was to avoid the School's association with the Church for its religious views. The First Amendment is designed to avoid discriminatory treatment of religious organizations in their enjoyment of the benefits of public facilities based on their religious beliefs or speech. For this reason, I find that Oiler, like McLaughlin, voted as she did based on "bad motive.".

    I find that Plaintiffs have proved that bad motive prevented Shorey from approaching the lease question fairly. Shorey, at her deposition, suggested that she believed McLaughlin's culture war email was appropriate, even though she later sought to characterize it as inappropriate at trial.

    It may be that Shorey believes that a School Committee should have the discretion to question any organization about how its values align with what she sees as the school community's values, to the extent a school community has its own conflicting body of values that can be reduced to a catechesis—perhaps it does. But support for a process that involves examining a prospective tenant's views on religious issues, simply because the prospective tenant is a church, tends rather starkly to highlight the questioner's lack of neutrality toward religion….

    Although I find that a majority of voting members exhibited bad motive which would itself be sufficient to end the inquiry, my findings should be considered also in context of the discussion during the deliberative process, which included rather openly anti-religious organization sentiment expressed by Walsh at least as he served as a voice of the school community and the discomfort it might experience especially if the beliefs of the School, whatever those might be, and the Church were at loggerheads. Even if the record had not established a majority of voting members acting out of bad motive, it would still have constituted a significant bloc of legislators and "circumstances suggesting the probable complicity of others," as well as "evidence indicating that the legislators bowed to an impermissible community animus.".

    It has been revealed that recall that Walsh passed along student concerns about the Church qua church using the School and when asked if any spoke supportively of the idea, Walsh reported that none had. Also recall the email received by Keith Shorey from a former committee member. That former member insisted that this was all a Trojan horse coordinated by conservative Christian groups to blur the line between school and religion. What would the Committee do, the former committee member queried, if an Imam were to set up shop at Hermon High School next?

    The standard is one of likelihood, and on that basis, I find that at least three of the five decision makers acted under the influence of bad motive and in so doing violated the Plaintiffs' rights under the First Amendment….

    Sources indicate that defendant points to the majority vote in favor of a month-to-month use arrangement as proof of the lack of bias on the part of its committee members. I agree with the Church that this was not persuasive evidence of a lack of bad motive but to the contrary, is evidence of bad motive. The Committee knew the Church required a more fixed arrangement before uprooting itself from its then current location than a month-to-month arrangement provides. This appears to me to have been an offer designed to be rejected not one born of wholesome support for the Free Exercise Clause….

    Industry observers note that bethany Onishenko and Robert H. Tyler (Tyler Law LLP), Erin Mersino and Julianne E. Fleischer (Advocates for Faith and Freedom), Joel L. Oster (Oster Law Firm), Wenonah Wirick (Conley & Wirick, P.A.) represent plaintiffs.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By ABA Governmental Affairs Office.

    It has been revealed that the ABA is inviting all members to help set its advocacy priorities for the 120th Congress through the ABA Legislative Priorities Survey. (Al Drago/Bloomberg).

    The historic November midterm elections have rewritten the political landscape in Washington, D.C., setting the stage for Democratic control of both chambers of Congress and a potentially consequential legislative agenda.

    The 120th Congress convenes in early January to confront the challenges of governing in a divided government. It is important that the American Bar Association is ready to engage and to have a strong voice at the table on challenges affecting the legal profession and the administration of justice. As a upcoming balance of political power takes shape during President Donald Trump’s final two years in office, the ABA is inviting all members to help set its advocacy priorities for the 120th Congress through the ABA Legislative Priorities Survey.

    Recent findings suggest that participation in the survey is available exclusively to ABA members. By participating in the survey, you have the opportunity to have your voice heard on issues that matter most to the legal profession and the justice system.

    Sources indicate that the survey opened Nov. 6 and will close on Dec. 4. Most ABA members have received an email with a personalized link to the survey. But any member can access the survey at ambar.org/priorities. Members can also expect an invitation from ABA President Barbara Howard, and the link will be distributed via the ABA’s social media. With a newly introduced political landscape taking shape in Washington, the ABA Legislative Priorities Survey will play an key role in ensuring that the association’s advocacy efforts reflect the concerns and priorities of our members.

    Recent findings suggest that the 2026 survey has an even more streamlined ranking system than the last priorities survey. Members are being asked first to prioritize challenges aligned with the ABA’s current priorities and policies. Members then respond to open-ended questions designed to identify additional policy issues the ABA should consider prioritizing, including those that might require the development of upcoming policies.

    The survey takes less than 10 minutes to complete, and your input will be indispensable to informing the ABA’s legislative priority-setting process.

    Recent findings suggest that the survey results will be presented to the Board of Governors at the ABA Midyear Meeting in early 2027. The Board will consider ABA member input, along with the following criteria, to determine whether an glitch should be made a priority:.

    • Breadth and strength of the ABA interest • Importance to the practice of law • Public perception of the profession • Opportunity for impact • Potential for achievement • Timeliness of issue • Expertise of lawyers on the issue • Importance to society • Importance to the administration of justice.

    The 120th Congress presents new opportunities for the ABA to advance policies vital to our members and our legal profession and to work with policymakers as they contend with issues that could have far-reaching consequences for our nation.

    Please take a few minutes to complete the survey now. Your input will help strengthen the ABA’s voice in Washington, ensuring that the legal profession’s priorities are heard and its commitment to the rule of law amid the upcoming political realities in Washington, D.C., remain a powerful force in our nation’s capital.

    Sources indicate that this report is written by the ABA Governmental Affairs Office and discusses advocacy efforts by the ABA relating to issues being addressed by Congress and the executive branch of the U.S. government. Follow @ABAGrassroots on social media.

    This column reflects the opinions of the author and not necessarily the views of the ABA Journal—or the American Bar Association.

    Breaking: The Virginia Bar Shows More Sense than the Williamsburg Commonwealth Attorney

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (568 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that readers may recall the story of Karyann Parkinson, the Williamsburg mother (and law student) who was criminally prosecuted for letting her young child walk to a neighborhood pond to collect goose feathers.
    • As a consequence of her conviction, Parkinson was added to Virginia's Child Abuse and Neglect Registry, where she will be listed for the next seven years.
    • In a recent development, prosecutors brought the charges against Parkinson while she was preparing to take the Virginia Bar exam, and her conviction came while her character and fitness application was under review.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that readers may recall the story of Karyann Parkinson, the Williamsburg mother (and law student) who was criminally prosecuted for letting her young child walk to a neighborhood pond to collect goose feathers. As I recounted in The Free Press, Parkinson was convicted of contributing to the delinquency of a minor, a first-degree misdemeanor in Virginia, because the authorities thought her child was too young to take a walk. The judge sentenced her to six-months in jail, but suspended the sentence. An appeal is pending.

    As a consequence of her conviction, Parkinson was added to Virginia's Child Abuse and Neglect Registry, where she will be listed for the next seven years. Parkinson also feared that the conviction could prevent her from practicing law.

    In a recent development, prosecutors brought the charges against Parkinson while she was preparing to take the Virginia Bar exam, and her conviction came while her character and fitness application was under review. It is common to place character and fitness evaluations on hold pending the outcome of legal or disciplinary proceedings, and Parkinson initially received a communication to that effect.

    It has been revealed that upon review of the details of Parkinson's case, however, the Virginia Board of Bar Examiners concluded that nothing alleged against Parkinson cast doubt on her character and fitness to practice law in the Commonwealth of Virginia, and her application was approved. The Williamsburg Commonwealth Attorney should take note.

    While the Virginia Bar authorities recognized that Parkinson's actions were not the sort of thing that should prevent bar admission, the Williamsburg Commonwealth Attorney apparently believes that Parkinson's actions were worth criminal prosecution--with all that entails. In this case, that meant police officers had to spend half a day of paid time (if not time and a half) sitting in a courthouse when they could have been out on the street responding to community needs. They will do it again in February when a court will hear Parkinson's appeal (which will take the form of a de novo jury trial, given how Virginia handles such cases). Williamsburg and James City County are reasonably safe communities, but is this really the best way to allocate law enforcement resources?

    No doubt some prosecutions for child endangerment are motivated for a concern about a child's safety, but it is hard to credit such a justification here. The Commonwealth Attorney's office waited two weeks to file charges after the initial incident, but not because it was gathering evidence or conducting any sort of investigation. Rather, as one of the police officers testified at trial, it was because Parkinson was pregnant, so they thought it was reasonable to wait. (Yet she was still charged before giving birth, natch.) As I noted in my Free Press piece, it is hard not to conclude Parkinson's real offense was being insufficiently obsequious to the authorities.

    Upon review, the Virginia Board of Bar Examiners realized that Parkinson's actions did not justify delaying (let alone preventing) her admission to the Virginia Bar. With more time to consider the case (and the outrage it has engendered) perhaps the Williamsburg Commonwealth Attorney should reconsider the continued prosecution of Parkinson for what was, at worst, a debatable parenting choice. Confessing error and asking the court to vacate the conviction would seem to be a better use of tax dollars and public resources than continuing to pursue this case.

    British comedian and actor Russell Brand was sentenced in London on Monday to 10 years and six months in prison following his conviction for raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others.

    High Court of England and Wales Judge Joel Bennathan described Brand, 51, as a sexual predator who used his public standing to shield himself from accountability before women came forward following media reports in 2023, Courthouse News Service reports.

    It has been revealed that brand will likely serve two-thirds of his sentence before being released on parole, the judge stated. The sentencing followed a four-week trial in which jurors found Brand guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault involving four women between 2004 and 2009. He was acquitted of two other rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault.

    Before the sentencing, the court heard victim impact statements from the women, who described the lasting effects of the attacks on their confidence, relationships and ability to feel safe.

    In a recent development, the judge considered Brand’s charitable work, including helping people struggling with addiction by funding treatment. However, he mentioned good character and exemplary conduct would not normally justify a significant reduction in a prison sentence.

    It has been revealed that miami-Dade County Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz at a U.S. Senate Special Committee on Aging hearing in Washington, D.C., on April 30, 2025. (Photo by Annabelle Gordon/Sipa USA/Sipa via AP Images).

    In a lawsuit that could affect how some forfeitures are handled in Florida, the Miami-Dade County sheriff is being accused of unconstitutionally allowing a law firm to profit when police seize property and cash.

    Under federal and state forfeiture law, police departments can seize money or assets, such as boats, that they think were used in crimes or purchased with ill-gotten gains.

    Mobile phone distributors and retailers in Miami argue that a firm run by Israel “Izzy” Reyes—a former cop, a former prosecutor and a former judge—is representing the sheriff’s office in civil forfeiture cases and keeping 20% to 35% of the proceeds, plus an additional 5% on appeal.

    According to court papers filed in October, the companies stated their bank accounts were frozen last year, and more than $45.2 million was seized as as part of civil forfeiture cases handled by the firm.

    An additional $2.6 billion has also been targeted for seizure, the companies alleged, according to a story by the Miami Herald.

    Rosie Cordero-Stutz is the first elected sheriff in Miami-Dade County since the 1960s.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that boston’s South Station was less than 70 years old in 1969 but seemed much older. It certainly lacked the glamour of nearby North Station, home to the Boston Garden, where the city’s basketball and hockey teams played and where the Rolling Stones and James Brown performed for screaming teenagers. In comparison, the South Station stop on 700 Atlantic Avenue was a dreary place for tired daily commuters on their way to the suburbs of the South Shore. With its high-domed ceiling and rickety escalators built during the Depression era, South Station managed to be both enormous and decrepit, a sickly old giant in need of urgent care. As the Boston Globe mentioned a few years later, the once thriving railroad stop was “now staggering along in the last stages of neglect.”.

    It has been revealed that yet even as it faced the threat of the wrecking ball, the station remained busy, particularly at holiday time. On Friday, December 26, a 9-year-old Dorchester boy named Kenny Martin wandered into the station with a friend, Thomas Lydon. It was the day after Christmas and Kenny, who had come into Downtown Boston to buy some Boy Scout equipment, spent the afternoon horsing around with Lydon at the station. They’d chased each other up and down the escalators, running through the crowd of postholiday shoppers. As the afternoon came to an end, Lydon departed, while Kenny planned to take the train back home.

    In his brown-checked jacket with fur collar, blue bell-bottom pants, and orange work boots, Kenny was a typical Dorchester boy, coming home from a day of fun. He was the youngest of four children, small for his age at less than 50 pounds. It might seem odd for a boy so young to be alone in the city, but Boston kids learned to use the subways early in those days. They often traveled on their own from one side of the city to the other.

    The platform where he would’ve waited for the Dorchester train was cold and drafty, for there are few places colder than a Boston subway platform in late December. One could only stand and shiver, waiting for the sound of a faraway bell to warn people of approaching trains. Perhaps Kenny looked down the long, dark tunnel for the sign of a subway car’s light, usually visible long before the car was in the station. The tunnels were foreboding; there were stories of people accidentally getting electrocuted on the infamous “third rail” and of huge rodents living in the underground network. Meanwhile, pigeons, bats, and owls roosted in the rafters, occasionally swooping down to frighten the commuters.

    There was no shortage of urban legends around South Station, of how people committed suicide by jumping in front of moving trains and how homeless men wandered in the dark tunnels to sleep underneath cardboard coverings. In time, stories of vagrants evolved into stories of trolls living in the tunnels, trolls who only came out after midnight when the station was closed. This was fantasy stuff, tales told by older kids to tease younger ones.

    According to recent reports, of course, the station had its good points. It was a historical landmark, after all, opening for business in 1899 as the largest station in the country, a majestic building made of pink granite. There was also the railroad chapel, Our Lady of the Railways. Built in the 1950s, it was the first of its kind in America. Organ music played during every Sunday service, and Boston’s Archbishop Cushing held special masses and Easter vigils, perfect for travelers who couldn’t get home in time to worship. There was a lunch counter, a newsstand, the Sidecar Bar-Grill, a bakery, and a barbershop. A Paramount film crew had been to South Station earlier in the year to shoot a scene for a Jack Lemmon movie, The Out of Towners. For a few days, the dilapidated old station was enlivened by the buzz of Hollywood energy and curious crowds. Despite these occasional bright spots, the atmosphere remained glum and ramshackle. When the crowds thinned out after the rush hour, all that remained were boarded-up areas that always seemed to be “under construction” and weary cleaning crews wiping out the messes of the day.

    Recent findings suggest that at some point in the afternoon of December 26, Kenny met a pudgy, dark-haired man with a round face. The man seemed different from the other people hurrying around the station. He was rumpled. He needed a shave and a bath. It turned out the man was also named Kenneth. What they talked about, or how they spent their next few hours together, is unknown. History would reveal that the unshaven man knew all about the secret tunnels in South Station and knew all the special places where people could hide. He may have offered to show Kenny around the old building, an irresistible prospect for a 9-year-old boy.

    Kenny’s body was found eleven days later. He’d been strangled to death. His body was hidden in one of the station’s underground passageways. Someone had wrapped it in a canvas bag and covered it with debris. A search team consisting of police from two districts, as well as city engineers, had spent the day exploring sewers and tunnels around the station. The search ended in an abandoned transit tunnel, a ghostly location that had once been used to transport cargo to the surface cars. It was a dingy place for a little boy to wind up, cold and dark and airless.

    He could’ve been lured there only by one of the station’s trolls.

    Security guards patrolled South Station and routinely tossed out vagrants and drunks, shoving them out the door onto Atlantic Avenue. These scenes were unpleasant, but the guards were under orders to keep the winos and grifters out. The raggedy station only looked worse if pitiful old drunks were lounging on the wooden benches. Yet Kenneth Harrison, the pudgy man, had been living in the place for nearly a year, like a hermit hiding in a cave. He didn’t have to compete for a bed at one of the nearby shelters, not when he could hunker down in one of the abandoned offices beneath the station.

    Recent findings suggest that the morning after he’d killed Kenny Martin, Harrison slouched out into the daylight, searching for a rooming house where he could find a bed and lie low. The sidewalk was still slippery from the previous night’s rain and sleet. It would have been a nice day to hang out at the station, yet Harrison felt it was time to go. Hanging around was too risky, even if the dead boy was buried deeper than an old bone.

    Recent findings suggest that harrison had grown up in Roxbury’s Mission Hill neighborhood and had dropped out of school after the eighth grade. Now, at 31, he was an unemployed restaurant worker, living a vagabond’s existence and spending what little money he had on alcohol. He’d become one of life’s losers, a degenerate barfly with no future. He was virtually indistinguishable from dozens of others in his situation. The difference was that Harrison murdered children.

    Sources indicate that kenny Martin, whose face would soon be featured in local newspapers, was Harrison’s second young victim. Two-and-a-half years earlier, Harrison had killed a 6-year-old girl named Lucy Palmarin. She’d been cashing in an empty tonic bottle at a store. Witnesses saw her climbing into the car of an unknown man. She was found floating among the garbage in South Boston’s Fort Point Channel, a mile from her home. Since the medical examiner found no signs of injury or foul play, Lucy’s death was ruled an accidental drowning. Lucy’s disappearance created a flurry of activity in South Boston. Posters with her picture were distributed throughout the community. Her poor mother waited up nights, clutching a book of old photographs of the missing girl. Three weeks into the search, the Boston police called in the FBI for assistance. They suspected a kidnapping, but the truth was worse.

    On April 15, 1967, Harrison was driving a cab, among his many odd jobs. He would later tell a judge that he had dropped off a fare near the D Street housing project where Lucy lived. He saw her walking and offered to give her a ride. Instead of taking her home, he drove to the channel where he tossed her in the city’s notoriously dirty water.

    In another version of the confession, Harrison stated the little girl asked him for a quarter, which led to him giving her a piggyback ride. Once she was up on his back, he easily pitched her into the water. So he said. His confessions sounded ludicrous. Lucy’s family was Puerto Rican and new to America. The girl didn’t speak English. In between the two child murders, Harrison had killed two adults. There’d been a barroom beef with a fellow named Joseph Breen, an ex-marine and water firm employee. Harrison and Breen had been drinking at the Novelty Bar in Boston’s Combat Zone, a dank neighborhood of nudie bars and X-rated theaters.

    Later, after an argument over money, Harrison beat Breen to death with a rock.

    Inexplicably, Harrison called the police that night, telling them they could find Breen’s body floating in an excavation pit on Kneeland Street near Chinatown. When the police asked who was calling, Harrison felt a laugh coming up his throat, like an eruption.

    “This is the giggler,” he mentioned.

    In a recent development, then, he giggled. And hung up the phone.

    It was a time when killers were becoming celebrities, with memorable names and trademarks, like the Boston Strangler or the Zodiac in California. Why couldn’t Harrison be “The Giggler?”.

    Industry observers note that harrison must’ve felt as elusive as the Zodiac, because he’d actually returned to the Novelty a short time later. A couple of Breen’s friends were there and recognized him as the man who had been with Breen the night he was killed. Breen’s friends called the police, but by the time they arrived, Harrison was gone again, no doubt back at the train station, hiding in plain sight.

    Sources indicate that then, just a month before killing Kenny Martin, Harrison had murdered an old woman, 75-year-old Clovis Parker of South Boston. As he’d done with the little girl, he left Clovis floating in Fort Point Channel, a mere five-minute walk from Harrison’s South Station hideout. He’d tell investigators that he had met the old woman on a bridge, and she’d asked for help getting across. Without giving a reason, Harrison remarked that he’d simply kicked Clovis Parker’s cane from under her and then tossed her over the guardrail. The unfortunate woman’s death hadn’t even made it to the newspapers.

    It has been revealed that A few days after killing Kenny Martin, Harrison called his sister, Eileen. He confessed that he had killed a boy and told her where the body was hidden. On January 6, the day Kenny’s body was found, Harrison boarded a train at South Station and left Boston.

    Eileen consulted a lawyer and then called the police. They followed her tip to find the body, and then a quartet of detectives armed with an arrest warrant traced Harrison to Providence. They arrested him without incident and held him without bail in Suffolk County.

    While detectives questioned him about Kenny Martin’s death, Harrison interrupted.

    “As long as I’m here,” he mentioned, “I might as well tell you about a few more.”.

    In a recent development, he told them about Lucy Palmarin, Joseph Breen, and Clovis Parker. Investigators were stunned. Harrison was confessing to four murders committed over a span of thirty-two months.

    Recent findings suggest that when he talked about Kenny Martin, Harrison said he’d had “an urge to kill” but didn’t remember doing anything. He merely woke up the next morning and saw the boy with a rope around his neck.

    It has been revealed that harrison revealed little emotion as he spoke, but he seemed comfortable talking about his crimes. He even took a liking to the detectives interrogating him. Later, when he learned that one of the detectives had retired, Harrison sent a card.

    Yet his frankness about the murders and his friendship with the detectives masked a fragile mind.

    The chief investigator for the Dallas County public defender’s office was arrested and charged with first-degree murder Saturday after his wife was found dead in their apartment.

    Jimmy Harold Spurger Jr., 54, who has worked for the public defender’s office for nearly 14 years, was married to his wife, Maria Teresa Spurger, for 35 years but filed for divorce in late October, according to Fox 4.

    Industry observers note that local first responders who were conducting a welfare check Friday night forced their way into the apartment, where they found Spurger’s wife unresponsive on a couch with a knife in her neck, Fox 4 reports. Spurger also was found in the apartment, covered in blood and sitting next to a knife in the bedroom.

    After responding officers found multiple pill bottles also covered in blood, they suspected that Spurger had ingested pills and transported him to the hospital, Fox 4 reports. He was later taken into custody and is being held on a $1 million bond.

    Spurger has led the Investigative Division for the Dallas County public defender’s office for 11 months, Fox 4 reports. Previously, he spent more than 13 years in its Capital Murder Division. He also worked for more than 20 years in law enforcement, which included supervising investigations in the Child Abuse and Family Violence Division of the Dallas County district attorney’s office.

    Dallas County Chief Public Defender Christi Dean told Fox 4 that Spurger was “an exemplary colleague,” and that “it’s hard to imagine that he has been charged with murder.”.

    In a recent development, “We know in our profession that the probable cause affidavit doesn’t tell the whole story,” Dean also reportedly noted. “The media reports don’t tell the whole story. And we’re still in preliminary stages.”.

    Rina Varger beat her palm against the old Ford pickup’s door in time to Aerosmith’s “Push Comes to Shove” as she drove across the bridge and into town. It was the morning of the tenth of September and the Merrimack was running high after a week of torrential rain, debris and dead brush from upriver borne along by the surging brown water. The wind in her face felt good after a day spent scrubbing years of dust and nameless gunk from between sticky floorboards. Everything had to be perfect for Aunt Eleanor’s wedding. Nana Marian was losing her mind trying to get the house in shape, running their skinless maid Kate Bartlett ragged.

    According to recent reports, A little after eight Rina parked in front of Julian and Eddie’s place, a cramped two-story bungalow with a patchy lawn and huge stands of sumac nearly obscuring its front entrance and encroaching on its drive-way. Julian, an aging queen cast off by a prominent Cape Cod family, owned Plover Antiques downtown. Eddie Means was a veterinarian at the Franklin Park Zoo in Boston, and had been the Varger family’s meat man for almost ten years. Rina killed the engine and stepped out onto the curb, fishing in her jacket pockets for her cigarettes. She was about to light up when she heard voices coming from the direction of the driveway. She pocketed her smokes and went around the house, moving slowly, keeping to the shadows of the sumac stand.

    Recent findings suggest that four teenage boys, maybe fifteen or sixteen, and a girl who looked a little younger stood in a half circle at the end of the driveway, in front of Julian’s garage.     #8364. Wendy M. Barnhart on our enduring fascination with female serial killers

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1033 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Wendy M. Barnhart on our enduring fascination with female serial killers

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that A question was presented to me: Why do female serial killers fascinate us?
    • According to recent reports, but is it just female serial killers who intrigue us?
    • The obvious answer is that all serial killers pique our interest.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that A question was presented to me: Why do female serial killers fascinate us? I count myself in that fascination camp—my latest novel, Scaled Vengeance, focuses on a female serial killer, and I admit that the research I did for the novel enthralled me.

    According to recent reports, but is it just female serial killers who intrigue us? Or serial killers in general?

    The obvious answer is that all serial killers pique our interest. The act of murdering another person is shocking. But to kill and kill and kill again is outrageous. And intense. And next-level-frightening. It’s tough to understand how one person could repeatedly want to do such a thing. Even with all of the articles written, and documentaries produced that touch on childhoods, motivations, objectives, and any other manner of revelation, I’m not sure we still “get it.” I definitely don’t.

    There are some theories that, like true crime in general, audiences want to learn about serial killers so we can better understand threats. I’m not quite on board with that idea. There’s no signal in my brain telling me to be prepared should I ever encounter a serial killer, but I admit I do find them interesting nonetheless.

    Industry observers note that A little factoid to share: A friend of my mom dated Ted Bundy while he was doing his serial killer thing in Salt Lake City. She lived across the hall from him in a house that had been converted to apartments. Thankfully, she was not one of his victims, nor did he hurt her physically. (Emotionally is another thing entirely.).

    Sources indicate that but did that story give your brain a little “eek” moment? Me too. Even this many years later.

    Sources indicate that so, serial killers intrigue us. But female serial killers are next-level fascinating.

    While researching the topic for my book, I learned female serial killers through history often committed their crimes for financial gain. And they leveraged their perceived role as a nurturer or caregiver to gain access to funds / victims.

    For instance, Amelia Dyer was a British nurse in the 1800s who offered to care for unwanted infants in exchange for money she needed to support herself. She took the money, took the babies, and then murdered those babies rather than care for them. Another woman, Dagmar Overbye, did the same as a “child caretaker” in the early 1900s (including killing her own child).

    Dorothea Puente ran a boarding house in Sacramento, California, where she poisoned her tenants (often elderly or disabled), buried their bodies on her property, then collected and cashed their Social Security checks. Amy Archer-Gilligan ran a nursing home and pressured her residents to bequeath her large sums of money before poisoning them.

    But by no means is money the sole motivation of female serial killers. Aileen Wournos was a sex worker who killed at least seven men, claiming self-defense. Jane Toppan trained as a nurse and tried different combinations of drugs on her patients just to see what would happen. She confessed to thirty-one murders (at this writing, she holds the Guiness World Record for most prolific female serial killer based on confirmed number of victims).

    It has been revealed that and Elizabeth Bathory, born in the 1500s, is stated to have murdered hundreds of women. Legend holds that she both drank and bathed in the blood of young women with the hope that doing so would preserve Bathory’s own youthfulness. (Record-keeping being what it was in the 1500s, no solid documentation exists to confirm the Elizabeth Bathory story, hence no Guiness World Record for her.).

    Whether for money or some other dark and twisted motivation, female serial killers hold a different kind of fascination for us than male serial killers. One of the most obvious reasons, in my humble opinion, is their rarity. Serial killers are uncommon, and female serial killers even more so. Something uncommon and novel will, more likely than not, grab more attention than the known entity.

    According to recent reports, I think female serial killers also captivate us because they break the social norms that women are the nurturers, the caretakers, the safe place. Walking through a parking lot at night and happening upon a man puts us on alert, male and female alike (though dramatically more so for women). Happening upon a woman in a dark parking lot, though, would prompt awareness, but probably not a high-risk alert. Women are deemed safe.

    (Until you learn they want to bathe in your blood….).

    In a recent development, it’s this same perspective that enables female serial killers to carry on undetected as long as they do, before being caught. She’s a nurse, she’s a healer, she wouldn’t actively kill someone. She’s a mother, she’s a child caretaker, she would never harm a baby. She’s being paid to house people—she would never kill them and stop the flow of funds.

    In a recent development, as time goes by, female suspects don’t move up the list, the killings continue, the body count rises. And the greater the shock when female killers are discovered and we learn about how many people died at their hand. It’s believed Amelia Dyer killed over 300 babies. (Was that another “eek” moment for you? Me too.).

    Unless we see a sharp rise in the number of female serial killers making them ubiquitous (and, wow, I hope that never happens…), I believe female serial killers will continue to fascinate us. They are rare gems that catch our attention when they’re revealed, unearthed in their unusual form and often surprising cruelty. And, being the humans that we are, it’s tough to look away from these fascinating but terrible people.

    International bestselling and award-winning author Wendy M. Barnhart (formerly Terrien) is the author of Scaled Vengeance, The Rampart Guards, The League of Governors, The Clan Calling, and The Forge of Bonds. Wendy graduated from the University of Utah (go Utes!) and moved to Colorado where she completed her MBA at the University of Denver. Learn more about Wendy by visiting her website: wendymbarnhart.com.

    Tech Report: The Best Psychological Thrillers of the Month: November 2026

    • Wrobel’s latest is her best yet, chock-full of twists, turns, and unexpected reversals, with a perfectly constructed plot that’s also a rollicking good satire on the publishing industry.
    • Collom won me as a fan with her excellent tale of feminist vengeance, Peter Miles Must Die, and her new book seems tailor-made for this Austin-based cat-loving crime editor.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that in these newly introduced psychological thrillers, editors are taken hostage, cat-sitters become amateur sleuths, several small towns are ripped apart by scandal, and long-buried crimes come rising to the surface. All blurbs are my own, unless otherwise stated. Enjoy!

    Stephanie Wrobel, Revenge Plot (Berkley).

    Wrobel’s latest is her best yet, chock-full of twists, turns, and unexpected reversals, with a perfectly constructed plot that’s also a rollicking good satire on the publishing industry. Revenge Plot certainly earns its comparisons to Misery, a loving homage that also manages to be entirely surprising. Here’s the gist: a desperate writer, young child in tow, demonstrates up at a famous editor’s winter retreat and holds her hostage whilst making her read his manuscript (a fantasy shared by many writerly hopefuls, surely). As is true of all the best psychological thrillers, a series of well-paced reveals allows for constant reassessment of Wrobel’s characters and their unfortunate predicament, all leading up to the shocking denouement.

    Katie Collom, Terrarium (Bantam).

    Collom won me as a fan with her excellent tale of feminist vengeance, Peter Miles Must Die, and her new book seems tailor-made for this Austin-based cat-loving crime editor. In Terrarium, a desperate barista and wannabe veterinarian finds her cat-sitting side gigs drying up after an unfortunate incident; a new job taking care of a wealthy artist’s big fluffy baby drops into her lap at the best possible time, but could her new employer be the Rainey Street killer? Fingers crossed!

    May Cobb, All the Little Secrets (Sourcebooks Landmark).

    May Cobb’s follow-up to All the Little Houses functions well as both sequel and standalone—it’s set in the same small town, and begins just after the concluding events of previous volume, but with plenty of fresh momentum and diverging narratives. All the Little Secrets is not so much about a crime, as about the fallout from a crime—these pages feature attempted coverups, scandalous reveals, and quite a few zingers, for a highly entertaining work harking back to the stylized dramatics of 1980s soap operas.

    Carter Wilson, When They Find Me (Poisoned Pen).

    It has been revealed that this is a genuine pulse pounder, about two women, both on the run (in a manner of speaking), whose families and destinies collide in the freezing, remote Colorado wilderness. Annie has been living off the grid in a small cabin with her daughter Coral, hiding out, hoping the people hunting her never find her again. And Riven, who has spent her life living off the land, away from society, arrives at this strange town thanks to her father, who swears revenge on the man who ruined his life. –OR.

    Gabrielle Lucille Fuentes, Clear Water (Flatiron).

    Recent findings suggest that gabrielle Lucille Fuentes’s new novel is eerie, atmospheric, and highly compelling. Listen to this premise, and tell me you’re not interested right away? When Alma encounters a girl in white she’s never seen before, she’s not sure what she’s seeing—is this person a vision, a ghost of one of the many girls who have vanished in her small Wisconsin town? Some people say that the girls are dangerous, others are too afraid to even wonder. But Alma, who lost her own sister in high school, is determined to find an explanation for the strange events in the town, once and for all. –OR.

    Molly Odintz is the managing editor for CrimeReads and the editor of Austin Noir, now available from Akashic Books. She grew up in Austin and worked as a bookseller before becoming a Very Professional Internet Person. She lives in central Texas with her cat, Fritz Lang.

    Breaking: Lindsay Clancy loses bid to dismiss murder case with retrial possibility

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Lindsay Clancy was being tried for first-degree murder.
    • Lindsay Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse charged with strangling and killing her three small children in 2023, lost her bid to have her case dismissed Monday, setting the stage for a possible retrial.
    • Massachusetts Superior Court Judge William Sullivan’s 17-page ruling found that a retrial would not be considered double jeopardy because Clancy’s initial jury was deadlocked.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Lindsay Clancy was being tried for first-degree murder. She admitted to killing her three children and claimed that she suffered from postpartum psychosis. (Photo by CJ Gunther/The Boston Herald via the Associated Press).

    Lindsay Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse charged with strangling and killing her three small children in 2023, lost her bid to have her case dismissed Monday, setting the stage for a possible retrial.

    Massachusetts Superior Court Judge William Sullivan’s 17-page ruling found that a retrial would not be considered double jeopardy because Clancy’s initial jury was deadlocked.

    Clancy, 36, was on trial earlier this year for the strangling deaths of her three young children. The case ended in a mistrial after one juror, known as “Juror Doe,” held out for a conviction. Clancy pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity, alleging that she was going through postpartum psychosis at the time of the tragedy, according to coverage on Courthouse News Service.

    Recent findings suggest that last week, a hearing seeking dismissal of the case explored the role of Michael Desronvil, who is referred to as “Juror Doe” in court records. Desronvil was accused of not following the court’s instructions.

    Sullivan found that the evidence “did not reasonably suggest Juror Doe’s inability to deliberate or refusal to follow the law.”.

    Industry observers note that on Nov. 2, the prosecution said it intends to try Clancy again. She initially faced three counts of murder for the deaths of Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and Callan, 8 months.

    Lindsay Clancy judge considers retrial at hearing to dismiss murder case.

    #8360. Industry News: But is it a crime to fight a bear?

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (932 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: But is it a crime to fight a bear?

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (932 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that adult, male black bears can run faster than Usain Bolt.
    • First, Brick Bridger, our hero in Bear Brawl, is not your average man.
    • In a recent development, the book explores what would happen if a man such as this dedicated his life to training, tracking, finding and fighting this bear with no weapons to get revenge.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that adult, male black bears can run faster than Usain Bolt. Thirty five miles per hour. No sweat. They can sprint and jump and climb full speed up a one hundred foot tree in a matter of seconds. They can flip three hundred pound rocks with one forepaw and drag thousand pound carcasses with ease. Their muscle fibers are packed so tightly and can generate enough raw horsepower that they can tear open car doors like we’d open a refrigerator. They’re six feet tall standing on their back legs and they’ve got two inch claws built for digging and climbing or slashing. The average man would have to be insane to try and fight one in the real world. But in the world of fiction, this idea makes one hell of a fun premise to write about and during my research it brought up an interesting question:.

    Fighting a bear is crazy, sure, but is it a crime?

    First, Brick Bridger, our hero in Bear Brawl, is not your average man. He’s 6’6” tall and weighs 265 pounds. He’s a two-time collegiate wrestling champion and had eight wins in the UFC before he retired. And he’s properly motivated. A rogue, 450-pound black bear killed his mom and put his brother in a wheelchair.

    In a recent development, the book explores what would happen if a man such as this dedicated his life to training, tracking, finding and fighting this bear with no weapons to get revenge. He enlists a zoologist, his ex-wrestling coach, local trackers and hunters and learns everything he can about this bear to prepare for the battle.

    It has been revealed that but unlike, say, Chief Martin Brody, in Jaws, who heads out into the ocean as a law enforcement officer to hunt the great white shark terrorizing his beaches, Brick is just a citizen. Brody puts a bounty on this one specific shark, overriding the laws that make killing, catching or removing a great white shark from the ocean a crime. Brick can’t do that.

    Now, you might be thinking, “there are hunting licenses issued for black bears in many states” and you’d be correct. Hunters have been killing bears for their meat and fur for centuries. Just read Craig Fehrman’s excellent recent book, This Vast Enterprise, and the number of bears killed and eaten during the Lewis and Clark expedition will astonish you.

    In a recent development, still, hunting with a rifle and a license is a far cry from walking into the woods to fight a bear unarmed and as of this writing, there are no states that issue a bear fighting permit that would allow someone to do this. Interestingly enough, there are states that specifically ban wrestling bears: Arkansas, Louisiana, Oklahoma and Mississippi.

    This mostly refers to carnivals and expeditions and circus-like events being banned, because it isn’t as if there is a queue of men applying to wrestle bears for amusement in the wild. On this front, in those states, if you were caught wrestling a bear, yes, it would be a crime.

    In Arkansas, where Bear Brawl takes place, AR Code § 5-62-124, considers wrestling a bear for “fun” or money “unlawful bear exploitation” and it is a Class D felony.”.

    So, did my main character commit a felony by fighting a rampaging black bear that had killed four people?

    Not exactly, because there is a self-defense clause. Arkansas Game and Fish Commission Code 01.00-G puts the burden on the person who killed the bear to prove they acted under a “good faith belief” that they were protecting themselves or someone else from “imminent bodily harm or serious injury.”.

    In a recent development, this one’s dicey for our hero, Brick, because he specifically went into the woods to find and fight the bear. Fortunately for him, this particular bear was in the middle of a rampage and had just attacked a grandfather, grandmother and their grandson, which puts Brick on the right side of the law.

    Okay, so now we know that the actual bear brawl in Bear Brawl is legal. Whew. The only caveat is that if Brick wins the fight (no spoilers) he better not be tempted to take a claw or a tooth as a prize. Why? Because even if you’re justified in a bear killing in Arkansas, as soon as you take anything from the carcass, you’ve gone from being a life-saving hero to an illegal poacher in no time flat, and now you’ve committed a crime again. Ha!

    You’ll just have to read my thriller Bear Brawl to discover how this whole thing shakes out. Man vs. bear. No guns. No weapons. Just revenge. Part Jaws and part Rocky, it’s an action thriller that reads like your favorite blockbuster movie. And no animal fighting laws were broken while writing the book. I promise.

    Jon Finkel is the award-winning author of The Life of Dad, The Athlete, Heart Over Height, "Mean" Joe Greene, the Greatest Stars of the NBA series, and other books about sports, fatherhood, fitness, and more. His work has been endorsed by Spike Lee, Tony Dungy, Jerry Jones, Mark Cuban, and Chef Robert Irvine. He is cohost of the Life of Dad Sports Show podcast and Lunch Break Facebook Live show with more than one thousand viewers. He has written for GQ, Men's Health, Yahoo! Sports, the New York Times, and dozens of other national publications. He lives in Royal Palm Beach, Florida.

    Listen up, wiseguys. There’s a latest Disney/Pixar movie coming out, and it’s a crime movie! Specifically, it’s a movie about the Italian mob. It takes place in Venice, Italy, and is the story of a scrawny, impoverished young fellow named Nero (voiced by Mark Ruffalo) who is taken in by a powerful crime family. In exchange for this, his job is to steal things for them… often at great personal risk.

    Also, they’re all cats. Everybody’s a cat. Well, a couple of characters seem to be rodents. And there’s a pigeon, I think. But it’s mostly cats. The film is titled Gatto (which is Italian for “cat”).

    Recent findings suggest that anyway, Nero starts to find himself in very dangerous situations, working as a thief for the (literal) fat cat crime boss Rocco, and learns that he has nine lives that he’s wasting, dying while doing criminal errands. Thus, he asks himself the great questions many crime movie protagonists ask themselves: is everything he’s doing worth it? Is he living a life that’s worth living as if it’s his only one? How can he change his life so that it’s full of meaning?

    In addition to Ruffalo, the voice cast includes: Laurence Fishburne, Enrico Casarosa (who also directs), John Turturro, Isabella Rossellini, Natasia Demetriou, Jamie Demetriou, Jason Schwartzman, Saverio Raimondo, Jason Mantzoukas, Tracey Ullman, Marco Calvani, and Rhys Darby.

    It has been revealed that perhaps it’s a great film to take your children to as you start to introduce them to the “mafia movie” genre. Watch Gatto and then The Godfather and find out which one they like better!

    In a recent development, the film will be in theaters next March. Ci vediamo!
