    #8358. 7 idiosyncratic novels that leave Laurie Cass in awe

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (983 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    7 idiosyncratic novels that leave Laurie Cass in awe

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (983 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When I came up with the topic for this post, I thought it would be the work of a few minutes to come up with half a dozen titles, parse out reasons why each one was included in the list, and conclude with a clever sentence or two.
    • What actually happened was I stared at my computer screen for an absurd amount of time, typing and deleting, typing and deleting.
    • Recent findings suggest that the end result is, in retrospect, overwhelmingly obvious: I could never write a book that isn’t mine to write.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When I came up with the topic for this post, I thought it would be the work of a few minutes to come up with half a dozen titles, parse out reasons why each one was included in the list, and conclude with a clever sentence or two.

    What actually happened was I stared at my computer screen for an absurd amount of time, typing and deleting, typing and deleting. When it became clear that I wasn’t getting anywhere, I got up and wandered over to my bookshelves and sat down in front of them to have a good long think.

    Recent findings suggest that the end result is, in retrospect, overwhelmingly obvious: I could never write a book that isn’t mine to write. Discovering what’s in you that can become a book is part of the joy of writing, and what an author brings to a manuscript is what makes it theirs and theirs alone.

    That remarked, there are books—and entire genres—that will forever be out of my authorial reach.

    Recent findings suggest that let’s start with one of my favorite books, Dissolution by C. J. Sansom. The main character of Matthew Shardlake is deeply complex, and his complicated history and personality twist together around and into the intricate plot. It’s set in 1537 England, during the reign of King Henry VIII, a period rife with fear and conflict.

    There is no way on this good green earth that I could write a book with anything remotely similar to the complexity of Dissolution. Not the tiniest sliver of a chance. If I didn’t have the same thing for breakfast every weekday, I wouldn’t remember what I had for breakfast; writing a book with so many layers is not something my brain is likely to take kindly to doing.

    In a recent development, and then there’s the research factor. Serious amounts of time are required to immerse yourself in the zillions of details it takes to write historicals. I love learning things, but until I retire from my day job, doing in-depth research is not in the cards.

    Miles Franklin, My Brilliant Career.

    Recent findings suggest that next on the list is My Brilliant Career by Miles Franklin. To write like that? As a teenager? Please. My teenaged writing output was embarrassingly bad poetry that is long lost to the mists of time, exactly where it belongs. Ms. Franklin’s talents were, and are, beyond mine. No way, no how, could I have written that.

    In a recent development, another one on the Beyond Me list has to be The Book Thief by Markus Zusak. A story narrated by Death? That I might be able to write, but a story as bone-deep sad as The Book Thief isn’t something I feel capable of doing. When writing, I tend to inhabit the heads of my main characters, and spending that much time in sorrow, sadness, and despair, would not be good for me on any level.

    I admire those who can do so and walk away intact, but  writing that intense is far outside my capacities.

    Alexander Dumas, The Count of Monte Cristo.

    I read this book for the first time as a teenager, and I flat out loved it. Reread it numerous times, and then put it away when I went off to college.

    Recent findings suggest that when I picked it up a few years ago, I still enjoyed the read and still feel it’s a quality book, but I noticed something I hadn’t as a youngster: there’s nothing funny in it. Not a word. The only things I can write don’t include humor are professional white papers and reports. And it’s possible that funny bits sneak into those, every so often. Writing a full-length novel with a total of no humor is not going to happen.

    Sources indicate that E. L. James, Fifty Shades of Grey.

    I included this on my Couldn’t Write list because of its reputation for explicit sex scenes. There are many, many other books that contain the act, and I don’t see how I could have written any of them. In what I write, all that happens off-book, if it happens at all. Fade to black at end of chapter works for me, and until an editor tells me differently, that’s how it’s going to stay.

    It has been revealed that I read this book in one sitting. Or more accurately, since I was in a hammock at the time, in one lying, but the point remains. I did not want to do *anything* until I found out what happened. The characters, the pacing, the stakes, the stark wonder of the discoveries—maybe I could wrap one of those elements into a book, two if I was lucky, but all of them together? Nope. That high-concept stuff is way outside my abilities.

    Recent findings suggest that plus there’s the science element. I’m geeky by nature, but the time spent researching would be a massive barrier, similar to the above-mentioned historical research.

    Helene Hanff, 84, Charing Cross Road.

    In a recent development, this book. This. Book. It captured my heart when I first read it decades ago, and it could well be what started me on a lifelong love affair with London. I don’t know what makes it such a lovely, lovely book; the lyrical quality of the correspondence? The gaps left to the reader to fill? The bittersweet tone you can almost taste?

    Industry observers note that I’m not sure, and it now occurs to me that I haven’t reread 84, Charing Cross Road in years. That whisper I hear, is it calling my name? Why, yes, I think it is. Excuse me, but I have to go.

    Laurie Cass is the national bestselling author of the Bookmobile Cat Mystery series.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    There have been plenty of law firm failures over the years. For instance, there was a run on closures thanks to the Great Recession, and Dewey & LeBoeuf’s 2012 failure sent shockwaves throughout the industry.

    But when Weil, Gotshal & Manges announced last month that it would be winding down operations, it felt different compared to the others before.

    After all, many of the BigLaw firms that went out of the business during the Great Recession had been overexposed in certain areas, and when the housing market crashed, so did their business. Dewey’s failure happened for a lot of reasons, mainly due to massive money guarantees to partners, an ill-advised merger, and alleged financial irregularities that resulted in criminal indictments.

    Weil Gotshal, though, had long been a firm with one of the best reputations on Wall Street, let alone the world. How did a firm like that end up joining the others on the dustheap? And could technology play a role in helping other firms avoid such a fate in the future?

    It has been revealed that in this episode of the Legal Rebels Podcast, Noah Waisberg talks to the ABA Journal’s Victor Li about those and other topics. Waisberg is the co-founder and the CEO of Zuva—an artificial intelligence contract analysis platform—and a longtime advocate of using technology to review contracts. He’s also a former Weil Gotshal associate, having worked there as a summer associate in 2005 and then as an associate from 2006 to 2010.

    Rivals race to rescue Weil Gotshal lawyers as firm heads toward closure.

    Weil Gotshal to wind down in shock fall for heavyweight firm.

    Noah Waisberg is the co-founder and the CEO of Zuva—an artificial intelligence contract analysis platform—and a longtime advocate of using technology to review contracts. He’s also a former Weil, Gotshal & Manges associate, having worked there as a summer associate in 2005 and then as an associate from 2006 to 2010. Before leading Zuva, Waisberg was the CEO of Kira Systems, the leading contract analysis company for professional service agencies, from its founding to its sale to Litera in 2021.

    #8356. How true crime both mesmerizes and misleads audiences

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1705 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    How true crime both mesmerizes and misleads audiences

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that I had the honor of serving as a Criminal Profiler for more than a decade of the twenty-two years I spent as an FBI Special Agent.
    • Then, as an FBI Agent, I investigated bank robberies, white collar crimes, civil rights violations, child sex crimes, serial murder and rape, child abductions, and terrorism.
    • In the DC Sniper case, for example, I witnessed firsthand what it was like to know that anyone could be shot dead, at any place, at any time, in the greater DC area.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that I had the honor of serving as a Criminal Profiler for more than a decade of the twenty-two years I spent as an FBI Special Agent. Before the FBI, I was a prosecutor for the Upcoming York City Law Department. While there, I tried cases from petty theft to sex crimes and extortion to attempted murder.

    Then, as an FBI Agent, I investigated bank robberies, white collar crimes, civil rights violations, child sex crimes, serial murder and rape, child abductions, and terrorism. I traveled across the country and around the world chasing the worst of the worst that humanity has to offer. Some of those offenders were among the most notorious criminals of our time.

    In the DC Sniper case, for example, I witnessed firsthand what it was like to know that anyone could be shot dead, at any place, at any time, in the greater DC area. That’s because people were being killed right in my own backyard.

    According to recent reports, from the start that case presented differently from other “spree killer” cases. Typically in spree cases, as the offender moves from shooting scene to shooting scene he decompensates and his criminal sophistication erodes. In other words, his crimes become more and more sloppy.

    According to recent reports, but here, the shooter made one shot/one kill, six times in a row while moving from location to location in rapid succession and no one ever even saw him. He was a ghost….

    Sources indicate that fortunately, though, his behavior leaked out enough information that we were able to build a profile of not one, but two snipers, working together for the first time in US history. One older with police or military training and experience, and the other a teen who had written the communications on a tarot card and on children’s note paper. In the end, shortly after our profile was released, the snipers were spotted by an alert trucker who immediately called 911 and ended their twenty-three-day reign of terror.

    Industry observers note that another notorious case involved JonBenét Ramsey, a six-year-old beauty pageant queen—who was reportedly kidnapped but was later found dead in the basement of her home. The case still remains officially unsolved decades later.

    In my opinion, this is not due to law enforcement incompetence, but because the family refused to be fully interviewed by law enforcement for several months, the father filed multiple law suits against investigators, and the prosecutor made a decision not to follow through with the murder indictments voted for by the grand jury.

    It has been revealed that in 2009, when I retired from the FBI and transitioned into full-time network television writing and producing, it was only natural that I gravitate toward what I knew best—crime. I formed a development and production company, XG Productions, with my brother Tim, also a retired FBI agent. Together, we endeavor to put crime victims first (not notorious offenders) and bring authenticity to the crime entertainment space.

    One of the most successful reveals I worked on as a writer/producer was the popular ABC/CBS prime time crime drama, Criminal Minds. In fact, we just finished shooting our nineteenth season at the time of this writing. I also worked on FBI, FBI Most Wanted, Blind Spot, Sleepy Hollow, Quantico, and many more. And XG also produced The Case Of: JonBenét Ramsey, The Case Of: Caylee Anthony, The Forgotten West Memphis Three, and INDIVISIBLE: Healing Hate.

    I published my first true crime book, Without Consent, in 2014. And since 2020, XG Productions has produced and published twenty-five Audible Original Docuseries. These include: Evil Has A Name, Paul Holes’ story of his relentless pursuit and identification of the Golden State Killer, with the help of the FBI’s Steve Kramer and Steve Busch. In the process of solving this decades-old cold case, they created Forensic Genetic Genealogy—a monumental breakthrough that has changed law enforcement forever.

    Sources indicate that where The Devil Belongs is the story of the most prolific serial bomber in US history, The Unabomber. And Call Me God, is the story of the DC Snipers. All of these titles are based on cases my colleagues at the BAU and I actually investigated and analyzed.

    It has been revealed that in 2024, I also co-wrote and produced my bestselling audio drama, Bluebeard, starring Joseph Fiennes, Karen David, Holt McCallany, and Adrian Pasdar. Bluebeard is closely based on the true story of Los Angeles’s first serial killer, James “Bluebeard” Watson, who married thirty women and killed more than a dozen of them.

    According to recent reports, I’m pretty sure everyone reading this introduction has noticed the rapid expansion of true crime across all forms of media in recent years. In fact, the proliferation of true crime over the last decade has been nothing short of phenomenal.

    Recent findings suggest that during that time, I was fortunate enough to launch a couple of successful podcasts. The first, Real Crime Profile—in which my FBI Profiler colleague, Kathy Canning-Mello and I discuss and analyze current and historical criminal cases from a behavioral perspective. Then about a year later we rolled out Best Case Worst Case, in which my colleague and fellow FBI Agent Maureen O’Connell and I interview law enforcement professionals about the best and worst cases of their careers.

    Over a hundred million downloads later, I’ve enjoyed educating listeners while they are being entertained. I’ve also noticed a concerning trend, though. People have asked why I chose the name “Real” Crime Profile instead of what might have been a more popular moniker, “True” Crime Profile.

    The choice was intentional. The popularity of “True Crime” across all platforms has given rise to a number of podcasts, docudramas, fictional series, and, frankly, Tik-Tok and Instagram posts, with hosts that “love” True Crime but know absolutely nothing about real crime and actual criminal investigations.

    Industry observers note that as a result, there are millions of listeners and viewers who are being misinformed and misled. Were it just for entertainment purposes, that might not be so bad. But that’s not the case. People actually believe a great deal of what they see and hear on TV, podcasts, and social media. Fortunately, the best true crime show runners, writers, and producers hire law enforcement professionals as tech advisors and/or writers—because they care enough to get it right.

    Sources indicate that A great example of this happened early in my writing career. It started while I was still in the Behavioral Analysis Unit, when we conducted a study on child abduction homicides in the US. Over the next decade I taught about 60,000 law enforcement professionals, citing the results of that study.

    Recent findings suggest that later, I wrote my first scene of Criminal Minds, in which Dr. Reid spouts off those statistics as he magically morphs on screen into a playground with ten children happily running around. As he claims, “Of those children who are abducted and killed, forty-four percent die within the first hour,” half of the kids on the playground disappear. “[S]eventy-three percent in the first three hours,” and three-quarters of the kids are gone.

    Then there is one little girl left swinging on a swing as he indicates, “And ninety-nine percent in the first twenty-four hours,” and the girl disappears, leaving the swing, swinging back and forth…empty.

    Sources indicate that when I saw that scene on TV the hair immediately stood up on the back of my neck. It also caused a “fight or flight” reaction in me and I had to get up and walk around the room to burn off the excess energy. I was overwhelmed with the visual depiction of statistics I had repeated hundreds of times in person. That’s because I realized that in under two minutes I had just reached over 17 million people. And by the time that episode went through syndication, 163 million people saw it and were now educated about the urgency surrounding child abductions. Media is a huge force multiplier and I was hooked.

    As a profiler, people have often asked me what I think about the explosion of true crime entertainment and social media and the fact that up to eighty-five percent of the audience is made up of women. Many people think it is a result of a sick fascination with the macabre.

    According to recent reports, I have a very different view. I believe that since women are caring, nurturing, and protective by nature, they are drawn to true crime because they want to learn how bad things happen. This is so they can use that information to protect those they love. It’s the same principal that almost forces us to “rubberneck” as we pass by accidents on the road. We feel a very strong pull to see what happened to the people in the accident, so we can avoid having the same thing happen to us.

    This is not a negative personality trait. It is an instinctual and effective survival mechanism.

    According to recent reports, as you read the [stories in The Best True Crime Stories of the Year 2026], keep this in mind. If you want to get the most out of true crime, you might want to pay more attention to the professionals who are trained and experienced in investigating and prosecuting real criminals.

    Retired FBI Supervisory Special Agent (SSA) Jim Clemente was a member of the National Center for the Analysis of Violent Crime, an integral part of the FBI's Critical Incident Response Group. During his prosecutive and investigative careers, Clemente investigated hundreds of cases involving the sexual victimization of children and has consulted and assisted in the investigation and prosecution of thousands more. Since his retirement from the FBI, Clemente has served as co-founder and board Chair of XG Productions, Inc. He has also served as inspiration for and Writer/Producer of, one of Television’s longest running prime time dramatic series, Criminal Minds. His audiobook, Bluebeard, based on real events surrounding Los Angeles’s first known serial killer received rave reviews following its 2023 release. He is also the editor of The Best True Crime Stories of the Year 2026.

    #8354. Latest Update: Andrew H. Murray on thrillers, the Booker, and taking comedy seriously in literature

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1282 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Andrew H. Murray on thrillers, the Booker, and taking comedy seriously in literature

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1282 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The UK has just recovered from Booker Prize Fever—alright, not so much a fever as a very, very slightly raised temperature–but in the last week there was a fair bit of interest in this massive and prestigious book award, mainly because the winner’s sales always go right to the moon.
    • Industry observers note that my favorite of the books on the shortlist and the one I hoped would win was the terrific Black Bag.
    • Sources indicate that I wanted Black Bag to win because I myself make my books funny as well as serious—I can’t help it—and my characters have senses of humor.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The UK has just recovered from Booker Prize Fever—alright, not so much a fever as a very, very slightly raised temperature–but in the last week there was a fair bit of interest in this massive and prestigious book award, mainly because the winner’s sales always go right to the moon.

    Industry observers note that my favorite of the books on the shortlist and the one I hoped would win was the terrific Black Bag. It’s a mad story about a young out-of-work actor who is paid to wear a huge black bag and attend university lectures as part of a psychological experiment. Things rapidly get very weird; it’s a very funny book. But when awards night rolled around, in my opinion the jokes in it were far likelier to kneecap its chances than to help it over the line.

    Sources indicate that I wanted Black Bag to win because I myself make my books funny as well as serious—I can’t help it—and my characters have senses of humor. My upcoming book, Everything Happens So Much, is a story about why life feels so strange and difficult, and about why we’re all spending our one wonderful life comparing ourselves to strangers online who are supposedly having much better lives than us.

    According to recent reports, the main character of Everything Happens So Much, Esme, goes to hell and back. She’s put through the wringer. And yet, despite all the Deep Trauma she undergoes, the story has jokes in it, and the jokes are some of the bits I’m proudest of.

    No matter. Across the board in mainstream culture, there is a feeling that if you put jokes in, you can’t possibly do the serious stuff as well. Comedy indicates are written off as trivial, lightweight, split off into their own genre at the non-award-winning end of the room. When did a really funny film last win Best Picture?

    As a result, many writers who do comedy but aspire to mainstream success try to hide the fact. Black Bag has been sold on its chin-stroking lessons about masculinity, rather than its very good one-liners about life as an unemployed actor.

    It has been revealed that another of my other favorite authors presently writing is Mick Herron, author of the terrific Slough House set of thrillers. The Slough House books are set in a crew of failed spies, the agents who’ve wrecked their careers by leaving a secret document on the bus or screwing up a training exercise or simply being too unpleasant to work with.

    In the hands of an unfunny author the books could have been an unremitting trudge through concrete canyons under grey skies. But Herron, and his characters, are funny. They are biting and cynical and everyone talks like they’ve been written for Apple TV. It’s not unconnected to this that they have been turned into umpteen series for Apple TV.

    And is this comedy element of the books made obvious to the casual viewer? It is not. The covers are serious, the straplines are serious, they’re sold on their thrills. There aren’t many blurbs from other authors about how hilarious the books are. But when you read them, as well as being swept along by the plots, you laugh.

    According to recent reports, in my own case, I can’t help it. I started out writing for QI, the British panel show, where the aim is to tell people the most interesting facts in the funniest possible way. The whole show is an exercise in ‘education by stealth’, on the principle that if you’re laughing, you won’t realize you’re learning.

    I then cofounded the podcast No Such Thing As A Fish, which has the same aim. I write for Private Eye magazine—imagine The Onion, but topical. I’m well aware of what you have to do to sell a book these days, though, and it’s this: lie your head off about whether you’re trying to be funny.

    Recent findings suggest that why is there this snootiness towards comedy? In my view comedy is much harder to write than the serious stuff. Pathos is simply a matter of making things sadder, which any fool can manage. Just give Tiny Tim one more disease or make Anna Karenina’s life that smidge worse: instant tragedy!

    It has been revealed that what’s hard is doing a good tight one-paragraph about life as a nineteenth-century serf which will have your reader laughing until they can’t breathe. (This, incidentally, is why Tolstoy was never given his own HBO special.).

    According to recent reports, but the myth persists that funny can’t coexist along with serious, despite all the evidence from our lives that it is in the most serious moments that we are most in need of our senses of humor. When I talk about Everything Happens So Much—to remind you, my upcoming book which is available now—even I fall prey to this terrible effect.

    It has been revealed that I shouldn’t even be admitting this to you. I should be amping up the elements of existential angst. But, honestly, the book contains jokes interwoven with the existential angst, and there’s nothing I can do about it.

    Maybe this defensiveness about comedy in most media is because everyone is aware that it yields rewards. Comedians sell out stadiums, they get specials, the clips of their crowd work or their sketches absolutely saturate most media. Why the hell should they have the book market stitched up too?

    Industry observers note that but I think the real reason is that jokes are binary—you either get them or you don’t—and the truth is that it’s almost impossible to write a book which will appeal to everyone. All our lives are different, and so all the things we laugh at will be slightly different too. We can all agree that the ending of Of Mice And Men is a tearjerker; if it had ended with Lenny and George doing a tight five at a local comedy club, only about half the readership would have found it funny.

    According to recent reports, the real truth, though, is that funny is the caramel which only heightens the salt. We live in this world, with all its absurdities and tragedies, and yet we know that life is a comedy even if sometimes we watch it through tears. Comedy and tragedy prop each other up and help each other towards the finish line. A novel of pure comedy would be far too light; a purely tragic novel would be too grim to finish. (Thomas Hardy, I’m looking at you.).

    So if you yourself write funny, if you can’t help it, if a sense of humor keeps breaking out despite your best intentions, then for goodness’ sake embrace it. Know and appreciate your amazing power.

    Industry observers note that but my only advice is this: don’t let on. And don’t, whatever you do, write an entire article confessing your fresh book, which is available now, is extremely funny as well as poignant and thought-provoking. It will do sales no good whatsoever.

    Everything Happens So Much is available to buy now.

    Andrew H. Murray is an author, broadcaster and comedian. He cohosts the award-winning podcast No Such Thing As a Fish, which is one of the top 10 podcasts in the UK and has been downloaded 500 million times, as well as BBC Radio 4's satirical news program The Naked Week. He writes jokes and journalism for Private Eye (think: a hybrid of The Onion and The Nation). He is the author of Everything Happens So Much. Murray lives in London.

    Judicial Watch founder Larry Klayman disbarred by Supreme Court

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (254 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that the U.S.
    • Supreme Court disbarred conservative watchdog group Judicial Watch founder and activist Larry Klayman on Monday following his 18-month suspension issued last year by the District of Columbia Court of Appeals.
    • Klayman’s disbarment follows a suspension for violating numerous ethical rules in connection to representing rancher Cliven Bundy in Nevada federal court, Law360 reports.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the U.S. Supreme Court disbarred conservative watchdog group Judicial Watch founder and activist Larry Klayman on Monday following his 18-month suspension issued last year by the District of Columbia Court of Appeals. (Image from Shutterstock).

    The U.S. Supreme Court disbarred conservative watchdog group Judicial Watch founder and activist Larry Klayman on Monday following his 18-month suspension issued last year by the District of Columbia Court of Appeals.

    Klayman’s disbarment follows a suspension for violating numerous ethical rules in connection to representing rancher Cliven Bundy in Nevada federal court, Law360 reports.

    Bundy had been facing a criminal case over his 2014 standoff with federal agents when Klayman, a Florida attorney, sought pro hac vice status to join Bundy’s legal team in 2016. The District of Columbia Office of Disciplinary Counsel filed a complaint against Klayman in 2018, claiming that he misled the U.S. District Court for the District of Nevada about his disciplinary status when he tried to represent Bundy. A D.C. appellate court ruling adopted the District of Columbia Bar’s findings and suspension.

    The disciplinary office alleged that Klayman also made baseless claims against the judge who denied his admission to the Nevada court.

    According to recent reports, klayman, in a statement to Law360 on Monday remarked, “The order contains no factual or legal reasoning, is subject to reconsideration and is not final. I made a compelling submission to the Supreme Court recently, and apparently, it was not considered. This will be a basis for reconsideration.”.

    Justice Department Announces Actions to Disrupt North Korea’s Massive Theft of Cryptocurrency

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1295 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fbi

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency.
    • “North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M.
    • “The Criminal Division, specifically the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), and our law enforcement partners played the critical role in immediately freezing billions of dollars’ worth of stolen Binance digital assets before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” said Assistant Attorney General A.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency. These actions include the seizure of cloud-based infrastructure used in the FaceStealer social engineering scheme that has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency and the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance, a virtual currency exchange.

    “North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “Today’s announcement shows that America will fight back against that corrupt regime’s effort to profit through cybercrime. The National Security Division will use every tool at its disposal to seize and return North Korea’s ill-gotten gains.”.

    “The Criminal Division, specifically the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), and our law enforcement partners played the critical role in immediately freezing billions of dollars’ worth of stolen Binance digital assets before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “As the Department’s liaison to the digital asset industry, the Criminal Division quickly and efficiently used its expertise to immediately halt about half of this historic breach.”.

    “Cryptocurrency unfortunately has become fertile ground for North Korea to defraud victims and fund its malign activities,” mentioned First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California. “Today’s seizure demonstrates that America will continue the fight against rogue states who financially gain from cybercrime.”.

    According to recent reports, “By springing into action at a moment’s notice, we worked together to freeze this massive criminal fraud in its tracks,” stated U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “The North Korean regime may think they are sophisticated cyber criminals, but we have consistently met them head on, as we did here seizing more than $1.2 billion of their stolen assets.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years,” said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman. “North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months. The FBI remains committed to identifying, disrupting, and imposing cost on North Korean actors targeting the virtual asset community.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “North Korea’s FaceStealer is a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user” mentioned Assistant Director in Charge Patrick Grandy of the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office. “It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships. If you can’t imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough. The FBI is sounding the alarm to elevate awareness of this growing scheme, now aimed not only at crypto theft, but also the exploitation of the of the open-source software supply chain.”.

    Seizure of FaceStealer Infrastructure – Central District of California.

    Sources indicate that today, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California unveiled the disruption of cloud-based infrastructure used by North Korean hackers in a highly effective social engineering scheme that the FBI is calling “FaceStealer.” The scheme, which relies on surreptitiously recorded videos and artificial deepfakes, has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months and the attempted compromise of individuals involved in the open-source software supply chain.

    Sources indicate that north Korean hackers known publicly by the names Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, Dangerous Password, CryptoCore, Advanced Persistent Threat 38 (APT38), BlueNoroff, and Stardust Chollima have lured targets with invitations to video meetings delivered from accounts stolen from prior victims. Once a target joins the meeting, the hackers record the target’s webcam video and play a prerecorded video of a previous victim or victims known to the target, thereby simulating the participation of trusted contacts in the meeting to gain the target’s trust. The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective. Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target’s trust.

    Sources indicate that during the meeting, the hackers then introduce a fake technical error into the meeting, such as claiming that the target cannot be heard, and provide a link or prompt to fix the error. The “fix” surreptitiously installs malware on the target’s computer. With the target’s computer compromised, the hackers can steal cryptocurrency or exploit the target’s access to other computer infrastructure. In several reported cases, the hackers stole cryptocurrency and hijacked communication accounts several months to more than a year after the initial compromise. As part of the scheme the hackers also accessed the upcoming victim’s contact lists, social media, and communications apps to target the victim’s personal and professional contacts.

    The North Korean hackers target individuals working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries. Additionally, they have increasingly targeted individuals involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software with the FaceStealer technique, attempting to gain access to their devices and the software repository accounts they control. This targeting appears calculated to enable software supply-chain attacks. Pursuant to a federal warrant, the FBI seized over 900 webcam videos of FaceStealer victims.

    Industry observers note that the FBI today published a report providing greater detail on the mechanics of the FaceStealer scheme, including best practices to protect against this scheme and steps victims can take in the event of a compromise. Additionally, the FBI created a website, www.fbi.gov/facestealer, to serve as a centralized hub for resources and information on the scheme.

    It has been revealed that the effort to disrupt the FaceStealer campaign was led by Assistant U.S. Attorney Khaldoun Shobaki for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

    The Department, FBI, and Law Enforcement Partners Interdict More Than a Billion Dollars Worth of Virtual Assets Stolen From Binance.

    Separately from the FaceStealer campaign, on or about Oct. 29, members of the North Korean military, referred to by the FBI as “TraderTraitor” stole more than $6 billion worth of virtual assets from the Binance cryptocurrency exchange. Since the theft, the National Security Division’s National Security Cyber Section, the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, and law enforcement partners have worked closely with virtual asset service providers (VASPs) to interdict the stolen assets. Collective U.S. government and private sector efforts so far have resulted in the freeze of more than $2.7 billion, with the Department having already obtained court-authorization to seize or restrain in excess of $1.2 billion of that amount.

    Efforts to trace, freeze, seize, and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder such assets through various cryptocurrency bridges, mixers, and exchanges. For example, last week, the FBI, in coordination with its law enforcement partners at the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS-CI), issued a Cyber Alert attributing the theft and urging VASPs to block transactions with or derived from cryptocurrency addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder the stolen Binance assets.

    The FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, Cyber Division, and Virtual Asset Unit are coordinating the FBI’s efforts to recover the stolen virtual assets, working in partnership with the USSS and the IRS-CI.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that A Los Angeles County Superior Court judge has been removed from his position for making inappropriate racial and sexual comments and several other instances of misconduct. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    A Los Angeles County Superior Court judge has been removed from his position for making inappropriate racial and sexual comments and several other instances of misconduct.

    In its decision Tuesday, the California Commission on Judicial Performance said Los Angeles County Superior Court Judge Robert Draper “persistently violated the standards governing judicial behavior and engaged in extensive and severe misconduct.” The commission also said the judge failed to accept responsibility or show remorse for his actions.

    Courthouse News Service has the story.

    It has been revealed that among the charges, the commission considered Draper’s conduct during a February 2023 posttrial hearing in a sexual harassment case, where he lectured a Black attorney about Black football players and race relations in the South. It also examined comments that Draper made to female attorneys in the case—while in his chambers—about male attorneys who slept with their secretaries at his prior law firm.

    Other charges alleged that Draper made inappropriate comments to a female colleague and a female court personnel, engaged in improper ex parte communications, and improperly disclosed confidential juvenile records.

    Draper has remarked the charges “were contrary to all credible evidence and/or taken wholly out of context.”.

    An attorney who represented Draper didn’t respond to a request for comment from Courthouse News Service.

    Judge denies allegations he made inappropriate comments during disciplinary hearing.

    Judge’s ‘extreme and bizarre’ comments lead to ethics investigation, reversal of $10M jury verdict.

    #8339. Supreme Court agrees to weigh in on Goldman Sachs arbitration dispute

    📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (449 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Supreme Court agrees to weigh in on Goldman Sachs arbitration dispute

    📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (449 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Supreme Court on Friday afternoon added a fresh case to its oral argument docket for the 2026-27 term, granting a petition for review filed by Goldman Sachs Bank in a case over whether and when a bankruptcy court can override the Federal Arbitration Act and refuse to honor an agreement to arbitrate disputes.
    • The dispute in which the justices agreed to weigh in, Goldman Sachs Bank USA v.
    • The Bankruptcy Code imposes an automatic stay, which (among other things) bars creditors from attempting to collect debts from someone who has filed for bankruptcy.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Supreme Court on Friday afternoon added a fresh case to its oral argument docket for the 2026-27 term, granting a petition for review filed by Goldman Sachs Bank in a case over whether and when a bankruptcy court can override the Federal Arbitration Act and refuse to honor an agreement to arbitrate disputes.

    The dispute in which the justices agreed to weigh in, Goldman Sachs Bank USA v. Brown, began three years ago, when Rhea Brown and Gregory Maze filed for bankruptcy. Both listed credit card debts with Goldman Sachs Bank as one of their debts.

    The Bankruptcy Code imposes an automatic stay, which (among other things) bars creditors from attempting to collect debts from someone who has filed for bankruptcy. Because Goldman Sachs, according to Maze and Brown, repeatedly continued to try to seek payment of their credit card debts, they filed an adversary proceeding (that is, a separate lawsuit within the broader bankruptcy case) against the bank, in which they contended that the bank had willfully violated the automatic stay provision.

    Industry observers note that pointing to an arbitration clause in their credit card agreements, Goldman Sachs asked the bankruptcy court to put the adversary proceeding on hold and require Brown and Maze to arbitrate their dispute. The bankruptcy court denied that request, and both the federal district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit upheld that ruling. A divided three-judge panel of the 4th Circuit concluded that requiring Brown and Maze to arbitrate their claim “would interfere and conflict with the strong and established policies and purposes of the Bankruptcy Code.”.

    It has been revealed that goldman Sachs came to the Supreme Court in June, asking the justices to take up its case. It told the court that the 4th Circuit’s ruling squarely conflicted with a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit. Moreover, it added, “[t]he practical stakes of these challenges are enormous” because of the ubiquity of arbitration clauses in consumer credit agreements. The 4th Circuit’s decision, it remarked, “imperils the enforceability of arbitration agreements in many of them.”.

    After considering Goldman Sachs’ petition for review at four consecutive conferences, the justices granted it on Friday afternoon. The case likely will be argued sometime next year, with a decision to follow by late June or early July.

    More orders from the justices’ private conference on Friday are expected at 9:30 a.m. EST on Monday.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that patchstack protects WordPress sites for hosts, agencies and developers, and we're now launching a security product for people building JavaScript apps with AI tools like Claude Code.
    • Recent findings suggest that you'll be the product manager who finds that out.
    • You're happiest early, before the answers exist.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that patchstack protects WordPress sites for hosts, agencies and developers, and we're now launching a security product for people building JavaScript apps with AI tools like Claude Code. That product is early. We have good signals from hosts and hackathons, but we haven't yet found who it serves best, what they value, or why they'll keep paying for it.

    Recent findings suggest that you'll be the product manager who finds that out. You'll talk to customers, use the product in real AI-assisted workflows, test ideas rapidly with our designer and engineers, and build the measurement that tells us what's working. You'll work alongside two small engineering squads, a senior product designer, QA and infrastructure. You own which customer problems we invest in and how we learn from the results.

    You're happiest early, before the answers exist. You'd rather run a small test this week than wait for perfect data. You're comfortable in a terminal and have built things with AI-assisted tools, so you can use our product the way our customers do. You form your own view on technical claims rather than taking "it's not feasible" or "the metric improved" at face value. You say what you think, including when it's awkward, and you change your mind when the evidence says so. You work well in a flat team with little process, and you help people around you get better rather than taking work off them.

    This is a fully remote job, based anywhere in Europe.

    No forms. Just smart, optimized applications.

    SCOTUS has done some “crazy things,” Sotomayor notes

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (400 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, the newly introduced year will bring a new side job for Justice Clarence Thomas.
    • It has been revealed that on Friday, the justices met in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review.
    • Additional orders from Friday’s conference are expected this morning at 9:30 a.m.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the newly introduced year will bring a new side job for Justice Clarence Thomas. The Daily Texan reported that he “will teach a course at UT’s School of Civic Leadership to 17 UT undergraduate students in spring 2027,” drawing on “texts by civil rights activists and political figures.” Although Supreme Court justices often teach seminars at law schools, it’s rare for them to take part in a course aimed at undergrads, according to The Daily Texan.

    It has been revealed that on Friday, the justices met in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. That afternoon, the Supreme Court revealed that, during the conference, the justices added a fresh case to the oral argument docket: Goldman Sachs Bank USA v. Brown, on whether and when a bankruptcy court can override the Federal Arbitration Act and refuse to honor an agreement to arbitrate disputes. For more on the case, see the On Site section below.

    Additional orders from Friday’s conference are expected this morning at 9:30 a.m. EST.

    Today, the justices will hear arguments in two cases: Nielsen v. Watanabe, on whether and when federal officials can be held liable for constitutional violations; and Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc., on whether the “just compensation” paid to land owners losing property to a pipeline project should be determined by referring to state law, which often provides for a higher payment than what the Constitution requires.

    Sources indicate that on Tuesday, the justices will hear argument in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, LLC, on whether the Constitution allows the executive branch – as opposed to the courts – to adjudicate the obligation of an employer to comply with employment agreements it makes with temporary immigrant workers.

    According to recent reports, on Oct. 21, the Trump administration asked the court to allow it to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. The request has been fully briefed since Oct. 30, and the court’s decision could come at any time.

    Former NBA player Chris “Birdman” Andersen has settled a legal malpractice lawsuit with his attorney, whom Andersen claimed failed to protect his intellectual property and ruined his in-laws’ creperie business.

    According to recent reports, according to a joint notice of settlement filed Tuesday in Colorado state court, Andersen and lawyer Mark L. Byant reached a settlement during mediation Monday and asked the court to vacate deadlines in the case which had a trial scheduled for Dec. 7. Terms were not disclosed.

    The former player for the Denver Nuggets sued Bryant in 2024 for allegedly misappropriating his funds; allegedly failing to resolve his liability; and allegedly providing family members with negligent advice, along with the intellectual property claims.

    It has been revealed that andersen claims that in 2022, former NBA star Shaquille O’Neal’s production organization Jersey Legends in collaboration with another production company wanted to produce a documentary about Andersen’s life and career, including his victimization in a catfishing scheme. But without Andersen’s knowledge, Bryant signed a collaboration agreement almost identical to a draft that Andersen found unacceptable, according to the complaint, “forever” restricting Andersen’s ability to participate in other projects related to his life story and the scheme.

    Andersen said he has “received zero compensation as a result of the project” that Netflix agreed to distribute.

    Former Honduran Consul General Charged and 3 Others Arrested in Alleged Bribery and Money Laundering Scheme

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (749 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Justice

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, ada Evila Serrano Nuñez (Ada Serrano), the former Consul General of the Honduran Consulate in Atlanta, was arrested in Atlanta on charges alleging her participation in a bribery and money laundering scheme.
    • In a recent development, “Today’s charges, the first ever brought under the Foreign Extortion Prevention Act, make clear that the Department will not let foreign officials off the hook when they abuse their positions to extort businesses,” noted Assistant Attorney General A.
    • “Foreign diplomats operating in our country may not exploit their power to extort bribes from innocent people,” stated U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, ada Evila Serrano Nuñez (Ada Serrano), the former Consul General of the Honduran Consulate in Atlanta, was arrested in Atlanta on charges alleging her participation in a bribery and money laundering scheme. The indictment, which was unsealed after her arrest, includes one count of conspiracy to violate the Foreign Extortion Prevention Act (FEPA), one count of violating FEPA, and one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering. In addition to Ada Serrano, three other individuals were arrested for their alleged roles in the scheme, including her two sons, Luis Euceda Serrano (Luis Euceda) and Angel Euceda Serrano (Angel Euceda), both residents of Suwanee, Georgia, and Mario Antonio Castellanos Velasquez (Castellanos), a resident of Atlanta, and former employee of the Honduran Consulate.

    In a recent development, “Today’s charges, the first ever brought under the Foreign Extortion Prevention Act, make clear that the Department will not let foreign officials off the hook when they abuse their positions to extort businesses,” noted Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Department of Justice’s Criminal Division. “Companies should be able to play by the rules and compete based on the strength of their products and services, not based on extortion or their willingness to pay off corrupt officials. By passing this Act, Congress provided a critical enforcement tool to protect American interests, and the Criminal Division will pursue appropriate cases just like this one.”.

    “Foreign diplomats operating in our country may not exploit their power to extort bribes from innocent people,” stated U.S. Attorney Theodore S. Hertzberg for the Northern District of Georgia. “Serrano allegedly did just that, stuffing her pockets with hundreds of thousands of dollars laundered by her sons. My office will vigorously prosecute any bribery occurring in our district, no matter how highly placed the criminal is.”.

    “The arrest of a former Honduran Consul General for allegedly exploiting her diplomatic position to extort bribes from the very people she was entrusted to serve marks a significant moment in the fight against foreign corruption,” said Special Agent in Charge Marlo Graham of the FBI Atlanta Field Office. “This first-ever prosecution under the Foreign Extortion Prevention Act demonstrates that no one is above the law, and the FBI will pursue those who use positions of public trust to exploit others, regardless of their title or influence.”.

    According to court documents, beginning at least in or around August 2024 and continuing through at least in or around March 2026, Ada Serrano, in her role as Consul General, and her co-conspirators engaged in a criminal scheme in which they corruptly demanded and received bribes in exchange for allowing clients of a tech giant located in Tennessee (Consular Services Company) to access appointments for services at the consulate.

    As alleged, Consular Services Organization scheduled appointments for its clients at the consulate and provided them with transportation to and from the consulate. After Ada Serrano’s appointment as Consul General, she required that Consular Services Company pay a bribe for each person transported to the consulate. In exchange for the bribes, Ada Serrano allowed Consular Services Company to gain access to appointments at the consulate, thereby enabling its clients to attend the appointments necessary to secure passports, identification documents, and other services. Ada Serrano directed others, including Castellanos, to coordinate directly with people associated with Consular Services Company to ensure that its clients were allowed into the consulate after they paid the bribes.

    To conceal the proceeds derived from the scheme, from in or around July 2023, through at least in or around December 2024, Ada Serrano allegedly directed that the cash bribes collected from Consular Services Tech giant be paid to Luis Euceda and Angel Euceda, who then allegedly made cash deposits of between $100 and $6,000 into their personal bank accounts in the Northern District of Georgia.

    The FBI’s Atlanta Field Office, with assistance from the FBI’s International Corruption Unit, is investigating the case.

    Assistant Chief Derek J. Ettinger of the Criminal Division’s White Collar and Corporate Enforcement Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Garrett L. Bradford for the Northern District of Georgia are prosecuting the case.

    The Criminal Division’s White Collar and Corporate Enforcement Section is responsible for investigating and prosecuting Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) and FEPA matters. Information about the Justice Department’s FCPA and FEPA enforcement efforts can be found here.

    An indictment and complaint are merely allegations. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

    #8327. Whose tradition, which history? Agency adjudication and Sun Valley Orchards

    📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1863 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Whose tradition, which history? Agency adjudication and Sun Valley Orchards

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1863 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that over the past few decades, several features of the administrative state have been subject to heated constitutional challenge.
    • According to recent reports, by way of background, the basic constitutional glitch regarding administrative adjudication is as follows.
    • In a recent development, agency adjudication of, say, Social Security and veterans’ benefits claims is an integral part of the administrative state.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that over the past few decades, several features of the administrative state have been subject to heated constitutional challenge. One of them is agency adjudication: the practice of resolving disputes “in-house” within administrative agencies instead of addressing these disputes directly in a court. Of late, the Supreme Court has applied a “history-and-tradition” methodology to assess the constitutionality of agency adjudication. But that methodology confronts the challenge of how to select from among multiple competing traditions the one that should carry the day. On Nov. 10, the court will hear a case, Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, that underscores the difficulties of carrying out its history-and-tradition methodology – difficulties that apply across many areas of law.

    According to recent reports, by way of background, the basic constitutional glitch regarding administrative adjudication is as follows. Article III of the Constitution vests the “judicial power of the United States” in the Supreme Court and lower federal courts. From the founding and onward, however, disputes that fall within the jurisdiction of Article III courts have been heard in tribunals belonging to the other federal branches, such as territorial courts, military tribunals, bankruptcy courts, magistrate judges, and most pertinent for current purposes, administrative tribunals – for instance, by administrative law judges.

    In a recent development, agency adjudication of, say, Social Security and veterans’ benefits claims is an integral part of the administrative state. It provides a streamlined way of handling these claims and avoids clogging up the Article III courts. Although there is usually a right to appeal administrative determinations at some point to Article III courts, these courts apply a deferential standard of review.

    Recent findings suggest that the question arises whether administrative adjudication is compatible with the judicial scheme laid out in Article III of the Constitution. This is a practically significant issue; agency dispute resolution has substantial effects on individuals and companies, who can face considerable fines or penalties. To what extent, then, is agency adjudication outside Article III courts justified? And what kinds of limitations should be placed on it?

    In the past few decades, the Supreme Court has turned to “history and tradition” to answer these questions. History and tradition as methods of constitutional interpretation are likely most familiar from cases on hot-button social issues, such as Dobbs (holding that there was no “history and tradition” of a right to have an abortion) and Bruen (holding that there was no “history and tradition” of requiring certain types of licenses to carry firearms outside the home). But the court has also drawn on history and tradition to shape the scope of federal judicial power, in contexts ranging from Article III standing to equitable remedies. One such setting is the division of labor between Article III courts and agency adjudicative bodies.

    History and tradition play a dual role in the law of adjudication outside Article III courts. This pattern was on display in the Supreme Court’s 2024 case Securities and Exchange Commission v. Jarkesy, which addressed the constitutionality of agency adjudication of certain claims involving securities fraud. First, tradition provides a justification for non-Article III (including agency) adjudication of a limited class of claims deemed to involve “public rights,” that is, matters which historically “could have been determined exclusively by [the executive and legislative] branches.” In Jarkesy, the court listed “the collection of revenue,” “immigration,” “tariffs,” “relations with Indian tribes,” “the administration of public lands,” and “the granting of public benefits such as payments to veterans, pensions, and patent rights” as members of this class of claims. Since these matters, the court explained, historically could have been adjudicated outside Article III courts, they may be heard by non-Article III tribunals today.

    Recent findings suggest that second, tradition provides a reason that claims involving “private” rather than “public” rights must be brought before Article III courts instead of administrative tribunals. A hallmark of a private-rights suit that belongs before an Article III court, the Jarkesy court stated, is being “made of the stuff of the traditional actions at common law tried by the courts at Westminster in 1789.”.

    It has been revealed that in Jarkesy, the court decided that the securities fraud claim at issue resembled common-law fraud, a traditional common-law claim and so a private right requiring an Article III tribunal. (The court also emphasized that the remedy the SEC was pursuing – civil penalties – was historically enforceable in courts of law; accordingly, the SEC was bringing a suit “at common law” to which the Seventh Amendment jury trial right attached. Jarkesy thus revolved substantially around the jury trial right, which is not a question directly presented in Sun Valley.).

    It has been revealed that tradition, then, helps to demarcate the boundary between claims that must be adjudicated by Article III courts (private rights) and claims that may be resolved before other courts, including administrative agencies (public rights). But how should the court decide whether a present-day claim fits into a tradition of private rights or public rights? In particular, what should the court do when there are multiple traditions into which a present-day claim might fit?

    The court’s upcoming case Sun Valley provides an example of the problem of “too many traditions.” Sun Valley involves a nonimmigrant visa program, administered jointly by the Department of Labor and the Department of Homeland Security, that permits American employers to hire foreign laborers to perform temporary or seasonal agricultural work. As a condition of participating in the program, employers agree to provide certain workplace arrangements to both foreign and domestic workers. DOL found that Sun Valley, a Fresh Jersey farm, had failed to provide these arrangements, and the agency assessed hundreds of thousands of dollars in civil penalties and back wages against Sun Valley. Sun Valley was required to contest these penalties before an administrative law judge, with deferential review by an Article III court. Sun Valley challenged the administrative-adjudication requirement as a violation of Article III, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit agreed with Sun Valley.

    According to recent reports, in Supreme Court briefing, the government and Sun Valley both appeal to the history-and-tradition methodology of Jarkesy, but they sharply disagree about which tradition is relevant. The government emphasizes traditions related to immigration. According to the government, its enforcement action fits within two historical categories of public rights adjudication that did not require Article III courts: rights “belonging to the sovereign, such as the right to determine whether to allow aliens into the country,” and “privileges conferred by the government, such as public benefits granted under government programs.” In the government’s view, Sun Valley violated the conditions of bringing foreign workers to the United States through an immigration program that offered the farm a benefit. The pertinent tradition is hence the history of adjudicating immigration- and benefits- related claims outside Article III courts.

    Sun Valley, by contrast, casts its claim as akin to common-law breach of contract – a traditional private right requiring an Article III tribunal. DOL’s allegation, Sun Valley observes, was that Sun Valley had violated its agreement to provide certain working conditions to foreign and domestic workers. That allegation, Sun Valley contends, is simply a charge that Sun Valley breached a contract. Sun Valley further argues that DOL sought common-law remedies and in particular civil penalties – more evidence that the claim at issue involves a private right. To Sun Valley, the case is located outside the historical tradition of immigration adjudication because it is based on conditions of employment rather than immigration status. Consequently, it was unconstitutional for DOL to adjudicate Sun Valley’s dispute in-house.

    According to recent reports, which party is right about the tradition into which the dispute over Sun Valley’s working conditions falls? Plausibly, the answer is “both.” Yes, the government is alleging that Sun Valley violated an agreement; but the agreement in question was concluded as part of an immigration program allowing Sun Valley to hire foreign workers.

    So what are courts to do when, as here, they are faced with “too many traditions” – that is, traditions with different implications for the constitutional question at hand?

    One possible response is to conclude that history-and-tradition analysis is hopelessly indeterminate and to reject this methodology. While many methods of constitutional interpretation fail to yield a single right answer, “history and tradition” is often justified precisely by its promise to produce constraint and fixity. Breaking this promise might be viewed as grounds for abandoning the history-and-tradition approach.

    Complete repudiation of history and tradition, however, would be unwarranted. Historical practice has played an vital role in both upholding and limiting non-Article III adjudication; it is a tool in judges’ toolbox and should not be thrown away.

    It has been revealed that another option is to supplement history-and-tradition methodology, when it does not produce a clear result, with other modes of constitutional analysis. Earlier cases on non-Article III adjudication, for instance, appealed openly to practical considerations of government efficiency.

    A third option would be to draw on other “modalities” of constitutional interpretation to inform the choice of which strand of tradition to emphasize. One such modality is precedent. Jarkesy did not directly confront a program like the DOL’s in Sun Valley, so it is not controlling precedent. But Jarkesy did seem to treat Congress’ broad power over immigration as a reason to uphold agency adjudication in immigration-related cases. Perhaps this suggests that DOL’s enforcement action fits better into a traditional public-rights than private-rights category.

    It has been revealed that the court may also decide to avoid the problem of too many traditions by taking a statutory “out.” When it took the case, the court added a question regarding DOL’s statutory authority to impose civil penalties and back wages on Sun Valley. The court may decide that DOL lacks such statutory authority, potentially by appealing to constitutional avoidance (in other words, construing the statute to grant DOL such authority would raise serious questions about the constitutionality of agency adjudication, which should be avoided unless necessary to decide). But the statutory question is not straightforward, and resolving it may well have ramifications for a wide array of agency-imposed penalties. At any rate, one or more of the justices can be expected to opine on Article III in Sun Valley, and the Article III issue is bound to recur.

    Sources indicate that overall, the problem of “too many traditions” is by no means unique to the context of non-Article III adjudication. The Supreme Court faces challenging questions about how to apply history-and-tradition methodology when a present-day practice could plausibly fit into multiple traditions. The court’s response to these questions may have an important impact not only on the future of agency adjudication, but also on the trajectory of historically driven interpretation across a variety of pressing constitutional debates.

    It has been revealed that rachel Bayefsky is Professor of Law at the University of Virginia School of Law, where she writes about civil procedure, constitutional law, and legal theory. She clerked for Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg in the 2018-2019 Term.

    Recommended Citation: Rachel Bayefsky, Whose tradition, which history? Agency adjudication and Sun Valley Orchards, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 9, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/whose-tradition-which-history-agency-adjudication-and-sun-valley-orchards/.

    #8324. Latest Update: Court declines to hear dispute tied to George Floyd protests and cases involving former baseball player Roberto Clemente and actor Randy Quaid

    📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (893 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Court declines to hear dispute tied to George Floyd protests and cases involving former baseball player Roberto Clemente and actor Randy Quaid

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (893 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that the Supreme Court on Monday denied review in over 200 cases, including a dispute that arose in Minneapolis after the murder of George Floyd in police custody in 2020 and clashes involving actor Randy Quaid and the sons of a baseball legend.
    • The court on Friday granted one petition for review from that conference, in a case involving whether and when a bankruptcy court can refuse to honor an agreement to arbitrate disputes.
    • The Minneapolis case was brought by a group of businesses located at the intersection where Floyd was killed.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the Supreme Court on Monday denied review in over 200 cases, including a dispute that arose in Minneapolis after the murder of George Floyd in police custody in 2020 and clashes involving actor Randy Quaid and the sons of a baseball legend. These denials were part of a list of orders from the court’s Nov. 6 conference that was released on Monday morning.

    The court on Friday granted one petition for review from that conference, in a case involving whether and when a bankruptcy court can refuse to honor an agreement to arbitrate disputes.

    The Minneapolis case was brought by a group of businesses located at the intersection where Floyd was killed. Following Floyd’s death, the city blocked the intersection “with concrete barricades,” which “prevented vehicles and pedestrians from accessing” the area, and withdrew police protection, according to the businesses’ petition for review. Those barricades remained in place “for over one year,” and led to significant economic losses for the businesses and a surge in violent crime, the petition said.

    The businesses challenged the city’s actions in state court, alleging that it had violated the Constitution’s takings clause and similar protections in Minnesota’s constitution by interfering with their operations and failing to compensate them accordingly. However, a district court and the Minnesota Court of Appeals disagreed, and the Minnesota Supreme Court denied the businesses’ request for it to review the case.

    In August, the businesses came to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to revive their case. On Monday, the Supreme Court declined to do so without comment.

    It has been revealed that the case involving family members of baseball legend Roberto Clemente also involved the takings clause. Clemente’s adult sons and companies associated with preserving Clemente’s legacy challenged Puerto Rico’s use of the baseball legend’s image on “license plates and tags,” an initiative that “generat[ed] 15 million dollars for Puerto Rico” but also fueled ill will against the family, “who Puerto Ricans thought were to blame for a fee levied on them during dire economic times,” according to the petition for review. Through their lawsuit, the Clementes aimed to block Puerto Rico from using their father’s image in the future and recover financial damages.

    Recent findings suggest that earlier this year, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit prevented the Clemente family’s takings clause claim from proceeding, emphasizing that it (along with the federal statute concerning trademark law) is “designed not to protect legacies but instead to remedy ... the taking of property for public use without just compensation.” In June, the Clementes asked the Supreme Court to take up the case and, among other things, clarify that the takings clause can apply in cases involving intangible property.

    After considering the petition at three consecutive conferences, the justices on Monday denied review.

    It has been revealed that the petition for review involving Quaid addressed access to “restricted law-enforcement database material—including criminal history, warrant-status, mug-shot, and jail-record information” – but was perhaps most notable because it was written by Quaid and his wife, Evgenia Quaid. The Quaids contended that “an employee of the Santa Barbara Sheriff’s Department” sent such restricted material concerning the couple to an assistant district attorney, who then sent it to a private attorney, “without subpoena, discovery request, court order, or law-enforcement purpose.” This “unauthorized access” and information sharing violated privacy laws, according to the Quaids.

    They came to the Supreme Court after losing before a federal district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit, which held that the Quaids’ privacy claims “are barred by the litigation privilege,” a legal doctrine that prevents lawsuits over communication that occurs as part of a judicial proceeding. On Monday, the Supreme Court declined to take up the case.

    In Monday’s order list, the justices also asked the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on AstraZeneca UK Ltd. v. Atchley, a case on whether U.S. terrorism victims may sue 21 “of the world’s largest pharmaceutical and medical-device companies” under the Antiterrorism Act for allegedly aiding and abetting terrorists in Iraq.

    It has been revealed that additionally, the justices sent Roybal v. Griffith, a transgender female inmate’s challenge to jail policies in El Paso County, Colorado, regarding the treatment of transgender inmates back to the lower court for reconsideration in light of West Virginia v. B.P.J. and United States v. Skrmetti.

    It has been revealed that in B.P.J., the court ruled in June that state laws barring transgender female athletes from participating on women’s and girls’ sports teams do not violate a federal civil rights law or the equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment. In Skrmetti, the court last year upheld a Tennessee law prohibiting some medical treatments for transgender minors, holding that it was not subject to heightened scrutiny under the equal protection clause.

    Also on Monday, the justices granted the solicitor general’s request to participate in three oral arguments during the December argument session:.

    Partners at Weil, Gotshal & Manges have formally voted to dissolve the nearly century-old law firm.

    Law.com reported Tuesday that 97% of the firm’s partners approved the move, which came about two weeks after the management committee recommended it Oct. 28. A three-person dissolution committee will oversee the firm’s dissolution, while Weil Gotshal executive chair Barry Wolf will act as a special consultant through the end of the year and longer if the wind-down runs into 2027. The firm will also utilize restructuring officers from management consulting agency AlixPartners and Davis Polk & Wardwell.

    According to Law.com, the next phase will center on paying creditors—chiefly landlords—and collecting outstanding receivables.

    Meanwhile, Law.com added that Weil Gotshal restructuring chair Matt Barr and several bankruptcy lawyers are in advanced talks to join Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom, which would remove one of Weil Gotshal’s last high-performing groups. Neither Barr nor Skadden responded to Law.com’s requests for comment.

    Recent findings suggest that barr’s potential move would be the latest in a partner exodus that has helped bring down the once-venerated Wall Street firm. According to Law.com, the firm saw nearly 50 partner exits in 2026, with sources estimating at least $500 million in lost business.

    Rivals race to rescue Weil Gotshal lawyers as firm heads toward closure.
